en: Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Chapter on the Six Sense Bases in the Saṃyutta Nikāya.
1. Connected Discourses on the Six Sense Bases (Saḷāyatanasaṃyutta) 1.
The Chapter on Impermanence (Aniccavagga) 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Internal Impermanence (Ajjhattāniccasuttavaṇṇanā)
1. In the first [discourse] of the Saḷāyatanavagga, regarding "the eye," there are two eyes: the eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*) and the physical eye (*maṃsacakkhu*).
Therein, the eye of knowledge is fivefold: the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*), the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), and the wisdom-eye (*paññācakkhu*).

Among these, what is called the Buddha-eye consists of both the knowledge of the underlying tendencies and latent dispositions (*āsayānusaya-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties in others (*indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa*).
That which is described as "surveying the world with the Buddha-eye" is the *buddhacakkhu*.
The *dhammacakkhu* refers to the three lower paths and the three fruits, as it is said: "The stainless, dust-free *dhammacakkhu* arose.
The *samantacakkhu* refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), as it is said: "Having ascended the palace, the one with all-seeing eyes (*samantacakkhu*)."
The "divine eye" (*dibbacakkhu*) is the knowledge that arises through the pervasion of light, which is described as "with the purified divine eye.
The "eye of wisdom" (*paññācakkhu*) is the knowledge that discerns the Four Noble Truths, which is described as "the eye arose.

The "fleshly eye" (*maṃsacakkhu*) is also twofold: the physical eye consisting of material components (*sasambhāracakkhu*) and the sensitive eye (*pasādacakkhu*). Of these, that which is within the eye-socket...
It is a lump of flesh surrounded by the eye-lids, wherein there are, in brief, thirteen constituent factors:
the four elements, color, odor, taste, nutritive essence, birth, life, existence, the eye-sensitivity, and the body-sensitivity.
In detail, however, the four elements, color, odor, taste, nutritive essence, and birth—these nine, by way of their fourfold origination, become thirty-six.
Vitality, physical existence, visual sensitivity, and tactile sensitivity—these four, being originated by kamma, constitute the forty constituent factors.

This is what is called the "eye with its constituents. Now, within this, there is a mere sensitivity capable of seeing forms, which is situated in the visual orb (the *dṛṣṭimaṇḍala*) surrounded by the black pupil (*kṛṣṇamaṇḍala*) and demarcated by the white circle (*śuklamaṇḍala*).
This is called the sensitive eye-faculty (*pasādacakkhu*). A detailed exposition of it, as well as of the ear and the other [faculties] that follow, has already been given in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Therein, taking this sensitive eye-faculty as the basis, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, the eye is impermanent," and so forth.
Regarding that, a detailed exposition is given according to the method beginning with: "It is impermanent for four reasons: because it possesses arising and passing away," and so on.
These have already been explained below. By "ear," the sensitive ear-faculty (*pasāda-sota*) alone is intended; likewise for the nose, tongue, and body.

By "mind" (*mano*), the consciousness that ranges through the three planes of existence during the process of reflection (*sammasana*) is meant. Thus, this sutta was spoken with the intention of instructing those who would understand when the three characteristics had been shown regarding the six internal bases (*ajjhattika-āyatana*).
2–3. Commentary on the *Ajjhattadukkhasutta* and others:

The second sutta was spoken by showing two characteristics, and the third by showing one characteristic, according to the inclination (*ajjhāsaya*) of those who would understand through such an exposition. As for the remaining suttas, however, they were either already observed by those [listeners] or will be observed by them through this much alone.
4–6. Commentary on the *Bāhirāniccasutta* and others.

4–6. In the fourth [section], visible form, odor, flavor, and tangible object have four modes of origination; sound has two modes of origination; and mental objects (*dhammā*) are the objects of the phenomena belonging to the three planes.
This too was spoken by way of those who gain understanding through the teaching that demonstrates the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*) regarding the six external sense bases.
In the fifth and sixth [sections], the method is exactly the same as what was stated in the second and third.
7–12. Commentary on the *Ajjhattānicca-atītānāgata-sutta* and others.

The seventh sutta and those following are taught with reference to those who, having observed the characteristics of impermanence and so forth in the past and future eyes and other sense bases, become exhausted by their intense grasping at present ones. In all other respects, the method is exactly as explained below.
The first chapter, the Chapter on Impermanence (*Aniccavagga*), is concluded.
2. Yamakavagga 1–4.
Commentary on the First Discourse on Formerly Unawakened, etc., 13–16.
Regarding the first and second [discourses] of the Yamaka-vagga: "Of the internal" (*ajjhattikānaṃ*) means "of those that are internal" by way of being internal within the internal.
Furthermore, their status as "internal" should be understood through the extreme strength and power of desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*).
For the six internal sense bases (*ajjhattikāyatana*) are like the interior of a house for human beings, and the six external sense bases (*bāhirāyatana*) are like the precincts of that house.
Just as desire and lust are extremely strong within their own home when it is filled with children, wife, wealth, and grain, so too is it there.
They do not allow anyone to enter; even by the mere sound of a vessel, those who are vigilant will say, "What is this?
In the same way, there is an excessive and powerful desire-and-lust (*chandarāga*) regarding the six internal bases (*ajjhattika-āyatana*).
Thus, because of this strength of desire-and-lust, they are called "internal. But in the vicinity of a house, it is not so.
He becomes strong; even when humans or four-footed creatures wander there, they do not stop him by force.
Although they do not stop him, being unwilling, they do not allow him to take even as much as a single head of cattle.
Thus, they have no excessive or powerful craving for those things. Likewise, he has no excessive or powerful craving for forms and so forth.
Therefore, these are called "external. However, the detailed discussion on the internal and external is already explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.
The remainder in both suttas follows the same method as stated above. The same applies to the third and fourth [suttas].
5–6. Commentary on the First *Noceassāda-sutta* and others.
17–18. “Released from” (*nissaṭā*) means gone out from. “Dissociated” (*visaṃyuttā*) means not bound.
“Completely liberated” (*vippamuttā*) means not intent upon [them] with a mind that has transcended limits (*vimariyādīkatena cetasā*), that is, with a mind free from limits.

For whatever defilements or cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) have not been abandoned, by that the minds of those in training (*sekhā*) are said to be limited; that which has been abandoned, by that they are free from limits.

But here, the meaning is that they dwelt with a mind that was "unbounded"—that is, because all defilements and the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) had been abandoned, it had transcended the boundaries of defilement and the cycle of existence.
The same method applies to the sixth [sutta] as well. Furthermore, it should be understood that in all six of these suttas, it is precisely the Four Noble Truths that are taught.
7–10. Commentary on the *Paṭhamābhinanda-sutta* and others. 19–22.

In the four suttas beginning with the seventh, only the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are discussed. Their sequential exposition, however, should be understood according to the method already stated below.
The second chapter, the *Yamakavagga*, is concluded.
3. The Chapter on All (Sabbavagga) 1. Commentary on the Discourse on All (Sabbasuttavaṇṇanā) 23.

Regarding the first [discourse] of the Chapter on All: "All, monks" (*sabbaṃ vo, bhikkhave*). "All" (*sabba*) is fourfold: all-in-all (*sabbasabba*), all as sense bases (*āyatanasabba*), all as personal existence (*sakkāyasabba*), and partial all (*padesasabba*). Therein—
“There is nothing here that he has not seen,
nor anything unknown or yet to be known;
he has directly realized everything that is to be understood.”
“The Tathāgata is the one with the all-around eye because of that”—this is called the "all-in-all" (sabbasabba).
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the all; listen to it”—this is called the "all as sense bases" (āyatanasabba).
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the exposition on the root of all phenomena”—this is called the "all as identity" (sakkāyasabba).
“Furthermore, when the first act of attention toward all phenomena arises as consciousness, mind, mentation... [and so on] ...the corresponding mind-element”—this is called the “all of a portion.

Thus, the mere five objects of sense are the “all of a portion. Phenomena belonging to the three planes are the “all of identity” (*sakkāya-sabba*). Phenomena belonging to the four planes are the “all of the bases” (*āyatana-sabba*).
Whatever is knowable is the “all of all” (*sabbasabba*). The “all of a portion” and the “all of identity” [are included therein].
It does not reach it; the "all" of the bases (*āyatana*) does not reach it; the "all" of the bases does not reach the "all-of-all.
Why? Because there is no such thing as a phenomenon that can be an object for omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
However, in this sutta, the "all" of the bases is intended.
“Having rejected” means having refused. “It would have speech as its sole basis” means it would consist merely of that which can be expressed by speech;
it would not be able to show that there exists some other distinct entity with its own intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma) beyond these twelve bases (āyatana).
And when questioned, it would not be able to provide an answer: “Which other thing is all-named? (i.e., what else is designated by the term ‘all’?)
When questioned, he would not be able to provide an answer by saying, "It is this. He would fall into distress (*vighāta*); that is, he would encounter suffering (*dukkha*).
In the phrase, "Just as, monks, in regard to what is not one's domain," the word *taṃ* is a mere particle. The word *yathā* expresses a reason; the meaning is:
because he was questioned regarding what is not his domain. For when beings are questioned regarding what is not their domain, there is only distress.
The intention is this: just as it is impossible to cross deep water by lifting with one's head a stone the size of a gabled house, and likewise impossible to drag down the moon and sun;
and one who exerts effort in such an impossible matter meets only with frustration—so too, in this case, one would meet only with frustration in an impossible matter.
2. Commentary on the *Pahāna-sutta* (Discourse on Abandoning) 24.
In the second [verse], "for the abandoning of all" means for the abandoning of everything. "Feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact":

this refers to the feelings that arise having made eye-contact the root condition—namely, the feelings of receiving (*sampaṭicchana*), investigating (*santīraṇa*), determining (*voṭṭhabbana*), and impulsion (*javana*).

But regarding that which is associated with eye-consciousness, there is simply nothing further to be said. This same method applies to the conditions for feeling and so forth in the ear-door and the others as well.
Herein, "mind" (*mano*) refers to the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*). "Mental objects" (*dhammā*) refers to the object.

"Mind-consciousness" (*manoviññāṇa*) refers to the impulsion (*javana*) together with the adverting consciousness. "Mind-contact" (*manosamphassa*) is the contact co-nascent with the life-continuum. "That which is felt" (*vedayita*) refers to the feeling co-nascent with the adverting consciousness.
Impulsion-feeling (*javana-vedanā*). However, there is nothing at all to be said regarding that which is associated with the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

Without displacing the life-continuum from its state as the life-continuum, "mind" (*mano*) should be understood as the life-continuum together with the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*). "Phenomena" (*dhammā*) refers to the object. "Mind-consciousness" (*manoviññāṇa*) is impulsion-consciousness (*javana-viññāṇa*).
"Mind-contact" (*manosamphassa*) is the contact co-nascent with the life-continuum. "Feeling" (*vedayita*) is [the feeling] co-nascent with the impulsion.

Feeling (*vedanā*). It is also permissible [to include] that which arises together with the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) along with the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*). Furthermore, whatever here is teaching, instruction, or knowledge, this is called "designation" (*paṇṇatti*).
3. Commentary on the Sutta of Higher Knowledge, Full Understanding, and Abandoning (*Abhiññā-pariññā-pahāna-sutta-vaṇṇanā*)
25. In the third [verse], "for the sake of direct knowledge, full understanding, and abandoning of all": this means for the purpose of abandoning after having directly known and fully understood all.

"Direct knowledge, full understanding, and what is to be abandoned" means that which is to be abandoned after having directly known and fully understood. The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated. 4.
Commentary on the First Discourse on Non-Understanding (*Aparijānanasutta*).

26. In the fourth [case], not fully knowing, not thoroughly understanding, not fading away from [passion for], and not abandoning; not fully knowing, not thoroughly understanding, not causing to fade away, and not abandoning.
And here, "not causing to fade away" means not making it disappear. Thus, in this sutta, all three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*) are explained.
For by the word "fully knowing" (*abhijāna*), the full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*) is explained; by "thoroughly understanding" (*parijāna*)—

By the word "by means of speech" is meant full understanding through investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*); by the two phrases "making it fade away" and "abandoning it," full understanding through abandoning (*pahānapariññā*) is indicated.
5. Commentary on the Second Aparijānana Sutta:
In the fifth [sutta], the phrase "phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness" indicates that one takes up exactly the same form (*rūpa*) as was previously mentioned.
In the previous section, both what has come into the range [of the senses] and what has not was included; here, however, it is that which has not come into the range.
This is the definitive conclusion here: in the previous section, both what had come into the range and what had not was indeed included;

but here, it refers specifically to the three aggregates associated with eye-consciousness. For these three are called "to be cognized by eye-consciousness" because they are to be cognized together with eye-consciousness.
The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
6. Commentary on the Āditta Sutta:
Regarding the sixth [phrase], "at Gayāsīsa," there is both a lotus pond and a river named Gayā not far from the village of Gayā.
There was also a boulder on the back [of Gayāsīsa] called Gayāsīsa, resembling the frontal globe of an elephant, where space was sufficient even for a thousand bhikkhus;
the Blessed One dwelt there. Therefore it is said, "at Gayāsīsa.
He addressed the bhikkhus because, having sought out a teaching appropriate for them, he intended to deliver that teaching.
In this regard, here is the sequential account: It is said that ninety-two aeons ago there was a king named Mahinda. His eldest son was named Phussa.
Having fulfilled the perfections, he was a being in his final existence; when his knowledge had reached full maturity, he ascended the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and realized omniscience.
The king’s youngest son became his chief disciple, as did the son of the royal chaplain.
[He became] the second disciple. The king thought: “My eldest son has gone forth and become a Buddha;
my youngest son is the foremost disciple; the son of the family priest is the second disciple. Thinking, “The Buddha is ours alone; the Dhamma is ours;
the Saṅgha is ours,” he had a monastery built, [extending] from the gate-tower of the monastery all the way to his own house on both sides.
Having surrounded it with small huts made of bamboo walls, and having had a canopy fastened above—
adorned with a network of fragrant garlands and flower wreaths inlaid with golden stars— and having spread silver-colored sand below and scattered flowers,
he caused the Blessed One to proceed along that path.
The Teacher, remaining right there in the monastery, put on his robe and went to the royal palace together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus through the inner curtain;
having finished his meal, he departed through the inner curtain. No one was able to give even as much alms-food as could fit in a ladle.
Thereupon, the citizens complained, "A Buddha has appeared in the world, yet we do not perform meritorious deeds."
"We are able to do so. For just as the moon and the sun provide light for all, so too do the Buddhas arise for the welfare of all;
yet this king draws all the meritorious intentions of everyone into himself alone.
Now, that king had three other sons. The citizens, having come together with them, deliberated.
“There is no conflict with the royal families; let us employ a stratagem.

They raised up bandits in the border regions and, having had a message brought back saying, “Several villages have been plundered,” they reported this to the king. The king summoned his sons and sent them forth, saying, “Sons, I am old;
go and pacify the bandits. The bandits, instead of dispersing here and there, remained concentrated.

They came right back to them. Having settled them in a village that was not a proper residence, they returned with the report, "The bandits have been pacified," and stood before the king after paying him homage.
The king, being pleased, said, "Sons, I grant you a boon. They accepted this and went to deliberate together with the citizens.
“The king has granted us a boon. What shall we take? “Noble sons, elephants, horses, and such things are not difficult for you to obtain;
however, the Jewel of the Buddha is rare, appearing only at certain times.
Accept the boon of attending upon your eldest brother, Phussa Buddha. Having agreed to do so with the citizens, they replied, “We shall do thus.”
Having bathed well and anointed themselves, they went into the presence of the king and requested, "Your Majesty, grant us a boon.
"What will you take, dear ones? "Your Majesty, we have no need for elephants, horses, and such;
grant us the boon of looking after our eldest brother, the Buddha Phussa. "This boon cannot be granted by me while I am alive," [the king replied].
“Give it,” he said, and covered both his ears. “Your Majesty, you have not been forced by us to give this boon;
it was given by you out of your own satisfaction. Your Majesty, can there be two different accounts regarding the royal family?
They spoke thus because they were speakers of truth. Since the king could not turn back, he said: “Sirs, for seven years, seven months, and seven days...”
“Having attended upon him, I will give it to you,” he said. “Very well, Your Majesty, give me a guarantee.
“For what purpose, dear sir, do you require a guarantee? “Your Majesty, for a guarantee that I shall not die for such a length of time. “Dear sir, you ask for an improper guarantee;
it is not possible to give such a guarantee, for the life of beings is like a drop of dew on the tip of a blade of grass.”
“If you do not grant us a guarantee, O King, what good will we have done if we die in the meantime?
“In that case, dear ones, grant me six years. “That is not possible, Sire.
“Then five, four, three, two, or one year? “Seven or six months? “… down to half a month. “Grant us at least half a month.”
"It is not possible, Your Majesty," [they replied]. "In that case, grant me for just seven days," he said.

"Very well, Your Majesty," they agreed, and accepted the request for seven days. The king performed the honors due to him during those very seven days—honors which would normally take seven years, seven months, and seven days to complete.
Then, in order to send the Teacher to his sons' dwelling place, he had the road eight usabhas wide decorated.
In the middle, having had a space four usabhas in measure trampled by elephants to make it resemble a *kasiṇa*-maṇḍala, he had it strewn with sand and covered with scattered flowers;
here and there he placed plantain trees and full water-pots.
Having had [the ground] cleared, he had banners and flags hoisted. At intervals of one *usabha* each, he had lotus ponds excavated;
later, on both sides, he had stalls for perfumes, garlands, and flowers set up.
In the middle section, on both sides of the decorated road which was four *usabhas* wide, he had stumps and thorns removed from two roads each, measuring two *usabhas* in width.
He had staff-lanterns made. The princes also, in the areas under their own jurisdiction, had a road sixteen usabhas long decorated in the same manner.
The king, having gone as far as the boundary of his own domain, the field-limit, paid homage to the Teacher and lamented:
"Sirs, go as if you were plucking out my right eye; having taken it thus, you have gone."
"But you should do what is appropriate for the Buddhas. Do not wander about negligent like drunkards," he said.
They replied, "We shall know, O Lord," and taking the Teacher with them, they went.

Having had a monastery built and dedicated it to the Teacher, they attended upon him there, sometimes at the seat of the elders, sometimes at the seat of the middle-ranking monks, and sometimes at the seat of the novices.
They remained there. As they examined the gift, it was exactly the same for all three people.
When the time for the commencement of the rains retreat drew near, they thought, "How indeed shall we ascertain the Teacher's intention?
Then this occurred to them: "The Buddhas are surely reverent toward the Dhamma, not reverent toward material things; we should establish ourselves in virtue."

Thinking, "We shall be able to grasp the Teacher’s intention," they summoned the men in charge of the offerings and said, "Sirs, continue to provide rice porridge, cooked rice, hard food, and so forth in this very manner and distribute the alms. Thus, they severed the obstacle of the preparations for the offering.
Then their eldest brother, taking five hundred men and establishing himself in the ten precepts, [donned] two saffron robes.
Having covered himself, he dwelt there using only allowable water.
The middle son, along with three hundred men, and the youngest, along with two hundred men, acted in exactly the same way. They attended upon the Teacher for as long as they lived.
The Teacher attained final Nibbāna in their very presence.
Having passed away from there, they wandered from the human world to the celestial world and from the celestial world back to the human world for ninety-two eons.
At the time of our Teacher, having descended from the celestial world, they were reborn in the human world.
Among them, the great minister who was occupied with the distribution of alms was reborn as King Bimbisāra of Aṅga and Magadha. They...
In the kingdom of that very king, they were born into a prominent brahmin family as a great clan.
The eldest was born as the eldest, the middle as the middle, and the youngest as the youngest.
Their attendant people also were born as their attendants. As they grew up, all three of them took those one thousand men and departed to become ascetics.
They lived right there on the bank of the river at Uruvelā. The inhabitants of Aṅga and Magadha brought them great honors month after month.

Then our Bodhisatta, having gone forth, gradually attained omniscience, set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, and having trained disciples such as Yasas and others, dispatched sixty arahants to the various directions for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma; he himself—
Taking his bowl and robe with the thought, "I shall discipline those three matted-hair brothers," he went to Uruvelā.
Having shattered their views through hundreds of miracles, he ordained them. Taking that thousand of ascetics wearing miraculous bowls and robes, he went to Gayāsīsa.
Seated there surrounded by them, he thought, "What kind of Dhamma discourse should I give to these?"
Thinking, "They are suitable," he reached the conclusion: "These men tend the sacrificial fire morning and evening.
I shall teach them by treating their twelve sense-bases as if they were burning and blazing; in this way, they will be able to attain Arhatship.
Then, in order to teach them the Dhamma accordingly, he spoke this Discourse on the Burning.
Therefore it was said: "He addressed the bhikkhus" means that, having sought out a teaching on the Dhamma suitable for them, he addressed them with the thought, "I shall teach that.
Therein, "blazing" (*āditta*) means burning and fully aflame. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
Thus, in this sutta, the characteristic of suffering (*dukkha-lakkhaṇa*) is taught.
7. Commentary on the *Addhabhūta-sutta* (The Overwhelmed) 29.

In the seventh [sutta], "addhabhūta" means overcome (*adhibhūta*), overwhelmed (*ajjhotthaṭa*); the meaning is "afflicted. In this sutta as well, only the characteristic of suffering (*dukkha-lakkhaṇa*) is explained.
8. Commentary on the *Samugghātasāruppa-sutta* (The Suitability for Eradication)
30. In the eighth [verse], "suitable for the uprooting of all conceiving" means it is appropriate for the eradication of all conceivings of craving, conceit, and views.

"Here" means in this teaching. "He does not conceive the eye" means he does not conceive of the eye as "I," or "mine," or "another," or "belonging to another. "He does not conceive in the eye" means [he does not conceive] "I am in the eye," or "mine..."
One does not conceive of "a possession and obstruction in the eye" or "another's possession and obstruction in the eye.
One does not conceive from the perspective of the eye thus:

"I have emerged from the eye," "my possession and obstruction has emerged from the eye," "another has emerged from the eye," or "another's possession and obstruction has emerged from the eye"—in this way as well.
"He does not conceive" means that he does not give rise to even one of the conceivings of craving, pride, or views.
"He does not conceive 'the eye is mine'" means he does not conceive "the eye is my own," that is, he does not give rise to the conceiving of craving which constitutes a sense of "mine-ness.
The rest is self-evident. In this sutta, insight is taught by bringing about the attainment of Arahatship through forty-four points.
9. Commentary on the First Sutta on What is Conducive to Eradication (Paṭhamasamugghātasappāyasuttavaṇṇanā) 31.

In the ninth [verse], "conducive to eradication" (*samugghātasappāya*) means that which is helpful for eradication. "Then it becomes otherwise" (*tato taṃ hoti aññathā*) means that from that point, it exists in a different manner.
"The world, subject to change and attached to existence, delights only in existence" (*aññathābhāvī bhavasatto loko bhavamevābhinandati*) refers to the state of being subject to change.
Even though it has become otherwise through undergoing transformation, this world— clinging, attached,
and fettered to the states of existence— rejoices only in existence. To whatever extent there are aggregates, elements, and bases, monks—
to whatever extent there are these aggregates, elements, and bases— that too [is not...].
"He conceives" means that even "all" does not conceive; this is shown again by summarizing what was already taken up below.
In this sutta, insight is explained after bringing about Arahantship in forty-eight instances.
10. Commentary on the Second Sutta on the Expedient for Eradication.

32. In the tenth [sutta], after showing the graspings of craving, conceit, and views by means of three sets of three phrases beginning with "This is mine," the teaching was given according to the method of three turnings.
Furthermore, in all three of these suttas, the sequence is such that the four paths are taught together with insight (vipassanā).
This concludes the third chapter, the "All Chapter."

4. Commentary on the Chapter on the Nature of Birth (Jātidhammavagga), §§ 33–42: In the Chapter on the Nature of Birth, "subject to birth" (*jātidhamma*) means having the nature of being born, having the essential characteristic of arising.

"Subject to aging" (*jarādhamma*) means having the essential characteristic of decaying. "Subject to illness" (*byādhidhamma*) means having the essential characteristic of illness by virtue of being the condition for the arising of illness. "Subject to death" (*maraṇadhamma*)...
"Subject to death" means having death as its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). "Subject to sorrow" means having sorrow as its intrinsic nature by way of being a condition for the arising of sorrow.

"Subject to defilement" means having the nature of being subject to defilement. "Subject to destruction" means having the nature of passing into destruction. The same method applies to "subject to vanishing" and so forth.
This is the fourth chapter: The Chapter on the Nature of Birth.
5. Commentary on the Chapter on All is Impermanent (Sabba-anicca-vagga), §§43–52.

Regarding the term *abhiññeyya* ("to be directly known") in the Chapter on Impermanence, it should be understood that the full understanding through knowledge (*ñāta-pariññā*) is explicitly mentioned, while the other two types of full understanding are implicitly included.

Furthermore, regarding the terms *pariññeyya* ("to be fully understood") and *pahātabba* ("to be abandoned"), only the full understanding through investigation (*tīraṇa-pariññā*) and the full understanding through abandoning (*pahāna-pariññā*) are explicitly mentioned, yet the others are likewise [implied].
It should be understood that both [types of full understanding] are indeed included. "To be realized" means to be made directly evident.

“This ‘remote forest’ is a designation for dwellings frequented by non-human beings.

At that moment, two young venomous snakes were playing on the roof of the cave. One of them fell and settled upon the Elder’s shoulder.

The poison entered him as if it were completely consuming the wick of a lamp.

When the Elder saw the poison’s progress, although it had only just fallen and had spread according to its natural limits, he resolved through the power of his psychic potency (iddhi), "May this body not perish in this cave," and addressed the monks: "Before this body perishes right here..."
"Scatters" means: as long as he does not scatter [the body], you should carry it outside; this is the meaning. "Alteration" (*aññathatta*) means the state of being otherwise.

It is said. In this sutta, the reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā) of those in training (sekha) and those beyond training (asekha) is explained.

87. "In the fourth [case], 'Channa' refers to the elder of that name; it does not refer to an elder who has gone forth from the home life.
