One should give. "The weapon" refers to a weapon that takes away life. "I do not desire" means I do not wish for it. "Served" means attended upon.
"With what is pleasing" means by bodily action and so forth that increases the mind. And herein, the seven types of trainees (sekha) are said to "serve";
the Arahant is said to be the "server"; and the Blessed One is said to be the one "served."
"Indeed, friend, this is fitting for a disciple," means, "friend, this is indeed appropriate for one called a disciple.
"Without reproach" means without recurrence and without reconnection. "Ask, friend Sāriputta; having heard, we shall know"—this is called the "Invitation of the Disciples" (*sāvakapavāraṇā*).
"This is mine," and so forth, are stated by way of the grasping of craving, conceit, and views. "Having seen cessation" means having seen its destruction and passing away.
"Having understood: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self,' I regard it as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
In these instances, the Elder Channa, when questioned by the Elder Sāriputta, answered by attributing the state of Arahantship to himself.
However, although the Elder Sāriputta knew his status as a worldling (*puthujjana*), he addressed him as "worldling."
Without saying either "one whose taints are destroyed" or "an arahant," he remained silent.
But the Elder Cunda, thinking, "I shall make him realize his state as an ordinary person (puthujjana)," gave him this exhortation.
In that context, "therefore" means because, being unable to endure the death-pain, he said, "I am taking up the knife."
He says this; therefore, he indicates that "the Venerable One is a worldling (puthujjana)," and thus you should attend to this as well.

Or else, because you have said, "Having seen the cessation of the six sense bases, I do not perceive the eye and so forth by way of the three types of grasping," therefore, this teaching of the Blessed One should also be attended to by the Venerable One—this indeed refers to the state of being a worldling.
He speaks while illuminating [the matter]. "At all times" means at every moment. "Of one who is dependent" means of one who is dependent on craving, conceit, and views.

"Shaken" means it is agitated. Just as this agitation now occurs for the Venerable One—who, being unable to endure the arisen feeling, has not abandoned the grasping that thinks, "I feel it; this is my feeling"—by this too...
He does not say, "You are just an ordinary person" (*puthujjana*).

"Tranquility" (*passaddhi*) means tranquility of body and mind; the meaning is that there is what is called the tranquility of the defilements (*kilesa*). "By way of inclination" (*natiyā*) means by way of the inclination of craving (*taṇhā-nati*).

"When non-existence" (*asati*) means when there is no obsession by attachment to a basis for the sake of becoming (*bhava*). "There is no coming or going" (*āgatigati na hoti*) means by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"Coming" means there is no going by way of death. "Death and rebirth" means death by way of passing away and rebirth by way of arising.
"Neither here nor beyond, nor in between the two" means it does not exist in this world, nor in the other world, nor in both places.
"This alone is the end of suffering" means this indeed is the end, this is the limit, of the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and the suffering of the defilements (*kilesa*).
There is no state of being an intermediate existence (*antarābhava*); this indeed is the meaning here.
As for those who, taking the expression "between both" (*ubhayamantarena*), maintain that there is an intermediate existence, their statement is pointless.
For the existence of an intermediate existence is explicitly rejected in the Abhidhamma. However, the word "between" (*antarena*) indicates an alternative formulation. Therefore...
This is the meaning here: "neither here nor hereafter" means "not both," according to another interpretation.
"He brought forth a weapon" means he brought forth a life-taking weapon; having brought it forth, he cut his windpipe.
Then, at that moment, the fear of death overcame him, and the sign of his future destination appeared. He [realized] his own state as a worldling (*puthujjana*).
Having understood this, with a heart moved by spiritual urgency, he established insight and, while discerning conditioned phenomena, attained Arahantship.

Having become one who has reached the summit, he attained final Nibbāna. Although this declaration was made while the Elder was still an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), by virtue of that very declaration, his final Nibbāna was rendered free from obstacles.
It was so. Therefore, the Blessed One took that very explanation and spoke it.

"Families of reproach" means families that should be visited. By this, the Elder [showed] that even while such male and female attendants exist, "Venerable Sir, that bhikkhu will attain final nibbāna in your teaching"—thus [he spoke] regarding the preliminary practice.

He asks this question while pointing out the fault of associating with families. Then the Blessed One, illustrating the absence of such association with families, said to him, "These, Sāriputta," and so forth.
It is said that in this context, the Elder’s state of non-association with families was well known.
The rest is clear throughout.
5–6. Commentary on the Puṇṇasutta, etc. 88–89.
In the fifth [verse], "that" refers to both that eye and visible forms. "From the arising of delight comes the arising of suffering":
through the convergence of craving, there is the convergence of the suffering of the five aggregates. Thus, at the six sense-doors, from the arising of delight...
By the phrase “the origin of suffering,” he showed the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) brought to its culmination by way of two truths.
In the second method, by [stating] “cessation” and “the path,” he showed the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*) brought to its culmination by way of two truths.
“By this, Puṇṇa”—this is a separate connection (*anusandhi*). Thus, first, the teaching was given by way of the cycle and the turning away, up to [the stage of] Arahantship.
Having thus included him, he now spoke the words beginning with "By this, you... in order to cause the Elder Puṇṇa to let out a lion’s roar in seven places.
"Fierce" means wicked and sinful. "Harsh" means cruel; "they will revile" means they will revile by means of the ten grounds for reviling.
"They will insult" means they will threaten, saying, "What kind of ascetic are you? We shall do this and that to you."
"Thus it will be for me in this matter": "In this way, it shall happen to me here. "With a staff" means with a four-cubit staff, or a khadira-wood staff, or a mallet-staff.
"With a weapon" means with a weapon such as one with a single-edged blade. "They seek out a weapon-taker" means they seek out a weapon that takes away life.
This is the Elder’s discourse on foulness (*asubha*) regarding the third *pārājika* offense.

This was said with reference to the monks' search for a weapon after they became disgusted with their own physical existence upon hearing [the teaching]. Regarding the phrase "by means of self-taming and tranquility" (*damūpasamena*):
here, "taming" (*dama*) is a name for the restraint of the sense faculties and so forth. As it is said:
"Tamed by truth, endowed with self-taming... (*saccena danto damasā upeto*).
“A master of the Vedanta who has lived the holy life.

Here, indeed, restraint of the sense faculties is called self-control (*dama*). “If there were truth, self-control, generosity, and patience—if more than these were found here,” in this passage wisdom is called self-control.
“By giving, by self-control, by restraint, and by speaking the truth,” in this passage the Uposatha observance is meant.
"Self-control" (*dama*) was thus stated. However, in this sutta, it should be understood that patience (*khanti*) is self-control; "peace" (*upasama*) is a synonym for that very same thing.

Now, as for the Venerable Puṇṇa—what was this Puṇṇa, and why did he wish to go there? He was indeed a resident of Sunāparanta, but having perceived that Sāvatthī was an unsuitable place for his dwelling, he wished to go there.
Herein is the sequential account: it is said that in a certain merchant village in the kingdom of Sunāparanta, these two were brothers.
Among them, sometimes the elder would take five hundred carts and go to the countryside to bring back goods,

and sometimes it was the younger brother. On this occasion, however, having left the younger brother at home, the elder brother took five hundred carts and, while traveling on a journey through the countryside,
eventually reached Sāvatthī, not far from the Jeta Grove.
Having halted the caravan of carts and finished his morning meal, he sat down in a comfortable spot surrounded by his attendants. At that time, the inhabitants of Sāvatthī,
having finished their morning meals and undertaken the observance of the Uposatha precepts, with their upper robes purified and carrying perfumes,
flowers, and other offerings in their hands, were inclined toward, directed toward, and leaning toward the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.
Having offered the sacrifice, they departed through the southern gate and proceeded toward Jetavana.
Seeing them, he asked a man, "Where are these people going? "What do you not know, noble sir?
The Jewels of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha have appeared in the world; this great multitude is going into the presence of the Teacher to hear a discourse on the Dhamma. To him—
The word “Buddha” pierced through his skin and hide, cutting right down to the marrow of his bones.

Surrounded by his own retinue, he went with that assembly to the monastery; standing at the edge of the gathering while the Teacher was teaching the Dhamma in a sweet voice, he heard the Dhamma and conceived the desire for the going-forth. Then—
When the Tathāgata, having perceived the proper time, dismissed the assembly, [the king] approached the Teacher, paid homage,
and invited him for the following day. On the second day, having caused a pavilion to be constructed, having prepared seats,
and having given a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he partook of his morning meal, undertook the observance precepts (uposathaṅga), and addressed the treasurer.
Having summoned him, he explained everything, saying, "This much wealth has been spent;
this much wealth has not been spent," and having handed over his entire estate with the words,
"Give this property to my younger brother," he went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher and became devoted to his meditation subject.
As he was attending to his meditation subject, it did not become clear to him. Thereupon he thought:
"This country is unsuitable for me; what if I were to go back to my own kingdom after receiving a meditation subject from the Teacher?
Then, having wandered for alms in the morning and emerged from seclusion in the evening, he set out.
Having approached the Blessed One, requested a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and uttered seven lion-roars, he departed.
Thus it was said: “Then the Venerable Puṇṇa...
lived. But where did he live? He lived in four places. First, having entered the kingdom of Suṇāparanta—
Having reached the mountain named Abbuhatthapabbata, he entered the merchant village for alms.
Then his younger brother, recognizing him, gave him alms and, having made a promise, saying, "Venerable sir, do not go elsewhere; please stay right here," he had him reside there.
From there, he went to the monastery named Samuddagirivihāra. There, a walking-path (caṅkama) was constructed, demarcated by iron magnets and stones.
There was no one at all capable of walking there. However, the waves of the ocean would come there, strike against the iron-stone rocks, and make a great noise.
The Elder, thinking, "May there be a comfortable dwelling for those who attend to their meditation subject," resolved by his supernormal power to make the ocean silent.
From there he went to the place named Mātulagiri. There too, a great multitude of birds gathered, and their noise was continuous, both by night and by day.
The Elder, thinking, "This place is not comfortable," went from there to the monastery named Makulakārāmavihāra.
That place was not too far from the merchant village nor too near; it was well-situated for coming and going, secluded, and free from noise.
The Elder, thinking, "This place is comfortable," established night-quarters, day-quarters, walking-paths, and so forth there, and entered the rains retreat.
In this manner, he dwelt in those four places.
Then, one day during that very same rains retreat, five hundred merchants set out by ship, intending to go to the other sea.

They loaded the goods onto the ship. On the day of embarking, the Elder’s younger brother, having fed the Elder and received the precepts from him, paid his respects and said, "Venerable sir, the ocean is indeed unreliable and fraught with many perils;
please keep us in your thoughts," and then he boarded the ship. As the ship was traveling at the highest speed, it reached a certain island.
They arrived. People, thinking, "We shall prepare our morning meal," disembarked on the island. But on that island there was nothing else; it was a sandalwood grove alone.
Then one man, having struck a tree with an axe and recognized it as red sandalwood, said: "Sirs, for the sake of gain..."
“Let us go to the other sea; there is no gain greater than this from here.
A small jar measuring only four finger-breadths is worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold. Let us take the goods suitable for trade and fill our jars with sandalwood.
So they did. The non-human beings dwelling in the Sandalwood Grove became angry and said, “These men are taking away our sandalwood grove.”
Thinking, "We shall have those who have been expelled executed," they said, "If they are executed right here, everything will become a single heap of corpses;
therefore, we shall sink their ship in the middle of the ocean.
Then, as soon as they had boarded their ship and traveled for a short while, they raised a tempest, and those non-human beings themselves manifested terrifying forms.
Terrified, the people paid homage to their respective deities.
The householder Cūḷapuṇṇaka, the younger brother of the Elder, stood paying homage to the Elder, thinking, "May my brother be my refuge.
It is said that at that very moment, the Elder, having reflected and perceived the impending calamity for them, leapt up into the air.
He stood facing them. As soon as the non-human beings saw the Elder, they departed, thinking, "The Venerable Puṇṇa the Elder is coming," and the storm subsided.
The Elder, having reassured them by saying, "Do not be afraid," asked, "Where do you wish to go?
"Venerable sir, we wish to go to our own place. The Elder stepped onto the deck of the ship and said, "This is the destination desired by these beings..."
"Let it go," he resolved. The merchants, having returned to their own place, informed their wives and children of what had occurred.

Saying, "Come, let us go for refuge to the Elder," those five hundred men, together with their five hundred women, established themselves in the Three Refuges and declared themselves lay disciples (*upāsakas*).
Then, having unloaded the goods from the ship, they [presented them] to the Elder.
Having set aside one portion, they said, "Venerable sir, this is your portion. The Elder replied, "I have no need for a separate portion;
however, has the Teacher ever been seen by you? "No, venerable sir.
"In that case, build a circular pavilion for the Teacher with this material. In this way, you shall see the Teacher. They said, "Very well."
"Venerable Sir," they said. Then, with that portion and their own portions, they began to construct the circular pavilion (maṇḍalamāḷa).
It is said that from the time it was commenced, the Teacher made use of it.
The guardian deities, seeing a radiance at night, perceived that "there are powerful devas [residing here]. The lay disciples [constructed] the circular pavilion...

Having completed the construction of dwellings for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and prepared the requisites for the offering, they informed the Elder: "Venerable sir, we have performed our duty; please summon the Teacher.
In the evening, the Elder went to Sāvatthī by means of his psychic power and said, "Venerable sir, the inhabitants of Vāṇijagāma desire to see you; have compassion for them."
"Please do so," he entreated the Blessed One. The Blessed One consented. The Elder returned to his own place.
The Blessed One then addressed the Elder Ānanda: "Ānanda, tomorrow we shall go for alms in the merchant village of Sunāparanta;
give a voting ticket to four hundred and ninety-nine bhikkhus. The Elder replied, "Very well, venerable sir," and [delivered it] to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Having reported this matter, he said, "Let those monks who travel through the air take voting tickets. On that day, the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna was the first to take a ticket.
The inhabitants of Vāṇijagāma, thinking, "The Teacher will surely arrive tomorrow," constructed a pavilion in the center of the village and prepared a hall for almsgiving.
Early in the morning, the Blessed One, having attended to his bodily needs, entered the Fragrant Chamber.
Having entered and attained the fruition-attainment (*phalasamāpatti*), he sat down. Sakka’s Pandukambala stone seat became hot.
He, reflecting on "What is this?", saw that the Teacher was going to Sunāparanta; he then addressed Vissakamma:
"Dear one, today the Blessed One will go for alms over three hundred yojanas. [Prepare] five hundred gabled houses..."
"Having built them, place them at the gateway of Jetavana, ready for departure. He did accordingly.
The gabled chamber (kūṭāgāra) of the Blessed One had four doors; those of the two chief disciples had two doors each; the others had one door each.
The Teacher, having emerged from the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī), entered the foremost gabled chamber among the series of chambers thus arranged.
Beginning with the two chief disciples, four hundred and ninety-nine bhikkhus also entered the gabled chambers.
One chamber remained empty, and all five hundred gabled chambers rose up into the air.
Upon reaching the mountain named Saccabandha, the Teacher caused the gabled chamber to remain suspended in the sky. On that mountain was Saccabandha...
The ascetic named Micchādiṭṭhika lived having attained the pinnacle of gain and fame while instilling wrong view in the great multitude;
yet, within him, like a lamp inside a jar, the supporting condition for the fruit of Arahatship was burning.
Seeing this, [the Buddha] went there with the thought, "I shall preach the Dhamma to him," and taught the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, the ascetic—

He attained arahantship. The higher knowledges (abhiññā) came to him by way of the Path itself. Having become an "Ehi-bhikkhu" (Come, monk), wearing robes and bowl produced by supernormal power (iddhimaya), he entered an empty gabled house (kūṭāgāra).
The Blessed One, together with five hundred monks who were staying in gabled houses, went to the merchant village and [reached] the gabled houses.

Having made himself invisible, he entered the village of the merchants. After the merchants had given a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, they led the Teacher to the Makula Monastery.

The Teacher entered the circular pavilion. While the Teacher was allaying the fatigue from his meal, the great multitude prepared their breakfast, undertook the precepts of the Uposatha, and remained there.
Taking many perfumes and flowers, he returned to the monastery for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. The Teacher preached the Dhamma;
the release of the great multitude from their bonds occurred, and there was a great clamor regarding the Buddha.
For the sake of gathering the great multitude, the Teacher remained right there for seven days, but at dawn, [he stayed] in the Great Fragrant Chamber itself.
He raised [the bowl]. At the conclusion of the Dhamma teaching over those seven days, there was the realization of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand living beings.
Having stayed there for seven days and walked for alms in the merchant village, he sent the Elder Puṇṇa back, saying, "You stay right here.
Between there and that place, there is a river named the Nammadā; he went to its bank. The Nammadā...
The Naga king went out to meet the Teacher, led him into the Naga abode, and paid honor to the Three Jewels.
After the Teacher had preached the Dhamma to him, he departed from the Naga abode. The king requested, "Venerable Sir, grant me something to be worshipped.
The Blessed One showed him the footprint-relic (*padacetiya*) on the bank of the Nammadā River; it remains covered whenever the waves come in.
When he had departed, [the heretics] were confounded. He received great honor. The Teacher then left that place and went to the Saccabandha mountain, where he said to Saccabandha:
"By you, the great multitude has been led down the path to the states of misery.
You must remain right here, cause them to abandon their false views, and establish them on the path to Nibbāna. He, too, requested to be allowed to attend upon him.
The Teacher displayed his footprint-relic on a solid rock as if stamping a mark upon a lump of moist clay.
From there, he went back to Jetavana. It was with reference to this matter that it was said: "In that very same rainy season," and so forth.
"He attained final Nibbāna" means he passed away into the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. For seven days, the great multitude [honored] the Elder.
Having performed the worship of the body, having gathered much fragrant wood, and having cremated the body, he took the relics and erected a cetiya.
"A number of bhikkhus" refers to the bhikkhus standing at the place of the elder’s cremation. The rest is clear everywhere.
The sixth [sutta] is likewise clear.
7–8. Commentary on the First *Ejā-sutta*, etc. 90–91.
In the seventh [verse], *ejā* means craving (*taṇhā*). For it is called *ejā* in the sense of moving (*calana*).

That very same [craving] is a disease (*roga*) in the sense of afflicting (*ābādhana*), a boil (*gaṇḍa*) in the sense of internal corruption (*anto-dussana*), and an arrow (*salla*) in the sense of piercing (*nikantana*). Therefore (*tasmā*), because *ejā* is indeed a disease...
"And the tumor and the dart; therefore. "One should not conceive [the eye]" and so forth is exactly as previously stated;
here too, everything has been shown by summarizing what was already included below. The eighth is exactly as previously stated.
9–10. Commentary on the First Sutta on Pairs, etc.
92–93. In the ninth [section], "dve-dvayaṃ" means two pairs. In the tenth, "itthaṃ dvayaṃ" means this pair is thus. "Moving and shaking" (calaṃ ceva byathaṃ ca):
because it does not stand firm in its own intrinsic nature, it moves and it shakes.
"Whatever cause and whatever condition": for eye-consciousness, the base and the object are both the cause and the condition. From what could it be permanent?

"Will it be?"—for what reason will it be permanent? But just as a son born from the womb of a male and female slave remains a slave to another, so too it is simply impermanent; this is the meaning. "Conjunction" (*saṅgati*) means going together.

"Assemblage" (*sannipāta*) means meeting together in one place. "Collection" (*samavāya*) means coming together in one place. By the phrase "this is called eye-contact," [it is shown that contact is not a separate entity].

Because it has arisen by means of a condition known as conjunction (*saṅgati*), meeting (*sannipāta*), and coincidence (*samavāya*), this is called "eye-contact" (*cakkhusamphassa*) precisely by the name of its condition.
That too is a cause: the basis and object of contact, and the three co-nascent aggregates—this is the cause. "Touched" (*phuṭṭha*)...

In the sense of "functioning," it is personal (*paccattaṃ*); the meaning is that feeling feels the very object touched by contact, volition intends, and perception perceives. Or alternatively, "touched" refers to the person possessing contact;
thus it is also said that one feels, intends, and perceives the object touched by contact through feeling and the other [mental factors]. Thus, in this sutta, there are thirty aggregates.
They have been explained. How so? First, in the case of the eye-door: the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the object (*ārammaṇa*) are the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*);

"that which feels what is touched" is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*); "that which wills" is the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*); "that which perceives" is the aggregate of perception (*saññākkhandha*);

and "that which cognizes" is the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*). This same method applies to the remaining doors as well. For even in the mind-door, the physical basis is exclusively...
The aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*); moreover, when there is a form as an object (*ārammaṇa*), that object is also the aggregate of form—thus there are six times thirty-five [factors].
In brief, however, these are five aggregates even across all six doors.
This discourse was taught with the intention of those who would understand when the five aggregates, along with their conditions, are explained in detail as "impermanent."
The Ninth Chapter: Channa. 10.
The Tenth Chapter: The Sixfold. 1. The Exposition on the Untamed and Unguarded.
94. In the first [sutta] of the Saḷavagga: “Untamed” means not tamed; “unguarded” means not protected; “unprotected” means not guarded;
“unrestrained” means not covered over. “They bring about suffering” means they bring about excessive suffering, such as that pertaining to the various realms beginning with the hells.
“They bring about happiness” means they bring about excessive happiness, such as the various stages of jhāna, the paths, and the fruits.
*Adhivāhati* is also a reading; it has the same meaning.
*Saḷeva* means "only six. *Asaṃvuto yattha dukkhaṃ nigacchati* means that in whichever sense-bases (*āyatana*) one lacks restraint, there one encounters suffering.
*Tesañca ye saṃvaraṇaṃ avediṃsu* refers to those who have known the restraint regarding those sense-bases.
They obtained [it]. "Dwelling untainted" means they dwell untainted, unsoiled.
"And what is tasted as 'delicious'" means that which possesses relish and is sweet.
"The two-fold contact in pleasure and pain, equanimity" means both pleasant contact and painful contact—these two contacts are equanimity; one should arouse only equanimity therein.
The meaning is as follows. There is also a reading: "the two types of contact, pleasure, pain, and equanimity. Alternatively, the meaning is:
"pleasure, pain, and equanimity caused by contact"; or, "one should be equanimous (*upekkhaka*) by not producing attachment toward pleasure and aversion toward pain.
"Neither attached nor opposed to anyone" means that one should be neither attached to nor opposed toward anyone whatsoever.
"Papañcasaññā" means that through the perception of defilements (*kilesasaññā*), it becomes what is called "papañca-perception.
"Itarītarā narā" refers to inferior beings who, while proliferating (*papañcayamānā*), approach the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). "Saññino" means sentient beings possessing perception.
"Manomayaṃ gehasitañca sabbaṃ" means all mental proliferation (*manomaya-vitakka*) based upon the house of the five strands of sensual pleasure.

"Having driven away" means having expelled and cast out. "He conducts himself based on renunciation" means that a bhikkhu of such a nature conducts himself by means of conduct grounded in renunciation.
"When well-cultivated in the six" means when [the mind] has been thoroughly developed in regard to the six objects.
"The mind of one touched does not waver anywhere" means that the mind of one touched by either a pleasant contact or a painful contact does not waver toward anything whatsoever.
"It does not tremble, it does not shake. "Become those who have gone to the further shore of birth and death"—that is, become those who go to *nibbāna*, the further shore of birth and death.
2. Commentary on the Māluṅkyaputta Sutta: 95. Regarding "Māluṅkyaputta":
he is the son of the brahmin woman Māluṅkyā. "In this" means in this request for your instruction.
By this, he both disparages and praises the Elder. How so? It is said that while this man was young, he was negligent regarding forms and other sense objects;
yet later, in his old age, desiring to dwell in the forest, he requested a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Then the Blessed One said: "What shall we say here about this youth?
Like Māluṅkyaputta, you too were negligent during your youth; now, in your old age..."
By speaking with the intention, "Having entered the forest, you should practice the duty of a recluse," he indeed disparages the Elder.
However, because the Elder was desirous of entering the forest and practicing the duty of a recluse even at an advanced age, the Blessed One said:
"What shall we say here regarding this youth? This Māluṅkyaputta of ours, even at an advanced age, [desires to enter the forest]..."
Having entered [the monastery], desiring to perform the duties of a recluse, he asks for a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), saying with this intention:
"Do you not exert yourself even in your youth?"—thus he encourages the Elder.
"Yatra hi nāma" means "he who indeed. "Kiñcāpi" means "even though it is known that 'I am old. If I...
"Though I am old, being old, I shall be able to practice the duty of a recluse;
therefore, may the Blessed One teach me," said [the elder] with this intention. Thus he spoke, disregarding his own aged state while commending the instruction.
"Never seen, never seen before" means not seen in this present existence, nor ever seen before in the past. "And you do not see" means...
He asks: "Even now you do not see [it], yet there is no such mental application on your part as 'may I see it'; could desire and the other [mental factors] arise for you in that regard?
In the phrase "in what is seen, merely the seen," it means that in the sense-sphere of visible form, when it is seen by the eye-consciousness, there will be merely the seen.
For visual consciousness sees in a visible form merely the form itself, not its nature as permanent and so forth;
thus, the meaning here is that by the remaining types of consciousness as well, my mind will be "merely what has been seen" (*diṭṭhamatta*).

Alternatively, "the seen" (*diṭṭha*) refers to visual consciousness, meaning the cognition of form within a form. "Mere" (*matta*) means measure; that which has "mere" as its measure is "merely what has been seen," namely, the mind.
The meaning is: "My consciousness will consist of eye-consciousness alone. This is what is intended:

just as eye-consciousness does not become attached, does not feel aversion, and does not become deluded toward a visible form that has come into its range, so too, through the absence of lust and other defilements, the impulsion (javana) will consist of eye-consciousness alone;
thinking, "I shall establish the impulsion within the measure of eye-consciousness itself. Alternatively, [it refers to] what is seen...
What is called "seen" is the form seen by eye-consciousness; what is called "merely seen" is the triad of consciousnesses—namely, receiving, investigating, and determining—that arise right there.

Thinking, "Just as it does not become lustful, hateful, or deluded, so too, when a form enters the range of perception, I shall arouse impulsion (javana) with that same measure consisting of receiving and the rest; I will not allow it to exceed that measure by way of lust and the like," [one practices].
"I shall allow it to arise"—this is the meaning here. The same method applies to what is heard and what is sensed.
Regarding "in the cognized, mere cognition": here, "cognized" refers to an object that has been cognized by the adverting of the mind-door;

in that which is cognized, "mere cognition" refers to the extent of the adverting itself. Just as one does not become attached or repelled by the adverting, [so too with the subsequent consciousness].

"He is not deluded" means that, by not allowing [the mind] to arise through passion and so forth, he will establish the mind by the measure of mere adverting (āvajjana) alone; this is the meaning here.
"When" (*yataḥ*) means whenever. "Then" (*tataḥ*) means at that time. "Not by that" means he will not be colored by that passion, nor corrupted by hatred, nor deluded by ignorance.
"Therefore, Māluṅkyaputta, you will not be there" means when you [are no longer affected] by that passion...

Or, if you are not impassioned by greed, or corrupted by hatred, or deluded by ignorance, then you will not be bound to, attached to, or established in that—whether it be what is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized. "Neither thus... and so forth has the same meaning as already stated.
"Mindfulness is lost" means mindfulness is destroyed. "And clinging to that" means having swallowed that object. Covetousness and cruelty...
"And covetousness and harmfulness. Alternatively, it should be construed with the phrase "increasing for him":
the meaning is that these two states—covetousness and harmfulness—increase for him.
"His mind is afflicted" means his mind is afflicted by covetousness and harmfulness. "Ācinato" means for one who is accumulating.
"Nibbāna is said to be far away": for such a person, what is called Nibbāna is declared to be distant.
"Having smelled" means having inhaled. "Having tasted" means having eaten, drunk, or licked. "Having touched" means having made physical contact.
"Possessed of mindfulness" means endowed with mindfulness known as *paṭissati*. "And the feeling of one who cultivates" refers to the supramundane feeling produced in association with the four paths.
*Sevantassa*: for one who cultivates [the path]. *Khīyati* means it goes to destruction. What is that? Both suffering and the multitude of defilements (*kilesa*). *Aññataro*:
a certain one among the eighty great disciples (*mahāsāvaka*). Thus, in this sutta, even by means of verses, only the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are explained.
3. Commentary on the *Parihānadhamma Sutta* (The Discourse on the Nature of Decline)
96. "Subject to decline" (*parihānadhamma*) means having the nature of declining. "Bases of mastery" (*abhibhāyatana*) means bases that have been mastered. "Covetous thoughts" (*sarasaṅkappa*):
here, they are called *sara* because they run; the meaning is that they rush. These are both *sara* (thoughts) and *saṅkappa* (intentions), hence "covetous thoughts.
"Conducive to fetters" (*saṃyojaniya*) means capable of binding, serving as a condition for bondage. "If that, O monk" (*tañce bhikkhu*) refers to that which has arisen in such a manner.
"Born of defilements" means that [defilement] or its object. "He endures" means he harbors it by taking it upon his mind.
"He does not abandon" means he does not abandon it through the abandoning of desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*). This should be applied to all the phrases in this manner.

"For this has been called a 'base of mastery' (*abhibhāyatana*) by the Blessed One" means that this has been described by the Buddha, the Blessed One, as a base that has mastered [the defilements]. Here...
By the person who, having asked about the Dhamma, analyzes it, the Dhamma is shown.
4. Commentary on the *Pamādavihārīsutta* 97.
In the fourth [sutta], "of one who is unrestrained" (*asaṃvutassa*) means of one who is not covered, not placed there after being closed and concealed. "He sprinkles" (*byāsiñcati*)...
It flows out; having become moistened by defilements, it proceeds. *Pāmojja* is weak rapture (*pīti*). *Pīti* is strong rapture.
*Passaddhi* is the subsiding of distress. "The states do not become manifest" means that the states of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) do not arise.
In this sutta, by asking about the person and then analyzing through the Dhamma, the person is shown by way of the Dhamma.
5. Commentary on the Saṃvara Sutta (98).
Regarding the fifth discourse, "And how, bhikkhus, is there non-restraint?":

this was not taught according to the order of the summary by omitting the first explanation of the path to be abandoned—as if saying, "Abandoning the left, one should take the right"—but rather out of skill in teaching.
It should be understood that this was stated by way of explaining the states that must first be abandoned. Here, having asked about the Dhamma, it is the Dhamma itself that is analyzed.
6. Commentary on the *Samādhi Sutta* (Sutta 99):

In the sixth [sutta], "concentration" (*samādhi*) means one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*). For this discourse was spoken by the Blessed One after he perceived that their one-pointedness of mind was declining; knowing that "for those who attain one-pointedness of mind, the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) will reach fulfillment," he spoke it.
7. Commentary on the *Paṭisallāna-sutta* (Sutta 100).

In the seventh [sutta], "seclusion" (*paṭisallāna*) means physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*). For this discourse was spoken by the Blessed One after he perceived that the teaching was declining due to a lack of physical seclusion, and knowing, "If these [monks] obtain physical seclusion, their meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) will reach fulfillment.
8–9. Commentary on the first *Na tumhākaṃ-sutta* and others.

101–102. The eighth [sutta] was spoken for those who understand by means of an illustration surrounding it, while the ninth was spoken according to the inclination of those who understand by way of the bare statement alone.
As for the meaning, in both cases it should be understood in the same manner as explained in the Khandhiya-vagga.
10. Commentary on the Udaka-sutta.
103. In the phrase *udako sudanti*, *sudanti* here is merely a particle. *Udako* is his name. In the phrase *idaṃ jātu vedagū*, *idaṃ* here is merely a particle;
or rather, he spoke thus while pointing out: "Listen to these words of mine. *Jātu vedagū* means:

"I am certainly a *vedagu* (one who has reached the end of knowledge); I have gone among those things to be known by means of knowledge termed 'veda' (*veda-saṅkhāta-ñāṇena*), or [I have attained] the *veda* itself."
"Gone" means attained; the meaning is: "I am wise. "All-conqueror" (Sabbajī) means he declares: "Having utterly conquered and overcome the entire cycle of existence (vaṭṭa), I stand firm.
"The root of the boil not yet scraped away" refers to the root of suffering not yet scraped away. "Scraped away" means it has been scraped away by me;
he indicates that he stands having dug it out.
"Born of mother and father" means produced from the semen and blood belonging to the mother and father, which have arisen from the mother and the father.
"Accumulated by rice and gruel" means built up and increased by means of boiled rice and gruel. "Subject to impermanence, to being covered, to being rubbed, to breaking, and to disintegration":
herein, this body, having come to be, [is characterized] in the sense of non-existence...
It is subject to impermanence; it is subject to being smeared with thin ointments for the purpose of counteracting foul odors;
it is subject to being massaged with light rubbing for the purpose of dispelling afflictions in the limbs and members;
or, as in childhood, it is subject to being pressed and rubbed in order to bring about the proper formation of various limbs that were deformed by dwelling in the womb while lying upon the thighs.

The meaning is that its nature is such that it is subject to being rubbed away; even when thus carefully maintained, its nature is such that it is liable to breaking and destruction, for it both breaks and scatters.

In this context, growth is described by the terms "born of mother and father," "accumulated from boiled rice and sour gruel," and "subject to rubbing away"; whereas impermanence, breaking, and destruction are described by the latter terms.
Decline. Alternatively, with the first three [phrases] there is arising, and with the latter eight there is passing away.
Thus, the distinctions of growth, decline, and production regarding the body composed of the four great elements have been shown. The remainder is of obvious meaning.
The tenth chapter, the Saḷavagga, is concluded.
The Second Fifty. 11.
The Chapter on the One Who Has Attained Security from Bondage (Yogakkhemivagga). 1. Commentary on the Discourse on the One Who Has Attained Security from Bondage (Yogakkhemisuttavaṇṇanā).

104. In the first discourse of the *Yogakkhemivagga*, "the discourse on the one who has attained security from bondage" (*yogakkhemipariyāya*) refers to that which is the cause for one who is secure from the four bonds.
"The discourse on the Dhamma" (*dhammapariyāya*) refers to the cause that is the Dhamma. "He declared the bond" (*akkhāsi yogaṃ*) means he spoke of the connection [to suffering].

Why is this? Is it because of its being declared, or because of its being abandoned? It is because of its being abandoned; for by mere declaration, one does not become "one who has attained security from bondage."
2–10. Commentary on the *Upādāyasutta* and others, 105–113.
In the second [sutta], pleasant and painful feeling (*vedanā-sukhadukkha*) is spoken of; however, that which is intended here is resultant (*vipāka*) pleasure and pain.

In the third, "of suffering" (*dukkhassa*) refers to the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*). In the fourth, "of the world" (*lokassa*) refers to the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāraloka*). In the fifth and those following...
Whatever needs to be said has already been stated according to the method in the Khandhiya-vagga.
The eleventh chapter is the Yogakkhemi-vagga.
12. The Lokakāmaguṇa-vagga.
1–2. Commentary on the First Sutta, *Āvāsagata*, etc. (114–115).
In the first [sutta] of the Chapter on Worldly Qualities (*Lokakāmaguṇavagga*), “gone to his dwelling” (*āvāsagato*) means gone to his place of residence.

“Fallen under the power of Māra” (*mārassa vasaṃ gato*) means fallen under the power of all three kinds of Māra. “The snare of Māra is fastened upon him” (*paṭimukko’ssa mārapāso*) means that the snare of Māra is fastened around his neck.
It was fastened and inserted. The second [sutta] is self-evident. 3.
Commentary on the Lokantagamanasutta: 116.

In the third [sutta], "of the world" (*lokassa*) means of the world-system (*cakkavāḷaloka*). "The end of the world" (*lokassa antaṃ*) means the end of the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāraloka*). "The dwelling" (*vihāraṃ*)...
"He will enter" means: "When I have entered the monastery, these bhikkhus will ask Ānanda about this summary;
he, having compared it with my omniscience, will explain it to them. Then I shall praise him;
and hearing my praise, the bhikkhus will approach Ānanda and listen to his words and place their trust in them."

Thinking, "They will conceive [such views], and that will lead to their harm and suffering for a long time," he did not analyze in detail the meaning of what had been spoken in brief; instead, he vanished from his seat and appeared in the Gandhakuṭī.
Thus it is said: "Having risen from his seat, he entered the vihāra."
"Commended by the Teacher" means praised by the Teacher. "By the wise" (*viññūnaṃ*): this genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental;
the meaning is "esteemed by wise fellow-celibates. "Is capable" (*pahoti*) means "is able. "Having passed even the root, having passed even the trunk":
the "pith" (*sāra*) may be located either in the root or in the trunk; [the phrase means] "having passed even that as well."
The meaning is: "In such a manner. "Possessing such attainment" means having such success; the meaning is "of this kind. "Having surpassed" means having transcended.
"Knowing he knows" means he knows precisely that which is to be known. "Seeing he sees" means he sees precisely that which is to be seen.
Or rather, unlike someone who grasps things erroneously—who, even though knowing, does not know, and even though seeing, does not see—it is not so [in this case].
The Blessed One. But the Blessed One knows what is to be known and sees what is to be seen.
Thus, in the sense of being the guide for vision, he is become like an eye (cakkhubhūta). In the sense of making things known, he is become like knowledge (ñāṇabhūta).

In the sense of having an unerring nature, or because he sets forth the Dhamma of the scriptures, or because he is the Dhamma consisting of those teachings uttered by speech after being reflected upon with the heart, he is become like the Dhamma (dhammabhūta). In the sense of being supreme, he is become like Brahma (brahmabhūta).
Alternatively, he is "become vision" (*cakkhubhūta*) because he has become [vision] itself, just like the eye. The meaning in these terms should be understood in this way.

Furthermore, he is a "speaker" (*vattā*) because he causes the Dhamma to proceed; he is a "proponent" (*pavattā*) because he sets it in motion. He is a "guide to the goal" (*atthassa ninnetā*) because of his capacity to demonstrate the goal by repeatedly extracting its significance.
He is a "giver of the Deathless" (*amatassa dātā*) because he teaches the practice for the attainment of the Deathless.
"To hold in high esteem" means that even one who causes [another] to request [something] again and again is said to hold it in high esteem.

Even one who speaks while making the matter difficult to understand—like someone drawing up sand from the foot of Mount Sineru while standing upon their own knowledge of the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa) of a trainee (sekha)—is indeed said to hold it in high esteem.
By saying "do not do so," it is meant: "Do not cause us to request again and again; speak to us by making it easy to understand."

"Whatever it may be for you" means "whatever belongs to you. "By means of the eye, friend, one perceives the world in the world and conceives of the world" means that the worldling, who has not abandoned views regarding the eye in the world, perceives and conceives of it as a "world" by way of the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*), and likewise by way of the world of world-systems (*cakkavāḷaloka*).
For apart from the twelve sense bases, such as the eye and so forth, that [conception] does not exist.
Either perception or conceit arises. Therefore it was said: "Friend, by means of the eye one is percipient of the world in the world, and conceited about the world.
And it is impossible to know, see, or reach an end to this world through its passing away.
However, in the sense of being subject to disintegration, there is the cessation of that very world—consisting of the eye and so forth—which is reckoned as Nibbāna.
It should be understood that until the end [of suffering] is reached, there can be no final termination of the suffering of saṃsāra.
Having thus answered the question, he now says: "Do not have any doubt because the question was asked by a disciple;
this Blessed One sits here having taken up the balance of omniscient knowledge. If you wish, go to him and be free from doubt."
Saying, "May you both go," he spoke the words beginning with "if they so desire.

"By these modes" means by these reasons: both by the reasons for the non-existence of a limit to the world-system (*cakkavāḷa-loka*) and by the reasons for reaching the limit of the world of formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*).
"By these phrases" means by these combinations of syllables. "By the phonemes" means by the individual letters.

"Paṇḍita" means endowed with wisdom (*paṇḍicca*). One is wise by virtue of four reasons: being skilled in the elements (*dhātu*), skilled in the sense-bases (*āyatana*), skilled in the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*), and skilled in what is a cause and what is not a cause.
"Mahāpañña" means endowed with great wisdom due to the capacity for receiving great meanings, great phenomena, great linguistic expressions, and great inspired insights.
"Yathā taṃ ānandena" means: it was said with reference to how Ānanda had explained it.
The meaning is: "Just as Ānanda has explained that, I too would explain it in exactly the same way. 4. Commentary on the *Kāmaguṇa Sutta* (The Discourse on the Strands of Sensual Pleasure)
117. In the fourth [case], "those which were mine" means those which were my own. "Formerly touched by the mind" means formerly experienced by consciousness.

"Therein my mind might frequently go" explains that it would arise on many occasions toward those five strands of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa) previously experienced—consisting of the three kinds of palaces, the three kinds of women, the various types of dances, and so forth—in which his mind frequently used to proceed.

Regarding the phrase "or in the present": here, at the time of his practice of striving, he shows that for six years he made the delightful objects of the five strands of sensual pleasure—consisting of what was seen, heard, and so forth—by means of flocks of birds and other creatures living in a forest thicket in full bloom; thus he demonstrates:
"Or such [objects] as these in the present would frequently arise. Regarding the phrase "or little in the future": in the future...

This shows that one might develop only a limited degree of restraint toward future objects of sensual pleasure by way of such [thoughts] as: “There will be a Buddha named Metteyya, a king named Saṅkha, and a royal capital named Ketumatī.

In this context, “by myself in my own person” means by me, being of a nature desiring my own welfare. “Heedfulness” refers to the practice of persistence regarding the mind in relation to the five strands of sensual pleasure.

Relinquishment (*avossagga*). Mindfulness (*sati*) means mindfulness that has grasped the object. Guarding (*ārakkha*) means: "This heedfulness (*appamāda*) and mindfulness must be made into a guard for the mind;
thus it was said by me. What is meant is: "These two states must be practiced for the sake of guarding.
Therefore, monks, those spheres (*āyatana*) should be known—because heedfulness is for the sake of guarding the mind.
And since there is nothing to be done through diligence or mindfulness once that sphere has been known, therefore that sphere must be known; the meaning is that the cause for this must be understood.
"The cessation of the six sense-bases" (saḷāyatananirodha) refers to Nibbāna; the meaning is that it was spoken with reference to that. For in Nibbāna...
The eye and so forth cease, and the perception of forms and so forth also cease. The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
5–6. Commentary on the *Sakkapañha-sutta* and others, §§118–119.

In the fifth [sutta], "in this very life" (*diṭṭheva dhamme*) means in this very personal existence (*attabhāva*). "They attain final Nibbāna" (*parinibbāyanti*) means by means of the Nibbāna of the defilements (*kilesaparinibbāna*).
"They attain final Nibbāna. "Consciousness is dependent on that" means that the consciousness of kamma is dependent on craving.
"Grasping at that" means the seizing of that; the meaning is that consciousness is accompanied by the grasping of craving.
The sixth [sutta] is self-evident. 7. Commentary on the Sāriputta-saddhivihārika-sutta.

120. "In the seventh [verse], 'will maintain' (*santānessati*) means he will connect [the mind]; he will not allow an interruption of his application (*yoga*) to occur. 8. Commentary on the *Rāhulovāda-sutta* 121.

In the eighth [verse], "conducive to the ripening of liberation" (*vimuttiparipācaniyā*) means those things which ripen liberation; thus they are "conducive to the ripening of liberation. "States" (*dhammā*) refers to fifteen states, which should be understood as being conducive to the purification of the faculties beginning with faith (*saddhindriya*). For this has been said:
“By avoiding persons who lack faith, by serving, associating with, and attending upon persons who have faith,
and by reflecting upon discourses that inspire confidence— in these three ways, the faculty of faith is purified.
By avoiding persons who are indolent, by serving, associating with, and attending upon persons who have aroused energy, and by reflecting upon the right efforts...”

The faculty of energy is purified by these three ways. By avoiding persons who are muddled in mindfulness, by associating with, befriending, and attending upon persons who are established in mindfulness, and by reflecting upon the foundations of mindfulness—by these three ways, the faculty of mindfulness is purified.
By avoiding persons who are unconcentrated, and by associating with persons who are concentrated...

For one who associates with [the wise], attends upon them, and reviews the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and liberations (vimokkha), the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) is purified through these three modes.

For one who avoids persons of poor wisdom, cultivates, associates with, and attends upon persons possessed of wisdom, and reviews the course of profound knowledge, the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) is purified through these three modes. Thus...

“By avoiding these five persons, by serving, associating with, and attending upon these five persons, and by reflecting upon these five discourses—in these fifteen ways, these five faculties are purified.
Furthermore, there are another fifteen states that ripen for liberation: the five faculties beginning with faith, and the perception of impermanence.

The perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of non-self in what is suffering, the perception of abandonment, and the perception of dispassion—these five perceptions conducive to penetration were taught to the Elder Meghiya as the five qualities beginning with having a virtuous friend.
At what time, then, did this thought occur to the Blessed One? At the time of the dawn watch, while surveying the world.

"Many thousands of deities": this refers to those deities who, together with the Venerable Rāhula while he was making his aspiration at the feet of the Blessed One Padumuttara during his time as the Nāga king Pālita,
also made their own aspirations— some deities dwelling on the earth, some dwelling in the atmosphere,
some belonging to the realm of the Four Great Kings, some in the world of the gods, and some in the Brahma-world.
They were reborn. On this day, however, they all gathered together in one place, in the Andhavana grove itself;

it is with reference to them that he said, "many thousands of deities. Regarding the term "Dhamma-eye" (*dhammacakkhu*), in this sutta it should be understood as referring to both the four paths and the four fruits. For among those deities, some were stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*).
Some were once-returners, some non-returners, and some were those whose taints were destroyed. Furthermore, there was no limit to the number of these deities by way of calculation.
The rest is clear everywhere.
9–10. Commentary on the Saṃyojanīyadhamma-sutta and others.
122–123. The ninth and tenth [chapters] are spoken by way of those who are capable of understanding when explained in terms of desirable objects.
The twelfth chapter, the Chapter on Worldly Qualities of Desire, is concluded.
13. The Chapter on Householders.
1–3. Commentary on the Vesālīsutta, etc. (124–126).
In the first [sutta] of the Householder Chapter, Ugga is the foremost among those who give choice gifts; he was thus designated by the Blessed One as being at the head of the ranks:
“Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples who give choice gifts, namely, the householder Ugga.”
[He] was set aside. The rest is exactly as stated in the other two [suttas] and in the third.
4–5. Commentary on the Bhāradvāja Sutta, etc., 127–128.
In the fourth [sutta], one who goes about seeking alms (*piṇḍa*) is called a *piṇḍola*. It is said that his wealth had completely perished.
He was a brahmin. Then, seeing the gain and honor received by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he went forth into homelessness after setting out for alms.
He wandered about carrying a large begging bowl;
with that bowl he drank rice-gruel until it was full, ate cakes until the bowl was full, and ate a meal until the bowl was full. Then, because of his habit of consuming expensive things—
They reported this to the Teacher. The Teacher did not permit him an alms-bowl bag. He would place his bowl upside down beneath his bed.
Even when placing it, he would set it down only after rubbing it; even when taking it up, he would pull it out only after rubbing it.
Over time, through that rubbing, it became worn away so that it could hold only as much as a single *nāḷika* measure of rice.
It happened. They then informed the Teacher, and the Teacher permitted him an alms-bowl and a bag for his robes.
At a later time, the Elder, having cultivated the development of the faculties, was established in the supreme fruit of Arahantship.
Thus, because he went forth for the sake of alms (*piṇḍa*), he was called *Piṇḍola*; and because of his clan, he was *Bhāradvāja*. Combining both together, he is called Piṇḍolabhāradvāja.
"He approached" means he approached surrounded by his high-ranking great ministers.

It is said that one day, after walking for alms in Sāvatthī and finishing his meal, the Elder thought, "I shall go through the air and sit for my midday rest in a cool place during the heat of the summer.
Having traveled thus, he entered a royal park called Udena’s Well (*udapāna*) located on the bank of the Ganges.
He sat for his midday rest at the foot of a certain tree, being fanned by a cool breeze from the water.
King Udena, having drunk the "great draught" for seven days, on the seventh day had the pleasure garden prepared;
then, accompanied by a great retinue, he went to the garden and lay down upon a bed spread out on an auspicious stone slab. To him—
A single female attendant sat massaging his feet. Gradually, the king fell asleep.
When he had fallen asleep, the female dancers thought, "He for whose sake we perform songs and the like has now entered sleep;
it is not proper to make a great noise at the time of sleep. Thus, each setting aside her own musical instrument, they departed for the park.
They departed. As they wandered about here and there eating various fruits and adorning themselves with flowers, they saw the Elder;
saying to one another, "Do not make a sound," they paid him homage and sat down.
The Elder preached a discourse on the Dhamma appropriate for them, beginning with the method: "Envy must be abandoned; stinginess must be dispelled."
That woman who had been sitting massaging the king’s feet stirred her feet and woke him up.
He asked, “Where have they gone? “What business do you have with them? They are sitting there surrounding a certain ascetic.
Enraged and seething like salt thrown onto a hot stove, the king stood up and said, “Those copper-colored ants...”
Thinking, "I will have him eat it," he went along and saw a nest of *tambaki* ants on an *asoka* tree.
He tried to pull it down with his hand, but was unable to grasp the branch. The ant-nest broke loose and fell upon the king's head;
his entire body became as if covered with a thick layer of salt and as if being consumed by flaming torches. The Elder perceived the king’s state of malice.

Having understood this, he leapt into the sky by means of his psychic power (*iddhi*). Those women also rose up, went into the presence of the king, and as if wiping his body, they fell one after another upon the ground;
seizing the ants that had fallen there, they threw them against his body, and all were pierced by the stings of their mouths:
"What is this? Other kings, upon seeing renunciants, pay them homage and ask questions..."
“They ask [about him], but this king has become desirous of having the nest of the ants broken upon his head.
Seeing his own transgression, the king summoned the park-keeper and asked: “Who is this renunciant?
Does he come here on other days as well? “Yes, Your Majesty,” he replied. “Inform me when he arrives here on such a day.”
The Elder also returned after only a few days and sat down at the foot of the tree.
Seeing him, the park-keeper thought, "This is a great gift for me," and went quickly to inform the king.
The king rose, silenced the sounds of conchs, drums, and other instruments, and went to the park together with his high-ranking ministers. Thus it is said: "He approached."
"Those who have not played with sensual pleasures" means those who have never previously engaged in the play of sensual desire; the meaning is that they have not enjoyed sensual pleasures.
"And they cause [the lineage] to endure" means they establish the tradition and cause it to continue for a long time.
"In mothers and mother-surrogates" means in those who are equal to a mother. For in the world, "mother," "sister," and "daughter"—these three are called objects of reverence.
He spoke thus to show that the mind could not find liberation when bound to a venerable object.

Then, seeing that his mind did not descend into that question, the Blessed One taught the meditation subject of the thirty-two aspects (*dvattiṃsākāra-kammaṭṭhāna*) for the purpose of binding the mind by means of attention to repulsiveness (*paṭikūla-manasikāra*).

"Those who have not developed the body" means those whose bodies, consisting of the five sense doors, have not been developed. "For them, that is difficult to do" means that for them, it is difficult to develop this meditation subject on the foul (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna).
Thus, seeing that his mind was not entering [into the object] even by this means, he spoke of the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara-sīla).
For when the mind is bound to the restraint of the sense faculties, it cannot find an opportunity to cause harm. Having heard this, the king—
Therein, with his mind immersed [in desire], he said, "O wonderful, Master Bhāradvāja!
and so forth. Regarding the phrases "with the body unguarded" and so on: one who plays with the hands and feet or twists the neck is said to have an unguarded body;
one who speaks various kinds of coarse words is said to have an unguarded speech; [and one who harbors] sensual thoughts and the like...

When one is engaged in discursive thought, it is said that one does not guard the mind. The meaning of the passage beginning with "with body guarded" should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated there.
"At that time, states of greed assailed me excessively" means that at that time, greed overcame me by prevailing over me.
"With mindfulness established" means with mindfulness directed to the body being well-established. Not...
“Maṃ tathā tasmiṃ samaye” means that at that time, greed does not arise in me as it did before;
this is the meaning. For the word *parisahanti*, the meaning is also simply “they arise. Thus, three bodies are mentioned in this sutta. How so?
For in the phrase “this very body,” the body born of karma (*karajakāya*) is mentioned; and in the phrase “the developed body,” [the mind-made body is mentioned].
Here, "body" refers to the body of the five sense-doors. In the phrase "with a guarded body," it refers to the physical body (copana-kāya);
the meaning is "bodily intimation" (kāya-viññatti). The fifth [section] is self-evident.
6. Commentary on the Ghosita Sutta.
129. Sixth: "And agreeable forms" means that agreeable forms exist. "And eye-consciousness" means that eye-consciousness exists.

"Contact to be experienced as pleasant" means the contact associated with eye-consciousness, which serves as a condition for pleasant feeling at the time of the impulsion (javana) by way of decisive support (upanissaya).
"Pleasant feeling" [arises] in dependence on one such contact by way of the impulsion process.
A pleasant feeling arises. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
Thus, twenty-three elements (*dhātu*) are explained in this sutta. How so? For here, the sensitivity of the eye is the eye-element (*cakkhudhātu*);
its object is the form-element (*rūpadhātu*); eye-consciousness is the consciousness-element (*viññāṇadhātu*); and that which is co-nascent with the eye-consciousness-element—
The three aggregates are the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*); thus, by way of four [elements] each in the five doors, there are twenty.
In the mind-door, the adverting consciousness is taken as the "mind-element" (*manodhātu*); both the object and the heart-base are the mental-object element;
and the mind-consciousness-element is that which is supported by the base. Thus, there are twenty-three. In this way, by way of these twenty-three elements...
This shows that the Blessed One has spoken of the diversity of the elements (*dhātunānatta*).
7–8. Commentary on the *Hāliddikāni-sutta* and others. 130–131.
In the seventh [sutta], regarding the phrase "he understands: 'this is agreeable, this is a woman,'" it refers to whatever agreeable form (*rūpa*) has been seen by him.

"It is thus" means he understands this very pleasant continuum in this way: "Dependent on eye-consciousness and a contact to be experienced as pleasant" refers both to the eye-consciousness itself and to that contact to be experienced as pleasant which, by way of the condition of decisive support,
the immediate condition, the contiguity condition, or the association condition, is a condition for pleasant feeling.
"Dependent upon [the mind], pleasant feeling arises. This same method applies everywhere.

Thus, in these two suttas, it should be understood that the mental-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) has the function of adverting, or else, being identical to the mind-element (*manodhātu*), it is spoken of by the name "mind-element. The eighth [sutta] is self-evident.
9. Commentary on the Lohicca Sutta.
132. In the ninth [case], in the city named Makkarakata, "in a forest hut" means in a separate hut built in the forest, not in a hut on the outskirts of a monastery.
"Young men" (māṇavaka) refers to those who were there even when they were old; because they were students (antevāsika), they are called "young men" even at an advanced age.
"They approached him" means that after learning their craft in the morning, they returned in the evening.
Thinking, "We shall fetch firewood for the teacher," they entered the forest and, while wandering about, approached that little hut.

"All around the hut" means all around, on every side of that hut. "Selayaka games" refers to the playful activities of walking back and forth here and there while holding one another's backs as they leap.
Regarding the passage beginning with *muṇḍakā*, it would have been appropriate to say "shaven ones, shaven ones" or "ascetics, ascetics";
however, they spoke thus—"shavelings, wretched ascetics"—in order to despise them. *Ibbhā* means householders. *Kaṇhā* means dark-skinned; the meaning is "black.
In the phrase *bandhupādāpaccā*, here *bandhu* refers to Brahmā. For Brahmins designate him as "grandfather" (*pitāmaha*). He is the progenitor (*apacca*) of the feet (*pādānam*).
“Born from the foot” means they were born from the back-foot of Brahmā; this is the intended meaning. It is said that their doctrine is:
“Brahmins emerged from the mouth of Brahmā, Kṣatriyas from his chest, Vaiśyas from his navel, Śūdras from his thighs, and ascetics (Śramaṇas) from his back-foot.
“Of the Bharatas” means of householders; for householders are called “Bharatas” because they support (bharanti) the kingdom.
...are so called. But these, speaking out of contempt, said, "The Bharatakas.

Having gone out from the monastery—[meaning] having tied up bundles of sticks in a delightful courtyard that was enclosed for the night-watch, strewn with sand as fine as silver plates, and having stirred up the sand while tossing them about, [they rubbed] hand against hand...

Taking his leaf-hut and wandering about, he thought: “These young men are playing excessively, crying out again and again, ‘These ones are honored by these Bharatas! These ones are honored by those Bharatas!
They do not even know that there are monks in the monastery; I shall show them that the monks are present. Having thus reflected, he emerged from the leaf-hut.

"Those who were supreme in virtue existed in former times"—this was said by him while recounting the virtues of the ancient brahmins, thinking that when the virtues of those possessing qualities are described, the absence of virtue in those lacking them will become evident. In this context, "supreme in virtue" means those for whom virtue is the eldest [quality].
For among them, virtue was the highest, not birth or lineage. "Those who remember what is ancient" refers to those who remember the ancient Dhamma of the brahmins.
They remember. Having overcome anger—having conquered anger—their gates became well-guarded and well-protected.
They delight in the Dhamma and in meditation—delighting in the tenfold path of wholesome action and in the eight meditative attainments (*jhānas*).
Having thus recounted the virtues of those of old, he now crushes the pride of the present-day brahmins, saying: "And these, having departed..."
He said, "We recite," and so forth. Therein, "having departed" (*vokkamitvā*) means having departed from these virtues.
Thinking "we recite" (*japāma*), that is, "we study," and thereby imagining themselves to be brahmins, they become intoxicated by this clan-name (*gotta*), thinking "we are brahmins.
Thus, they conduct themselves unevenly; the meaning is that they perform uneven bodily actions and so forth. "With various punishments" (*puthu-atta-daṇḍā*): *puthu*...
"Punishments for various offenses" (*puthuatta-daṇḍā*) means punishments for these various [offenses]; the sense is that diverse types of punishments have been taken up.

"Among those with craving and those free from craving" (*sataṇhātaṇhesu*) means among those who possess craving and those who do not. "For one who does not guard the doors, they are in vain" means that for one whose doors are unrestrained, all undertakings of vows become futile;
this he illustrates. How so? "Just as wealth obtained by a man in a dream"—just as in a dream...
The various kinds of wealth obtained by a man, such as gems, pearls, and so forth, become useless;
having awakened, he sees nothing at all—this is the meaning of "they become useless.
"Fasting" means not taking food for one or two days, and so on. "And lying on the bare ground" means on a patch of earth strewn with green grass.
"Sleeping, bathing at dawn, and the three Vedas": this means that having entered the water at dawn, there is both the act of bathing and the three Vedas.
"A rough hide, matted hair, and mud": this refers to the harsh sensation of the antelope skin (*ajinacamma*) as well as the mass of matted hair (*jaṭākalāpa*) and the mud;
"mud" here means dental plaque. "Mantras, virtue and observance, and austerity": this refers to the mantras and what is known as the "goat-virtue" (*ajasīla*) and "cow-virtue" (*gosīla*).
"Virtue" (*sīla*) refers to conduct known as *ajava* and *tagova*, and "vow" (*vata*). This, he says, is now the "austerity" (*tapo*) of the brahmins.

"Deceit and the crooked staff": the meaning is that deceit (*kohañña*)—which conceals faults like a hidden well—and the crooked staff (the sense being a crooked staff taken from one of the *udumbara*, *palāsa*, or *velu* trees). "Water-sprinklings" (*udakācamanāni*).
"And with water" refers to the cleansing of the face. "These are the colors of the brahmins" shows that these are the colors of the brahmins' requisites and belongings.

"The cultivation of some small thing" means the cultivation of some small thing has been performed; or this very reading [is correct], meaning it was performed for the sake of increasing material gain (*āmisakiñcikkha*).
Thus, having now crushed the pride of the brahmins, he spoke the words beginning with "and their minds were well-composed," while praising the ancient brahmins once again.

In this context, "well-composed" (*susamāhita*) shows that the minds of those brahmins were well-composed through access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) and absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*).
"Untroubled" (*akhila*) means gentle and not stiff. "That path leads to the attainment of Brahmā" (*so maggo brahmapattiyā*)—that...
He spoke thus while pointing out that this is the path to the supreme attainment, whereas as for you, what are you called, O brahmins?
"Have they come here? means: have they indeed arrived here? "Is intent upon" means:

through the influence of the defilements, one becomes intent, that is, greedy. "Is corrupted" means: through the influence of ill-will, the mind becomes putrid. "Of limited mind" means: due to the non-presence of mindfulness.

"With a defiled mind" means having a limited mind. "Liberation of mind" refers to the concentration of fruition (*phalasamādhi*). "Liberation by wisdom" refers to the wisdom of fruition (*phalapaññā*).
"With a measureless mind" means having a measureless mind due to a mind free from defilements through the presence of mindfulness.
10. Commentary on the *Verahaccāni Sutta*
133. In the tenth [chapter], at the city named Kāmaṇḍāyanti. *Yaggha* is a particle used for the purpose of exhortation. The remainder is self-evident.
The thirteenth chapter, the Section on Householders (Gahapativagga).
14. The Section on Devadaha (Devadahavagga).
1. Commentary on the Devadaha Sutta (134).

In the first chapter of the Devadaha Vagga, "Devadaha" is the name of a town derived in the neuter gender. "Manoramā" means those that delight the mind; the meaning is "agreeable. "Amanoramā" means disagreeable.
2. Commentary on the Khaṇa Sutta.
135. Regarding "In the second [section], those called 'possessing the six bases of contact'": there are no separate hells specifically named "possessing the six bases of contact.
For indeed, the designation of the six doors as bases of contact exists in all thirty-one great hells alike.

However, this was stated with reference to the great Avīci hell. As for "heavens," here too it is specifically the Tāvatiṃsa realm that is intended; [this refers to] the world of the devas of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
However, there is no lack of the designation of even a single sixfold sense-base (cha-phassāyatana) therein. What does this illustrate?

Because one is overwhelmed by absolute suffering in hell, and because one is overwhelmed by absolute pleasure in the world of the gods due to negligence arising from a preoccupation with constant play and delight, it is impossible to dwell in the holy life of the Path. The human world, however, is a mixture of pleasure and pain.
Right here, both the states of loss and the heavenly realms are made known. This is called the field of action for the holy life of the path, and it has been gained by you.
Therefore, these human aggregates that you have obtained are your gain;
and this human state that you have attained is the opportune moment, the right time for dwelling in the holy life. For it has been said by the ancients:
“This is the land of action; here the development of the path occurs.
Here there are many grounds for a sense of spiritual urgency.
Toward objects that inspire such urgency, [one should apply oneself].”
"Being filled with a sense of spiritual urgency, apply yourself thoroughly.

**Commentary on the First Discourse on Delighting in Form (Paṭhamarūpārāmasutta), Verse 136:** In the third verse, "delighting in form" (*rūpasammuditā*) means those who are delighted and gladdened by forms. "Suffering" (*dukkhā*) means those who are suffering. "Happiness" (*sukha*) refers to the happiness of Nibbāna.
"Sukhito" means happy. "Kevalā" means entire. "Yāvatatthīti vuccatī" means as much as is said to exist.
In the phrase "ete vo," the particle *vo* is merely an expletive. This is contrary to the world;
that vision which belongs to the wise who see thus is contrary to—that is, opposed to—the entire world. The world...
For while [fools] imagine the five aggregates to be permanent, pleasant, self, and beautiful, the wise [regard them] as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul.
"They say they are pleasant" means they speak of them as pleasant; "the wise know them as pleasant" means they understand them as pleasant. All this was said with reference to Nibbāna alone.
"Deluded herein" means deluded regarding this Nibbāna. "Ignorant" means fools. For all ninety-six types of sectarian teachers...
They have the perception, "We shall reach Nibbāna," yet they do not even know what this so-called "Nibbāna" is.

"Enveloped" (*nivutānaṃ*) means being shrouded and obstructed by the hindrances of the defilements (*kilesa-nīvaraṇa*). "Darkness for those who do not see" means that for those who do not see, there is darkness.
Why is it so for them? For it is for those who do not see either Nibbāna or the vision of Nibbāna that such darkness exists.
For fools, even Nibbāna and the vision of Nibbāna are perpetually shrouded in gloom and darkness—like the lunar disk obscured by a dark cloud, or like a bowl covered with a lid.
But for the wise, noble persons who see with the vision of wisdom, it is opened up, as if they were looking upon light. Thus, for the wise, it is revealed through the vision of their discernment.
Nirvana is as open as light. "They do not perceive it though it is near;

they are creatures unskilled in the Dhamma"—this means that nirvana is near because it is to be attained immediately after delimiting any particular portion within one's own body, such as the head-hairs or body-hairs, or from the cessation of one's own aggregates. Thus, it is near.
Even though they have entered the path, people who are unskilled in the dharma of what is the path and what is not the path—or in the dharma of the Four Noble Truths—do not know it.
"By those who have not entered Māra’s realm" means by those who have not entered the triple-world cycle, which is Māra’s dwelling place.
"Who indeed other than the noble ones? means: setting aside the noble ones, who else is worthy to know the state of Nibbāna? "They attain final Nibbāna through perfect knowledge."

Having understood correctly through the wisdom of arahantship, they immediately become free from taints (*anāsava*) and attain final nibbāna through the nibbāna of the defilements (*kilesaparinibbāna*).
Alternatively, having become free from taints through right knowledge, they attain final nibbāna at the end through the nibbāna of the aggregates (*khandhaparinibbāna*).

As one reflects on the cause, an evil conviction arises; that mode of grasping, thinking "there is a purpose," is called the acceptance of the contemplation of views (diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti).
