The Chapter on the Ocean. 1.
Commentary on the First Discourse on the Ocean.
228. In the first [sutta] of the *Samuddavagga*, it is said: "Bhikkhus, the eye is a sea for a person.
Whether in the sense of being difficult to fill or in the sense of being a gathering place (*samuddana*), it is the eye itself that is the sea.

For even from the earth up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma-world, the blue and other objects of perception that converge upon it cannot bring it to a state of fullness; thus, it is a sea in the sense of being difficult to fill.
It is an ocean (*samudda*). It is called an ocean in the sense of "surging" (*samuddati*), for it surges toward various objects such as blue forms and so forth;

and because it proceeds with a movement full of defilement, acting as the cause for the arising of afflictions as it flows on unrestrained, it is an ocean in the sense of "flowing together" (*samuddana*).
Its "impetus consisting of form" is like the immeasurable impetus of waves belonging to that ocean of the eye.
The immeasurable material force consisting of form should be understood by way of the objects of perception—blue and so forth—that flow together.

"He who endures that material force" means he who, by remaining in a state of equanimity, endures that material force which has flowed into the ocean of the eye—that is, he endures it without giving rise to the defilements of lust and so forth:
namely, lust for pleasant forms, hatred toward unpleasant ones, and delusion regarding those not looked upon with indifference.

In the phrases beginning with "with waves" (*sa-ūmi*), it is "with waves" because of the waves of the defilements (*kilesa*). It is "with whirlpools" (*sāvaṭṭa*) because of the whirlpools of the defilements. It is "with crocodiles" (*sagāha*) because of the crocodiles of the defilements.

It is "with sea-monsters" (*sarakkhasa*) because of the sea-monsters of the defilements. And by way of anger and distress, it is "with waves. For this has been said: "Bhikkhus, 'fear of waves' is a designation for anger and distress.
By way of the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), it is "with whirlpools. For this has been said: "'The whirlpool and the crocodile'..."
“Monks, this is a designation for these five strands of sensual pleasure. With reference to women, it is “with crocodiles” and “with rākṣasas.
For it has been said: “Monks, ‘crocodile-rākṣasa’ is a designation for a woman. The same method applies to the remaining sections as well.
“He has crossed over that which is fearful and difficult to traverse” means he has transcended that which is fearful due to the danger of waves and difficult to surmount.
“Gone to the end of the world” means he has reached the end of the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). “One who has gone beyond” is said to mean one who has gone to Nibbāna.
2–3. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Ocean, etc. (Suttas 229–230).
In the second [discourse], “the ocean” is called an ocean in the sense of being an ocean; it is so called in the sense of agitating (*kiledana*) and in the sense of moistening (*temana*).
It has been said. "For the most part" means excluding the noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*). "Heaped together" means soaked, drenched, and submerged.
"Become like a tangled skein," and so forth, has already been explained in detail below. "One who has abandoned death" means one who stands having abandoned the three kinds of death.
"Without substrate" means free from the three substrates (*upadhi*). "For the sake of non-becoming" means for the sake of *nibbāna*. He has confounded the King of Death.
Just as one does not know his destination, even so has he gone, having deluded the King of Death. The third [sutta] is exactly as described above. 4–6.

In the fourth, it exists in the sense of being unabandoned; therefore it says, "that is unabandoned. "Limited" means even [a tree] the size of a mountain...
"Unattractive form that does not provoke lust is called 'limited' (paritta)"; this shows that even such forms as these overwhelm his mind.
"What need is there to speak of those that are excessive?"—this means that what need is there to mention that an attractive object, a thing that provokes lust, overwhelms his mind?
And in this context, even something the size of a fingernail or the back of a fingernail, such as a gem or a pearl, if it is provocative of lust...
It should be understood that the object (*vatthu*) is indeed an excessive object (*adhimattārammaṇa*). "A young man" (*dahara*) and so forth—these three are merely synonyms for one another.
"He should strike" (*ābhindeyya*) means he should hit or break it. In the fifth [case], "both of those" (*tadubhayaṃ*) refers to both of them. The sixth is self-evident. 7.

234. In the seventh [section], "in many ways" means by means of many reasons. "Itipāyaṃ" means "this is thus. In this sutta, the characteristic of non-self is taught by way of impermanence.
8. Commentary on the Ādittapariyāya Sutta (The Fire Sermon) 235.

In the eighth [section], "grasping the sign according to the secondary characteristics" means grasping it by way of the secondary characteristics, such as: "The hands are beautiful; the feet are beautiful."
Grasping the sign (*nimittaggāha*). For "grasping the sign" is grasping by way of synthesis; "grasping the secondary characteristics" (*anubyañjanaggāha*) is grasping by way of analysis.

Grasping the sign is like a crocodile (*kumbhīla*), which seizes everything at once; grasping the secondary characteristics is like a bloodhound (*rattapāsa*), which analyzes and seizes each individual part, such as the hands and feet.
These two modes of grasping are found even within a single impulsive moment (*ekajavanavāra*), as well as across different impulsive moments (*nānājavanavāra*).
There is simply nothing that can be said [about it].
"Attached to the gratification of the sign" means bound and fettered by the gratification of the sign. "Consciousness" refers to kamma-consciousness.
"If one should pass away at that time" means that there is no one who passes away with a defiled mind.
It exists. For indeed, the passing away of all beings occurs by means of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) alone. However, he spoke thus in order to demonstrate the fear of the defilements;
or rather, it was stated in this way according to the specific occasion.

For when an object has come into the range of the eye-door, a mind that is lustful, or hateful, or deluded, having experienced the flavor of that object, enters the life-continuum. In the life-continuum...
Having stood [there], he undergoes death. At that time, for one who is dying, only two destinations are to be expected;
it is with reference to this occasion that this was said.
"Monks, this indeed is the danger"—namely, that one must experience this in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years.
"Perceiving it as suffering, I say thus: 'I wish to have my eyes anointed with a red-hot iron rod.
In this manner, the meaning is to be understood in all instances. 'With an iron spike' means with an iron needle.
'Completely rubbed' means having pierced both ear-holes and being rubbed against the ground."

On the third occasion, "completely destroyed" means it is completely destroyed by way of being cut and caused to fall through the act of inserting a nail-cutter, lifting [the object], and then striking it while moving it.
On the fourth occasion, "completely destroyed" means it is completely destroyed by way of cutting the root of the bond and causing it to fall.
On the fifth occasion, "completely destroyed" means having torn away the sensitive body-tissue with a sharp spear.
It is completely destroyed by falling away. Regarding the term "sword," it should be understood here as a large staff or club.

"Sleeping" refers to falling asleep after having lain down. By the phrase "one who has fallen under the sway of such thoughts might cause a schism in the Saṅgha," it is shown that these thoughts bring about evil karma extending even to the point of a schism in the Saṅgha. The rest here is self-evident.
9–10. Commentary on the First Simile of the Hands and Feet, etc. (Suttas 236–237).
In the ninth sutta, "when there are hands, monks," means when hands are present.

In the tenth, when it is said "there is not," this is stated according to the inclination of those who are capable of understanding. And in both of these cases, it is precisely the pleasure and pain that are the result [of kamma].

19. The Chapter on the Venomous Snake.
1. Commentary on the Simile of the Venomous Snake (Āsīvisopamasutta) 238.

Regarding the first [discourse] in the Chapter on the Venomous Snake: "He addressed the bhikkhus" means that he surrounded all those who were traveling alone, in pairs, in threes, in fours, or in fives, who lived in common, who were diligent and well-prepared, and who were engaged in the meditation subject of the characteristic of suffering.
He addressed the bhikkhus who were seated as practitioners of yoga. For this sutta was spoken with reference to the inclinations of individuals (*puggalajjhāsayena*).

It was spoken specifically concerning those individuals who are "to be known through elaboration" (*vipañcitaññū*), who dwell in various directions, and who are practitioners of the meditation subject on the characteristic of suffering (*dukkhalakkhaṇakammaṭṭhānika*);

these individuals, having arrived at the time of attendance, sat surrounding the Teacher. Even so, it applies to all four types of individuals, beginning with those "to be known through a brief indication" (*ugghaṭitaññū*).

This is indeed a condition for individuals. For a person of quick understanding (*ugghaṭitaññū*) will attain *arahantship* by the mere setting forth of the matrix (*mātikā*) of this discourse; a person who understands through elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*) by the detailed exposition of the matrix;
and a person to be guided (*neyyapuggala*) by reciting this very discourse, questioning it, attending to it wisely, and associating with and relying upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitta*).
"By attending upon [him], he will attain Arahantship. This discourse, which has words as its limit, will serve as a latent impression (*vāsanā*) for him in the future.

Having thus understood the beneficial nature of [the teaching] for all, the Blessed One—with great exertion, like one lifting Mount Sineru, like one expanding the sky, and like one shaking the Cakkavāḷa mountains—said: "Bhikkhus, just as..."
He began this Discourse on the Simile of the Venomous Snake.
Therein, "four venomous snakes" refers to these four: Kaṭṭhamukha, Pūtimukha, Aggimukha, and Satthamukha.
Of these, one bitten by Kaṭṭhamukha finds his entire body as rigid as a dry log, [especially] at the joints and limbs.
It remains as if pierced by an iron stake of extreme intensity.
When bitten by one with a putrid mouth, it reaches a state of putrefaction like a ripe, rotten jackfruit and oozes out; it becomes like water poured into a sieve.
When bitten by one with a fiery mouth, the entire body is consumed by flames and scattered like a handful of ashes or a handful of husks.
When one is bitten by the Seven-Faced [serpent], the entire body breaks apart;
it becomes like the site of a lightning strike or like a joint that has been gnawed by a great toothpick. Thus are the four venomous serpents classified according to their poison.

However, through the variations in the force of their poison, these become sixteen. For the Wood-Mouthed [serpent] is one whose poison is active upon being bitten, upon being seen, and upon being touched.
The *vātavisā* (wind-poison) is fourfold. For by it, whether bitten, seen, touched, or even if the body is merely struck by its wind, the body becomes stiff in the manner described.
The same method applies to the others as well. Thus, there are sixteen [types] by way of the transformations caused by the force of the poison.
Again, there are sixty-four by way of the designation of individuals (*puggalapaṇṇatti*). How so? First, among the *kaṭṭhamukhas*, there is the *daṭṭhavisa* (bitten-poison).

It is fourfold: one whose poison has entered but is not fierce, one whose poison is fierce but has not entered, one whose poison has both entered and is fierce, and one whose poison has neither entered nor is fierce.

Among these, that person whose poison is said to have "ascended quickly—like a fire from a well-kindled grass torch—taking hold of the eyes, taking hold of the shoulders, and taking hold of the head" [is the first].
It enters [the body] like the venom of a jewel-serpent (maṇisappa) and so forth;
however, by reciting a mantra, blowing into the ear, and striking with a staff, it descends and remains right at the place of the bite—this is called "one whose venom has arrived but is not fierce.
But as for that whose venom ascends slowly, at each stage where it has ascended, it is like cold water.

It is like the venom of water-snakes and the like; even after twelve years have passed, it manifests as boils, pustules, and so forth on the back of the ears, the back of the shoulders, and other parts; and when mantra-recitations and such are performed, it does not descend quickly.
This is called "fierce-venom" (*ghoravisa*), not "descended-venom" (*āgatavisa*). However, that whose venom ascends quickly but does not descend quickly—
Like the venom of the *aneḷaka* snake and others, this is both "venom that has reached" (*āgatavisa*) and "fierce venom" (*ghoravisa*).

However, that whose venom is mild—such as the venom of the *otāriya*, *nīla*, *sappa*, *dhamma*, *nisappa*, and so on, which enters with ease even when being introduced—is called "neither venom that has reached nor fierce venom.
By this method, those such as the "wood-mouthed" (*kaṭṭhamukha*) venomous snakes [are included] among the "putrid-mouthed" (*pūtimukha*) and others.
And those such as the venomous snakes are to be understood in this way. Thus, by way of the designation of individuals (*puggalapaṇṇatti*), there are sixty-four.
Among these, by dividing each one fourfold according to the mode of birth (*yoni*)—beginning with "nāgas born from eggs" and so forth—there are two hundred and fifty-six.
When those born from moisture and those born from heat are doubled, they become five hundred and twelve.
These, when doubled by way of those with desirable forms and those with undesirable forms, amount to twenty-four hundred and forty.
Furthermore, when condensed in reverse order from the path already traversed, they become only four, by way of the "charcoal-mouth" and so forth. Referring to these, the Blessed One said:
"Bhikkhus, it is just as if there were four venomous snakes. For these are taken here according to their families.

In this context, "venomous snakes" (*āsīvisa*) refers to those whose venom is poured out (*āsitta-visa*), those whose venom is eaten (*asita-visa*), and those whose venom is like a sword (*asi-sadisa-visa*).
"Those whose venom is poured out" means their venom is as if placed by being poured over the entire body;
the meaning is that their venom is poured upon both another's body and one's own. "Those whose venom is eaten" means whatever is eaten or consumed by them [becomes poisoned].
It becomes poison itself; therefore, because they have poison that is "eaten" (āsita), they are called *āsīvisa* (venomous snakes).

Alternatively, the word-meaning here should be understood as follows: they are *āsīvisa* because they possess poison (*visa*) similar to a sword (*asi*), which is sharp and capable of cutting through the vital organs.
They are *uggateja* because they possess intense heat (*teja*), that is, powerful heat. They are *ghoravisa* because their poison is difficult to suppress.
"They would speak thus" means they would speak in this way for the purpose of having [the snakes] cared for. For kings, having had venomous serpents caught, might say:
"We shall have such thieves bitten by these and then kill them; or, at the time of besieging a city, we shall throw them into the enemy army;
or, when unable to crush the enemy force, we shall eat fine food, mount excellent couches, and [use] these [snakes] against ourselves..."
"Having been bitten, we shall die according to our own will rather than falling into the power of our enemies," they say, and thus they cause venomous snakes to be kept.

Those who do not wish to kill the thief immediately, desiring instead that "he may die after having experienced suffering for a long time," speak to that man as follows: "O man, these are the four venomous snakes for you."
In that context, "from time to time" means at various times. "Should be laid down" means should be made to lie down.
"This or that person" refers to anyone among those such as Kaṭṭhamukha and others. "Whatever is to be done by you, good man, do that"—this should be understood as the speech of the attendant.
It is said that after having thus placed the venomous snake [upon him], he said, "This is your attendant."
They announced that four venomous snakes had been placed in four baskets. Then, one snake emerged and approached;
following the man’s right foot, it climbed up, coiled itself from the wrist of his right hand, and lay down at the base of his right ear with its hood spread, hissing.
Another snake followed the same path up his left foot and did likewise to his left hand.
Having coiled around him, he lay down making his hood at the base of the opening of the left ear, performing a "good birth.
The third emerged, climbed up toward the front, coiled around the belly, made his hood at the base of the throat, and lay down performing a "good birth.
The fourth climbed up along the back, coiled around the neck, and placed his hood upon the top of the head.
Having successfully brought about the birth, he lay down.

Thus, while the four venomous snakes had been born from the very hairs on his body, a servant attending to that man saw him and asked, "What have you obtained, sir? Thereupon, he replied, "These, sir, are in my hands..."

When it was said, "The King gave certain special ornaments: like bracelets on his arms, like armlets on his belly, like a waist-wrap garment, like earrings on his ears, like strings of pearls on his neck, and like a crest-ornament on his head," he replied:
"O blind fool, do not think thus: 'The King, being pleased with me, gave this...'"
“An ornament has been given,” he said. “You are a thief who has committed an offense against the king, and these four venomous snakes are difficult to tend and difficult to care for:
when one wishes to rise, another wishes to bathe; when one wishes to bathe, another wishes to eat;
and when one wishes to eat, another wishes to lie down. Among them, whichever one’s desire is not fulfilled—”
“Having bitten right there, it kills. “But, sir, if that is the case, is there any way to safety?
“Yes,” he would say, “once you have recognized the distracted state of the king’s men, fleeing is the way to safety;
do whatever must be done. Thus he would speak.

Having heard that, and seeing that the four venomous snakes were in a state of negligence and that the king’s men had withdrawn, he wrapped his right hand with his left, placed the hood upon the tip of his right ear, and slowly removed [the first snake] as if stroking the body of the sleeping venomous snake.
By this same method, he removed the remaining ones as well. Then, for them—
He would flee in fear. Then those venomous snakes, thinking, "This man has been given to us by our king," would come pursuing him.
It was with reference to this that it was said: "Then, monks, that man, terrified of the four venomous snakes...
would flee. But as that man was fleeing, looking back again and again at the path he had come by, the king thought, "That man has fled."
Having heard this, he would think, "Who indeed will be able to track him down and kill him?
While searching, he finds five men who are his own enemies and dispatches them, saying, "Go, track him down and kill him.
Then, his spies, having learned of that development, report it to him. He becomes even more terrified and flees. This is the meaning.
"Intending this, they would speak thus," and so forth, was said.
Regarding the sixth, the "intermediate murderer": "First he fled, eluding the venomous snakes that pursued him here and there;
now, pursued by five enemies, he flees even more effectively—it is not possible for him [to be caught] in this way."
"But it is possible to entice him; therefore, from his childhood, let a murderer who has been intimate with him—having eaten and drunk together with him—be sent as an intermediary.
When the ministers had spoken thus, the king sought out and dispatched a murderer to act as an intermediary.
Thus, as he was returning and looking back to see if the village were empty, he smelled the footprints again and again;
then, seeing four venomous snakes, five murderous enemies rushing toward him with speed, and a sixth murderer lurking in between, he said:
"Turn back, sir! Do not flee! You shall live happily, enjoying sensual pleasures together with your wife and children."
Seeing him approaching, fleeing here and there even more desperately, he might see a single hovel facing him in a border district—an empty village.
"He would enter it as empty" means that because it is devoid of wealth, grain, beds, chairs, and so forth, he would enter it as truly empty;
"tucchakaṃ" and "suññakaṃ" are synonyms for this very word. "He would touch it" means...
Thinking, "If there is water, I will drink; if there is food, I will eat," he would open the vessel, insert his hand inside, and feel about it.
Then they would say to him: "Having failed to obtain anything even in one of the six houses, [he stands] alone in the middle of the village."
There was a tree with dense shade; seeing a curved plank spread out there, he thought, "I shall sit here for now," and went there.
As he sat, fanned by a very gentle breeze, he experienced even that slight comfort as a state of peace and bliss.
Then, certain well-wishers who had learned of his situation from outside arrived and [spoke] thus to that man:
They would say: "Now, O man!"—that is, "O man, now.
"Robbers who plunder villages" refers to six village-plundering robbers who have come [thinking], "Whatever we shall obtain here, we will either seize it or cause it to be killed.
"A water-flood" means deep and wide water; for there may be water that is deep but not wide, or wide but not deep.
It is not called "the ocean" because it is deep and wide; rather, that is its very name.
It is "dangerous and fearful" by way of the four venomous snakes, the five assassins, the sixth person who moves among them, and the six village-destroying thieves.
It is "safe and fearless" due to the absence of those very same venomous snakes and so forth.
It would be secure, fearless, a magnificent and excellent park with abundant food and drink, resembling a city of the gods.
Yet there would be no boat for crossing; that is, there would be no boat established for crossing such that one could think, "By means of this boat we shall go from the near shore to the far shore.
Or there might be a bridge for crossing, meaning one of the following: a wooden bridge, a pedestrian bridge, or a cart bridge.
Or there might not even be a northern bridge. "He stands, O brahmin"—surely this one is not a brahmin. Why then did he call him a brahmin?
Because he has driven away (*bāhitattā*) so many adversaries; or, turning back from his teaching, he spoke thus in order to point out a single brahmin who had destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*).
But when he had thus crossed over, the four venomous serpents said: "Truly, you have not been caught by us; today you shall be roasted! (*murumurāya*)...
“Having consumed his life, we shall cast him away. The five adversaries thought, “Alas, you have not been captured by us!
Today, having surrounded you and cut your limbs one by one, we shall go before the king and receive a hundred or a thousand [pieces of gold].
The sixth, the intermediary, thought, “Alas, you have not been captured by me! Today, with a sword the color of crystal, I shall cut off your head.”
“Having obtained the position of commander-in-chief, may I enjoy prosperity. The six thieves thought, “Indeed, you have not been won over by us;
today, after having you subjected to various forms of torture, we shall cause much wealth to be brought [to us].
Being unable to descend into the water and unable to go further because they had angered the king’s command, they would wither away right there and die.
"Similes occur to me"—thus should the correlation of the similes be understood from the beginning:
for action (kamma) is to be regarded as like the king, and the worldling dependent on the cycle of existence (vaṭṭanissita puthujjana) is like the man who offended the king.
The four great elements (mahābhūta) are like the four venomous snakes; and the time when that king entrusted [the man] to the four venomous snakes is like...
At the very moment of rebirth-linking for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), it is at that time that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are assigned by karma.

Just as the time when one is told "flee! is like the time when the Teacher said to this bhikkhu: "Come out, O man, while these venomous snakes are in a state of negligence and the king's men are in a state of distraction; do whatever you must do, my good man."
Having explained the meditation subject of the great elements, it was said: "Become disenchanted with these four great elements and become dispassionate;

in this way you will be liberated from the cycle of existence. Having heard these words of the man who acted for his welfare, and taking advantage of the moment when the four venomous snakes were inattentive and the king’s men were absent, he went out and departed by whatever path led away.
Just as fleeing [from danger], this bhikkhu’s “fleeing by means of knowledge” consists in his fleeing after receiving a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from the Teacher,
for the sake of being liberated from the venomous snakes of the great elements (mahābhūta).
Now follows the discourse on the four great elements, which is a designation for these four great elements, beginning with "the earth element" and "the water element."
Furthermore, the discussion on the five aggregates of clinging and the discussion on the sense bases should be understood according to the method set forth in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
In this context, the earth element is to be regarded as like a wood-mouthed viper, while the remaining elements are like a putrid-mouthed snake, a fire-mouthed snake, and a weapon-mouthed snake.
For just as the entire body of one bitten by a wood-mouthed viper becomes rigid, so too...

Also by the provocation of the earth element. And just as [the wound] of one bitten by a "putrid-mouth" snake and the like oozes, burns, and festers, so too does it do by the provocation of the water element, the fire element, and the air element. Therefore the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā said:
"The body becomes rigid when bitten by a 'wood-mouth' snake."
Through the provocation of the earth element, he becomes like one with a mouth of wood.
Or, like one bitten by a putrid-mouthed creature, the body becomes putrid;
through the provocation of the water element, he becomes like one with a putrid mouth.
“The body becomes scorched, as if struck by the mouth of fire;
through the provocation of the fire element, it becomes like the mouth of fire itself.
The body becomes cut, as if struck by the edge of a blade.”
"Through the provocation of the air element, he becomes like one with a sword in his mouth.
Thus, in this regard, the similarity should first be understood in its specific sense.

In its general sense, however, [the similarity is established] by way of their abode, the transformation caused by the force of the poison, the grasping of harm, the difficulty of attending to them, and the difficulty of approaching them.
Their resemblance to venomous snakes should be understood through these reasons: because of ingratitude, because they act without distinction, and because they possess endless faults and calamities.
In this context, "habitat" means that for venomous snakes, the anthill is their habitat, and it is there that they dwell;
likewise, for the great elements, the body is their anthill-habitat. Furthermore, for venomous snakes, trees, hollows, thickets of grass and leaves, and places of refuse are also habitats.
For these [creatures] also dwell within it. Furthermore, for the great elements (*mahābhūta*), the body’s hollows, the body’s thickets, and the body’s refuse-heaps are their abodes (*āsaya*).
Thus, first of all, similarity should be understood by way of abode.

Regarding “by way of the transformation caused by the force of poison”: there are four types of venomous snakes (*āsīvisa*) according to their lineage, such as the *Kaṭṭhamukha* and others. Among them, each one—

When analyzed according to the transformation caused by poison, it is fourfold, beginning with that which is from being bitten. The great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are also fourfold, distinguished as earth and so forth according to their individual characteristics.
Herein, each one is fourfold according to its origination from kamma and so on.
Thus, similarity should be understood by way of the transformation caused by the force of poison.

"By way of grasping what is harmful": those who grasp at a venomous snake grasp five harmful things—they grasp a foul odor, they grasp impurity, they grasp disease, they grasp poison, and they grasp death.
Those who grasp at the great primary elements also grasp five harmful things—they grasp a foul odor, they grasp impurity, they grasp disease... [and so on].
They take on aging; they take on death. Therefore the ancients said:
“Whoever takes up a snake, A foul-smelling, thickly smeared, and most venomous one— These five things in the world Are taken up by those who delight in snakes.”
“Foul odor, impurity, disease, poison, and death as the fifth—
these five things are harmful, like a snake smeared with filth.
In the same way, unwholesome, blind, foolish worldlings [are likewise].”
“Five things that are harmful are grasped by those born into existence who delight in becoming:
foul odor, impurity, disease, old age, and death as the fifth.
These five are harmful, like snakes smeared with filth.”
Thus, their similarity should be understood by way of grasping what is harmful.
Regarding "difficult to attend upon": those venomous snakes are difficult to attend upon; when one wishes to rise, another wishes to bathe;
when that one wishes to bathe, another wishes to eat; and when that one wishes to eat, yet another wishes to lie down.

Among those [venomous snakes], whichever one’s intention is not fulfilled, that very snake bites and kills right there. However, these venomous snakes are even more difficult to treat than the *bhūta* spirits.

For when a medicine is administered for the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*), the water element (*āpodhātu*) becomes disturbed; and while he is administering medicine for that very same [element], the fire element (*tejodhātu*) becomes disturbed.
Thus, while medicine is being prepared for one element, another becomes disturbed.
Thus, its similarity [to a venomous snake] should be understood by way of being difficult to attend upon.
As for "difficult to approach": venomous snakes are indeed difficult to approach; seeing a venomous snake at the front of a house, they flee toward the back;
seeing one at the back, they flee toward the front; and seeing one in the middle of the house, they enter a room.
Having seen [the body] in the womb, they climb onto beds and chairs. The great primary elements (mahābhūtāni) are even more difficult to approach than that.
For when one is afflicted by such a disease as leprosy, the ears, nose, and so forth fall off after being cut away;
the body breaks apart and blue flies swarm around it; the stench of the body wafts from afar. Even while that person is being reviled and lamenting...
They are unable to approach him out of anger, nor out of compassion; instead, they cover their noses and spit, avoiding him from afar.

In this same way, the same point should be illustrated by other diseases such as fistula, abdominal tumors, and wind-diseases—those conditions that produce a state of loathsomeness and disgust. Thus, similarity should be understood by way of being difficult to approach.

Regarding "ungratefulness": for venomous snakes are ungrateful; even when being bathed, fed, honored with perfumes and garlands, and carried about in a basket, they seek only an opportunity to strike.
Wherever they find such an opportunity, they bite and kill right there. Even more ungrateful than venomous snakes are the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
For these have no sense of "having done" [any service]; even when being bathed with cool, warm, or pure water;
even when being honored with perfumes, garlands, and the like; even when being attended with soft garments, soft beds, soft gardens, and so forth;
and even when being fed choice food or given choice drink—they seek only an opportunity [to break free]. Wherever...

They find an opportunity, and having become provoked right there, they bring about ruin and disaster. Thus, similarity should be understood by way of ungratefulness. By way of acting without distinction:
for venomous snakes do not make distinctions such as "this one is a khattiya, or a brahmin, or a vessa, or a sudra, or a householder, or a renunciant";
rather, they bite and kill whoever happens to come near. So too with the great elements.
They make no distinction, thinking: "Is this a khattiya, a brahmin, a vessa, or a sudra; a householder or one gone forth;
a deva or a human; Māra or Brahmā; devoid of virtue or possessed of virtue?
For if shame were to arise in them at the thought, "This one is virtuous," then they would have felt shame toward the Tathāgata, the Supreme Person in the world with its devas.

...they would produce [shame]. Or, if shame were to arise in them by way of such considerations as, "This one is of great wisdom," "This one is of great psychic power," or "This one is a practitioner of the ascetic virtues (dhutavāda)," they would produce shame toward elders such as the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma.

Or, if fear were to arise in them [thinking], "This one is devoid of virtue, cruel, and stubborn," [then they would feel it] toward those who are devoid of virtue, cruel, and stubborn in the world including the devas.
They would fear Devadatta, the foremost of teachers, yet they feel neither shame nor fear;
instead, having become angry, they bring about some kind of ruin and calamity. In this way, their lack of distinction and their similarity should be understood.
Regarding "the limitlessness of faults and misfortunes": for there is no measure to the faults and misfortunes that arise depending upon a venomous snake.
For instance, having bitten them, these [beings] make them one-eyed, hunchbacked, paraplegic, or lame; thus they display immeasurable misfortunes.
Even when spirits are provoked, there is no misfortune they will not inflict, such as making one blind or otherwise impaired;
their harmful afflictions are immeasurable. In this way, their similarity [to other dangers] should be understood through their infinite faults and calamities.

Now, here the meditation subject should be explained by way of the four great elements up to the stage of Arahantship; that has already been explained in the *Visuddhimagga* in the "Description of the Definition of the Four Elements.

Regarding the passage, "Bhikkhus, 'five murderers and enemies' is a designation for the five aggregates of clinging," the similarity of the aggregates to murderers and enemies should be understood in two ways. For the aggregates [are like murderers] both to one another...
They strike one another, and when they exist, what is called "striking" is discerned. How so? First, material form strikes both material form and non-material form;
likewise, non-material form strikes both non-material form and material form. How?

For this earth element, when breaking up, breaks up only by taking the other three elements with it; the same principle applies to the water element and the others as well. Thus, first, material form...
It is form itself that destroys. However, when the aggregate of form breaks up, it breaks up only by taking along the four immaterial aggregates;
thus, form destroys the immaterial as well. When the aggregate of feeling breaks up, it breaks up only by taking along the aggregates of perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The same principle applies to the aggregate of perception and the others as well. Thus, the immaterial destroys only the immaterial.
At the moment of dissolution, however, the four immaterial aggregates (arūpakkhandhā), while dissolving, dissolve only by taking the physical basis (vatthurūpa) along with them;
thus, the immaterial destroys the material as well. In this way, they are "killers" (vadhakā) because they destroy one another.
Furthermore, where the aggregates exist, there occur cutting, breaking, killing, binding, and so forth, but not elsewhere. Thus...
When the aggregates exist, killing is discerned; thus they are called "killers.

Now, having divided the five aggregates into two sections by way of the material and the immaterial—or beginning with the discernment of the material or the mental—this meditation subject should be explained up to the stage of Arahantship; that has already been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.
“Bhikkhus, ‘the sixth assassin moving within, with sword raised’ is a designation for delight-and-lust (*nandī-rāga*).
Herein, the similarity of delight-and-lust to an assassin with sword raised should be understood in two ways: by its striking down the head of wisdom and by its dealing a blow from behind.
How so? For when a desirable object comes into range at the eye-door, that [delight-and-lust]...”
Dependent upon an object, greed arises; at that point, it is said to have "fallen upon the head of wisdom.
This same method applies to the ear-door and the other sense-doors as well. Thus, first of all, their similarity should be understood by way of causing the head of wisdom to fall.
Furthermore, this delight-and-lust leads one toward the four modes of birth, such as the egg-born and so forth. Based on that approach to birth, there are twenty-five great fears and thirty-two...
And since the instruments of torture have already arrived, his likeness to an executioner with sword raised should be understood from this method of thorough investigation.
Thus, even by way of delight-and-lust (*nandī-rāga*), the meditation subject has indeed been explained for a single bhikkhu. How so?
For this delight-and-lust is the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*); having defined it as the aggregate of mental formations, one should [then define] the feeling associated with it.
The aggregate of feeling, perception is the aggregate of perception, consciousness is the aggregate of consciousness, and their bases and objects are the aggregate of form;

thus one defines the five aggregates. Now, having defined those five aggregates by way of name-and-form, and having developed insight starting from the search for their conditions, he proceeds step by step...
"One attains arahantship"—thus has the meditation subject been explained by way of delight-and-lust (*nandī-rāga*).
The similarity of the six internal bases to an empty village is already found in the Canon itself.
Here, however, is the method for the meditation subject: just as those six thieves, having entered an empty village with six walls, [wandered] here and there...
Just as those wandering about find nothing and become indifferent to the village, even so the bhikkhu, searching by way of adherence within the six internal bases,
sees nothing to be grasped as "I" or "mine," and thus becomes indifferent to them. Thinking,
"I shall establish insight," he [examines] the eye-sensitivity and the rest by means of the meditation subject of derived form.
Having grasped them, he defines them thus: "This is the aggregate of form," and the mind-base as "the immaterial aggregate.

Thus, having defined all these by way of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and having sought their conditions and developed insight, he contemplates formations and gradually establishes himself in Arahantship. This is for one person.
The meditation subject has been explained for the bhikkhu up to the stage of arahantship.
Now, demonstrating the similarity between [certain people] and external village-robbers, he said: "Robbers who plunder villages," and so forth.
In that context, the locative case in *manāpāmanāpesu* is used in the sense of the instrumental; thus, the meaning is "by means of what is pleasant and unpleasant. Therein, regarding the robbers...
When they are plundering a village, five things occur: first, the thieves stand surrounding the village and set fire to it, producing a crackling sound;
then the people take their portable wealth and go outside;
then, for the sake of the goods, they engage in hand-to-hand combat with them; and some among them receive blows.
Some fall upon the spots where they were struck; as for the rest who remain unhurt, they bind them, lead them to their own dwelling place, bind them with ropes and the like, and enjoy them as slaves.
In this context, it is like village-robbers surrounding a village and setting fire to it: [the mind] [engages] with objects at the six doors.
When [the object] comes within range, the arising of the fever of defilement (*kilesa-pariḷāha*) should be understood as being like going outside having taken one's essential wealth in hand.
At that moment, abandoning wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*) and possessing unwholesome states is like reaching out and touching the goods for their sake;
it is the time of incurring offenses such as *dukkaṭa*, *dubbhāsita*, *pācittiya*, and *thullaccaya*, just like the moment of receiving a blow.
The time of committing a *saṅghādisesa* offense is like the moment after receiving a blow, when one has fallen at the site of the blow;

the time of having committed a *pārājika* offense and ceasing to be a recluse is like the time of taking the rest of the people, binding them, leading them to a place of residence, and using them for the enjoyment of a slave;

and the times of the minor, medium, and major precepts (*cūḷasīla*, *majjhimasīla*, *mahāsīla*) while depending on that very same object, even as everyone is looking on, are likewise [to be understood].
This is the time for breaking the training, renouncing it, and returning to the state of a householder.

In that regard, one should understand the mass of suffering pertaining to the present life as he supports his wife and children, and the mass of suffering pertaining to the future life as he is reborn in a state of deprivation after death.
These external sense bases are also taught for the purpose of a single bhikkhu’s meditation subject; for herein, visible forms and so forth—

The four derived forms (upādārūpa) are the tangible base (phoṭṭhabbāyatana), the three elements (dhātu), and those four [elements] together with the water element within the mental-object base (dhammāyatana).
By way of delimitation, there is the space element (ākāsadhātu); by way of lightness and so forth, there are lightness and the rest.
Thus, all this—both primary elements (bhūta) and derived form—is the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha). Feeling and the other [mental aggregates] have that as their object.
The four immaterial aggregates. Therein, "the aggregate of form is *rūpa*, and the four immaterial aggregates are *nāman*.
Having thus defined name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the meditation subject for one who practices according to the previous method is explained as extending up to Arahantship.
Regarding the term "floods" (*oghānaṃ*): here, the meaning of "flood" is that which is difficult to cross over. For these [floods]—having fulfilled the restraint of virtue [lead to] Arahantship...
Having generated the aspiration, “I shall reach [the further shore],” one must cross by relying on spiritual friends and applying oneself rightly;

for they are difficult to cross by whatever means. In the sense of being difficult to cross, they are called *ogha* (floods). These too are taught as the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) for a single bhikkhu.
For all four of these are, in fact, a single aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*). The rest [is explained] under craving with delight (*nandīrāga*).
It should be elaborated by applying it in the same manner as previously stated.

"This is a designation for personality" (sakkāya): for personality too is fraught with danger and peril due to the four great elements and so forth, just as the near shore of a river of water is due to venomous snakes and the like;
and that [personality] is [overcome] by a single bhikkhu solely through the means of his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
It has been explained. For *sakkāya* (the existing body) consists of the five aggregates of the three planes, and these, in brief, are simply name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Thus, having begun here with the definition of name-and-form, the meditation subject should be expanded in detail up to the stage of Arahantship.
This is a designation for Nibbāna; for Nibbāna is like the further shore of a great ocean of water, being free from the four great elements and so forth.
"Secure and fearless. This is a designation for the arousal of energy (*vīriyārambha*).

Here, taking "energy" (*vīriya*) to mean precisely the exertion (*vāyāma*) mentioned below in order to demonstrate the activity of the mind, he shows it. "Crossed over, gone to the further shore": having crossed over, he has reached the further shore.
In this regard, just as one standing on the near shore which is fraught with danger, desiring to cross the ocean of water, might stay for a few days—
One should not board the boat as if one were merely playing in the water after having prepared it slowly;
for by acting thus, one meets with disaster even before having boarded. In the same way, one who wishes to cross the ocean of defilements must not indulge in delay, thinking, "I am still young;
I will construct the raft of the Eightfold Path when I am old. Acting in this manner—
For even before reaching old age, one meets with destruction; and even having reached it, one is unable to do [anything].
However, having recollected the *Bhaddekaratta* and other such teachings, this raft of the Noble Path must be bound together with speed.
And just as one binding a raft requires the full use of both hands and feet—since one who has a lame foot or a crippled foot cannot do so—one must likewise possess all the necessary factors.
Just as one who cannot stand firm, or as those with webbed hands and the like who cannot grasp blades of grass or leaves,
so too for one binding this boat of the Noble Path, the perfection of both the feet of virtue and the hand of faith must be sought.
For indeed, one who is immoral, lacking faith, and thus unestablished in the Teaching— disbelieving in the practice— cannot [succeed] with the boat of the Noble Path.

One is able to bind it. Just as one who, though possessing complete hands and feet, is weak and afflicted by disease and thus unable to bind a raft—only one endowed with strength being able to do so—in the same way, one who possesses virtue and faith but is lazy and indolent is unable to bind this raft of the path;
only one who has aroused energy is able to do so. Therefore, one who desires to bind this [raft] must be energetic.

It must be so. Just as that man, having bound together a raft and standing on the bank, fixes his mind with the thought, "This ocean of water, a yojana wide, must be crossed by me through my own personal effort," even so the yogi, descending from the walking-path, resolves:
"Today, having crossed the ocean of defilements which are to be slain by the four paths, I shall establish myself in Arhatship."
The mind should be bound.
And just as that man, while crossing the ocean by means of a raft, having gone a distance of one *gāvuta* and then turning back to look, knows:
"I have passed one part; three parts remain," so too [he goes] another *gāvuta*.
Having gone and turned back to look, he knows, "I have passed two [measures], two remain.
Having gone another *gāvuta* and turned back to look, he knows, "I have passed three, one remains.
Having passed that as well and turned back to look, he knows, "All four of my storehouses have been passed," and he [sees] that raft with his foot.
Having stepped onto it, having cast himself toward the stream, and having crossed over, he stands on the bank.

In the same way, this bhikkhu, crossing the ocean of defilements by relying on the raft of the Noble Path, has crossed over the defilements to be abandoned by the first path via the path of stream-entry;
standing in the fruit immediately following that path, he turns back and looks with reviewing knowledge, [seeing]: "Of the defilements to be abandoned by the four paths..."
He knows: "One portion has been abandoned; the other three remain.

Again, in the same manner, having combined the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment and comprehending formations, he crosses over the defilements to be abandoned by the second path via the once-returning path.
Established in the fruit immediately following that path, he turns back with the knowledge of review and, looking back, [sees] those [defilements] to be abandoned by the four paths...
He knows: "Two portions of my defilements have been abandoned; the other two remain.

Again, likewise, having integrated the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment, and contemplating formations, he crosses over the defilements to be abandoned by the third path via the non-returning path (*anāgāmimagga*).
Established in the fruit immediately following that path, he turns back and looks with reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*), [seeing] those [defilements] to be abandoned by the four paths...
He knows: "Three portions of my defilements have been abandoned; one remains.

Then, likewise combining the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment, while contemplating formations, he crosses over the defilements to be abandoned by the fourth path via the path of arahantship.
Established in the fruit immediately following that path, he turns back and looks with reviewing knowledge, knowing: "All defilements have been abandoned by me."
Just as that man, having sent that raft adrift on the current, crossed over and stood on dry land, entered a city,
and having ascended to the top of a magnificent palace, sits with a one-pointed mind and a joyful heart, thinking,
"By this much indeed have I been delivered from misfortune"— whether on that very seat or elsewhere, such as at night-stations or day-stations, wherever it may be.
Seated, thinking, "By this much indeed have I been released from what was harmful," he enters the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) having Nibbāna as its object;
with a one-pointed mind and a joyful heart, he sits. Or rather, it is with reference to this that it was said:
"Crossed over, gone to the further shore, standing on dry land—this, monks, is a designation for an Arahant. Thus, first of all, are the various meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) here.
These have been explained; however, having synthesized them all, they should be shown as being one and the same.
Even when shown as one, they must be resolved specifically by way of the five aggregates.
How so? For herein, the four great elements are internal, while the five sense-bases are external.
The fifteen subtle forms within the sense base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) constitute a portion of the personal existence (*sakkāya*); this is the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*).

The sense base of mind (*manāyatana*), the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*), a portion of the sense base of mental phenomena, and the four floods (*ogha*)—these constitute a portion of the personal existence; these are the four immaterial aggregates (*arūpino khandhā*).
Therein, the aggregate of form is "form" (*rūpa*), and the four immaterial aggregates are "name" (*nāma*); this is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

For him, delight-and-lust (*nandī-rāga*), the flood of sense-desire (*kāmogha*), the flood of existence (*bhavogha*), a portion of the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*), and a portion of the personality-view (*sakkāya*)—these are the conditions.
Thus, one defines name-and-form as being with conditions.

Having defined name-and-form as being with conditions, and having applied the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*), he increases insight and, by comprehending formations (*saṅkhāra*), attains arahantship.
This is the gateway to liberation for a single bhikkhu.

Therein, the four great elements, the five aggregates of clinging, the eleven internal and external bases, a portion of the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*), the flood of views, the flood of ignorance, and a portion of the identity-view—this is the truth of suffering; while delight and lust constitute a portion of the base of mental phenomena.

The flood of sensual desire (*kāmogha*), the flood of existence (*bhavogha*), and a portion of identity-view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) constitute the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*); Nibbāna, designated as the further shore, is the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*);
and the Noble Path is the truth of the path (*maggasacca*). Therein, two truths are the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and two are the unrolling of the round (*vivaṭṭa*);
two are mundane (*lokiya*) and two are supramundane (*lokuttara*). Having thus analyzed the four truths in sixteen aspects and sixty thousand methods, [he taught them].
"Should be shown. At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred bhikkhus who were capable of understanding through detailed exposition (vipañcitaññū) were established in Arahatship.
Furthermore, this sutta was spoken by way of the characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa).
2. Commentary on the Rathopama-sutta (The Simile of the Chariot).
239. "Abounding in pleasure and joy" (sukhasomanassabahulo) means that one possesses both bodily pleasure (*kāyika-sukha*) and mental joy (*cetasika-somanassa*) in abundance;
thus, one is "abounding in pleasure and joy. "The basis for it has been undertaken" means that the cause for it is complete.
"For the destruction of the taints" (*āsavānaṃ khayāya*): here, "destruction of the taints" refers to the path of Arahatship; the meaning is "for the sake of that."
"A goad placed crosswise in the middle of the chariot" means a goad set across the center of the chariot. "Wherever he wishes" means whichever direction he desires.
"In whatever way he wishes" means whichever mode of travel he desires. "He would drive it forward" means he would impel it.
"He would drive it backward" means he would turn it back. "For protection" means for the purpose of guarding. "For restraint" means for the purpose of suppressing speed. "For taming" means...
"For the sake of freedom from attachment. "For the sake of peace" means for the sake of the pacification of the defilements (*kilesa*).

"In just this way" refers here to how, when an unskilled charioteer yokes untamed horses and drives the chariot along an uneven path, not only are the wheels broken, but also the axle and the horses' hooves, and he himself meets with ruin and disaster.

He reaches [the goal], yet he is not able to proceed according to his every desire; in the same way, a bhikkhu who does not guard the doors of the six sense faculties is not able to experience the pleasure of the ascetic life according to his every desire.
Just as a skilled charioteer, having yoked the horses to the reins, lowered the chariot onto level ground, and taken up the reins, [directs] the horses...
Just as one who, having established mindfulness on the nostrils, takes up a goad, and having made it effective, urges on [the elephant] by directing it with whatever movement is desired;
even so, a bhikkhu who guards the doors of the six sense faculties experiences whatever ascetic delight he desires in this teaching.
If he wishes to direct his knowledge toward the contemplation of impermanence, he directs it toward that.
Knowledge proceeds. This same method applies to the contemplation of suffering and so forth.
"One who knows the measure in food" means one who knows the proper amount regarding food. In this regard, there are two measures: the measure of receiving and the measure of consumption.
Regarding the measure of receiving, the authority of the donor should be understood; as for the object to be given...
One must know one’s own capacity; one must know one’s own strength.
For such a bhikkhu, if the gift to be given is abundant but the donor wishes to give little, he takes little according to the donor.
If the gift to be given is small but the donor wishes to give much, he takes little according to the gift. If the gift to be given is abundant and the donor...
Desiring to give much, he takes a measured amount after considering his own strength. Through that moderation in accepting,
he produces unarisen gain and makes what has arisen stable, just like the seven-year-old novice during the time of the righteous Great King Tissa.
It is said that they brought molasses for the king in five hundred carts. The king, thinking, "This is a pleasing gift;
I will not eat it without the noble ones," sent two hundred and fifty carts to the Mahāvihāra and went himself after having eaten his morning meal.
When the drum was struck, twelve thousand bhikkhus assembled. The king stood to one side.
Having summoned the monastery attendant, he said: "In the king's name, a single bowlful is the measure for alms;
give only after filling whatever vessel has been taken. If anyone standing in line to receive a portion does not take it, inform me.
Then, a certain great elder, having come from Cetiya Mountain with the intention of worshipping the Great Bodhi Tree and the Great Cetiya, [arrived at] the monastery.
As he was entering, seeing the monks taking sugar at the site of the great pavilion, he said to a novice who was coming up behind him, "Do you have no need for sugar?
"Yes, venerable sir, I have none," replied the novice. "We are exhausted from the journey;
even a single portion of food the size of a wood-apple would be enough for us. Then the novice brought out his bowl.
It was the elder’s turn according to the sequence of seniority. The monastery attendant, having filled the vessel to the brim, lifted it up;
the novice moved his finger. "Dear novice, for the alms-giving of royal families, filling the vessel is the standard measure;
take what fills the bowl. "Yes, lay follower, kings indeed have great expectations, but for our preceptor, this much alone is sufficient."
Having heard his words, the king asked, "What is the novice saying, sir? and went into his presence.
The monastery attendant said, "Master, the novice’s bowl is small; he does not take much. The king said, "Venerable sir, fill the bowl that has been brought and give it to him.
[The attendant replied,] "Great King, kings indeed have great expectations; [if you do so,] the bowl will be lifted up..."
“They wish to give [the fruit] only after filling [the bowl], but for our preceptor, this much alone will suffice. The king thought:
“This is a seven-year-old boy; even today, the scent of milk does not leave his mouth.
He does not say, ‘Having filled a jar or a basket, we shall eat it tomorrow or the day after. It is possible that he may enter the Buddha’s teaching.”
“...to take possession of,” he commanded his men, saying, “Sirs, I am pleased with the novice;
bring another two hundred and fifty wagons as well and give them to the Saṅgha.
Then one day, that same king, desiring to eat partridge meat, thought: “If I [were to have it] roasted on coals...”
Thinking, "I will tell another that I wish to eat partridge meat, and they will eradicate the partridges within a radius of a league," he spent three years enduring the arisen thirst.
Then, pus formed in his ears; unable to endure it any longer, he thought, "Is there anyone among us..."
“Is there a lay follower who is an attendant and a guardian of virtue? he asked. “Yes, Your Majesty, there is; one named Tissa guards his virtue without breach.
Then, wishing to test him, the king summoned him. He came, paid homage to the king, and stood before him.
Then the king said to him, “Are you, dear son, named Tissa? “Yes, Your Majesty,” he replied. “In that case, go,” the king said. As he was leaving—
Having gone and had a cock brought, he commanded a man: "Go, tell Tissa: 'Cook this with three broths and serve it to us.
He went and spoke accordingly. He replied: "Sir, if this were dead—as I understand it—then I would cook and serve it. But as for taking life..."
"I will not do it. He returned and reported this to the king.
The king sent him again, saying, "Go once more. He went and said, "Sir, attending upon a king is a heavy burden;
do not do this. It is still possible to undertake the precepts again; please cook [the meal]. Then Tissa said to him:
“Sir, for one single individual existence there is certainly but one death; I will not commit the taking of life.
He reported this again to the king. The king sent him a third time, and when he still would not accept, he had him summoned and questioned him in person.
He gave the same answer to the king. Then the king commanded his men: “This man [is a thorn] to the king...”
“He incurs my displeasure; go, place him in the executioner’s basket and cut off his head! But in private, she gave them this instruction:
“After you have led him away and intimidated him, place his head in the executioner’s basket and return to report it to me.”
Having laid him down in that executioner’s basket, they placed the cock in his hands.
He, placing it against his chest, released it, saying: "Dear one, I give my life to you; I take your life from you.
Go, free from fear. The cock, spreading its wings, flew through the air and alighted upon a banyan tree.
He hid himself. That place where safety was granted to the cock became known as Kukkuṭagiri.
When the king heard of this occurrence, he summoned the minister’s son, adorned him with all his ornaments, and said:
"Dear son, I tested you for this very purpose; for me, who desired to eat partridge meat, [three]..."
“Years have passed; will you be able to serve me after having purified [the meat] in three ways?
“That indeed is my work, Your Majesty,” he replied. Having departed and standing in the gateway, he saw a man entering early in the morning carrying three partridges.
He gave him two kahāpaṇas, took the partridges, and purified them.
Having perfumed it with cumin and other spices and cooked it until well-done over glowing coals, he presented it to the king.

While seated on the royal couch of state upon the great terrace, the king took one piece, cut off a small portion, and placed it in his mouth; at that very moment, it pervaded his seventeen thousand channels.
At that time, recollecting the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, [the king thought]: "A world-ruling monarch such as I [should not eat] partridge meat..."
“Desiring to eat, he did not receive it for three years; while the Saṅgha of monks was not cooking, how could he have obtained it?
At the very moment the sugar-candy was placed in his mouth, he threw it to the ground. The minister’s son fell upon his knees and caught it with his mouth.
The king said, “Go away, dear one! I know your innocence; for this reason, by me...”
Having said, "This has been discarded," he told him, "Keep the remainder protected just as it is.
On the following day, the elder who was a court attendant entered for alms. When the minister’s son saw him, he took his bowl and brought him into the royal palace.
Another elder who had gone forth in old age followed behind the elder like an attendant monk.
He entered. The Elder thought, "This must be the monk summoned by the king," and became negligent.
The minister’s son also thought, "This must be the Elder’s attendant," and fell into negligence. After seating them both, they gave them rice gruel.
When the gruel had been drunk, the king brought forward two partridges. The Elder took one, and the other also took one. The king said, "There is a portion remaining..."
"It is not proper to eat without having asked for permission," he said, and asked the Great Elder. The Elder covered his hand [to signal consent], and the elder monk accepted.
The King, feeling dissatisfied, followed the Elder as he departed with his bowl after finishing his meal, and said:
"Venerable Sir, it is proper for those coming from a family home to come taking a monk who has learned the proper conduct."
At that moment, the Elder realized, "This man has not been summoned by the king.
On the following day, he entered taking his attendant novice with him. Then, as before, the king presented him with a partridge after he had drunk his rice gruel.
The Elder took one [portion], but the novice, flicking his finger, had it cut in the middle so that there was only a single portion.
He took it. The king presented that portion to the Great Elder. The Great Elder covered his hand, and the novice did likewise.
Sitting not far away, the king ate it, cutting it into small pieces, and said, "By virtue of the training we have undertaken, we were able to eat one and a half partridges.
As soon as he had finished eating the meat, pus flowed from his ears.
He went out. Then, having rinsed his mouth, he approached the novice and said, "I am pleased, dear one;
I give you eight regular meals. [The novice replied,] "Great King, I give them to my preceptor. "I will give you another eight," [the king said]. "Those I give to our teacher," [he replied].
"I will give you yet another eight," [the king said]. "Those I give to those who share my preceptor," [he replied].
"I give. "I give another eight as well. "I give those to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. "I give another eight as well. The novice accepted.
Thus, one who understands the measure of acceptance not only brings about unarisen gain but also makes that which has arisen stable.
This is called the measure of acceptance. In this regard, the measure of use is as follows:
The purpose of reflection is that the purpose of consuming food only after one has reflected—thinking, "I eat this food for this specific purpose"—is indeed the measure of moderate consumption;
that alone is intended here. For this very reason, he said, "with wise reflection," and so forth;
however, the other [type of reflection] is also permissible.

Regarding "the lion’s posture" (*sīhaseyyā*): here there are four postures—the posture of those who enjoy sensual pleasures, the posture of the departed, the lion’s posture, and the posture of the Tathāgata.
Among these, "for the most part, monks, those who enjoy sensual pleasures lie on their left side"—this is the posture of those who enjoy sensual pleasures;
for among them, there is generally no such thing as lying on the right side.

“Monks, for the most part, the hungry ghosts (petas) lie on their backs”—this is the *peta*-posture. Because they have little flesh and blood, being merely a mass of knotted bones, the hungry ghosts are unable to lie on one side; they lie only on their backs.
“Monks, for the most part, Sīha, the king of beasts, lies on his right side, having tucked his tail between his thighs”—this is the *sīha*-posture.
Because he abounds in vital energy (*tejas*), Sīha, the king of beasts, [places] his two forefeet together...
Having placed one hind foot in one spot and inserted the tail between the thighs, and having observed the positions where the toes of the front and hind feet rest,
he lies down placing his head upon the tops of his two front feet; even when waking after sleeping for a whole day,
he wakes without alarm, but rather lifts his head [to observe] the front feet and so forth.

He observes the place where he stands. If he finds that he has left some spot, he becomes displeased, thinking, "This is not worthy of your birth and your courageous nature," and lies down right there;
he does not set out for his almsround. But if he finds that he has not left it, he thinks, "This is worthy of your birth and your courageous nature."
Joyful and elated, he rises, stretches like a lion, shakes his shaggy mane, roars three times the lion’s roar, and sets out for his almsround.

However, the reclining posture of the fourth jhāna is called the “Tathāgata-posture. Among these, it is the lion’s posture that is intended here; for this is indeed called the supreme posture because its physical demeanor is suffused with fiery energy (*tejo*).
"Foot upon foot" means placing the left foot upon the right foot. "Having placed over" (*accādhāya*) means having placed it slightly beyond; that is, having set it down with a small overlap.
For if the ankle were to rub against the ankle, or the knee against the knee, pain would arise frequently, the mind would not become one-pointed, and the bed would become uncomfortable.
Therefore, one should place it so that they do not touch, having overlapped them accordingly.
When [the body] is thus placed, no painful sensation arises, the mind becomes one-pointed, and the bed becomes comfortable. Therefore, he prepares his bed in this way.
"Mindful and clearly comprehending" means being endowed with both mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sampajañña*). How is it that while sleeping he is mindful and clearly comprehending?
By not abandoning mindfulness and clear comprehension. For throughout the day and all through the night, he remains thus.
Having purified his mind of obstructive states, at the end of the first watch of the night, he descends from the walking path and washes his feet;
even while washing them, he does not abandon his basic meditation subject. Without abandoning it, he opens the door, sits on his bed, and falls asleep without abandoning it.
Upon waking, however, he wakes up having grasped his basic meditation subject once again.
In this way, even while falling asleep, he remains mindful and clearly comprehending. However, they did not approve of the view that this constitutes the "element of knowledge.

Rather, having purified his mind in the manner already described, at the conclusion of the first watch of the night, thinking, "I shall rest my acquired body by means of sleep," he descends from the walking path and washes his feet without abandoning his primary meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), [and likewise] the door.

If, however, having sat on a couch and abandoned his primary meditation subject (*mūlakammaṭṭhāna*), he falls asleep while gradually reflecting on his lodging, thinking, "Only aggregates strike against aggregates; only elements strike against elements," then upon waking, he wakes up having taken up that very primary meditation subject.
Thus, even while falling asleep, he remains mindful and clearly comprehending (*sato sampajāno*).
It should be understood that [the name] "becomes" is used.
Thus, in this sutta, only insight (vipassanā) in its prior stage consisting of three factors has been explained.
Without, however, resting content with just this much, the bhikkhu should unify those very same faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment, and further develop insight.
"He attains arahantship. In this manner, the teaching should be expounded up to the stage of arahantship.
3. Commentary on the Kummopama Sutta (The Simile of the Turtle).
240. In the third [simile], "turtle" refers to a bony turtle; "tortoise" is a synonym for the same. "On the bank of a river" means by a river.
On the bank. "Intent upon his range" means being eager, striving, and bound to that [range] with the thought, "If I obtain some fruit or other, I shall eat it.
"Having put together" means having placed them inside as if in a casket. "He remains" means he stays there.
"They put together" means they place them together while setting them down. This is what is meant: just as a tortoise [withdraws its limbs].
Just as one cooking [food] in his own skull does not give the jackal an opening and the jackal cannot overpower him, so too,
a bhikkhu who contains his own mental reflections within the skull of his own object does not give the Māra of the defilements an opening, and Māra cannot overpower him.
"Independent" means independent of the supports of craving and views. "Not harming another" means not causing harm to any other person.
"Parinibbūta" means parinibbūta by means of the parinibbāna of the defilements.
"One would not reproach anyone" means that one would not reproach any other person for failure in virtue, failure in conduct, or out of a desire to exalt oneself at the expense of another.
Or, rather than wishing to disparage them, one should not revile them; instead, having established five qualities within oneself, one should think:
"I will speak at the proper time, not at an improper time; I will speak what is true, not what is false; I will speak gently, not harshly;
I will speak what is beneficial, not what is unbeneficial; I will speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not..."
"Free from faults"—thus he dwells with a mind established in the nature of uplifting.
4. Commentary on the First Simile of the Log: 241.
"He saw"—sitting upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared on the bank of the Ganges, he saw. "Being carried away"—means...
Having been cut into four pieces and placed within a mountain range, it became thoroughly dried by wind and sun;
then, when a rain-cloud poured down, it was submerged by the water and gradually fell into the current of the river Gaṅgā, being carried away by that stream.
He addressed the bhikkhus: "Having made a comparison with this log of wood, [consider] one who has gone forth out of faith in my teaching..."
“I shall show you a son of good family,” he addressed [the king] out of a desire to teach the Dhamma. As for the phrase,

“that great log of wood being carried away by the current of the river Gaṅgā,” this was begun in order to point out the eight obstacles that prevent one who has entered the stream— being free from the eight defects— from reaching the ocean.
In this regard, its freedom from eight defects should be understood as follows: Suppose a single log of wood grows on a mountainside not far from the river Ganges;
entwined by various creepers, it withers into yellow leaves and, being devoured by termites and other insects, comes to non-existence right there at that spot.
But suppose that same log of wood descends into the Ganges and, at its bends...
Having reached the ocean, it cannot shine upon the jewel-colored surface of the waves.
Another tree grows on the bank of the Ganges with its roots outside and branches inside;
although from time to time it touches the water with its drooping branches, because its roots are outside, it merely plays among the bends of the river after having descended into the Ganges.
Having reached the ocean, it cannot shine upon the surface of the waves, which have the color of jewels.
Another tree was born in the middle of the Ganges; because its roots were firm, it was well-established.

Its branches that extended outward were entwined by various creepers. Because of its firm roots and because it was bound by creepers on the outside, even this tree, having descended into the Ganges... [and so forth].
One does not obtain it. Another, covered by sand right where it fell, reaches a state of putrefaction; this one also, having entered the Ganges... [as before] ...does not obtain it.

Another, because it grew between two rocks, stands motionless as if firmly embedded; it splits every incoming stream of water into two; this one, because it is well-established between the rocks, having entered the Ganges... [as before] ...does not obtain it.
Another stands bound by creepers, filling the sky in an open space.

Having waited for one or two years, it becomes moistened once or twice when the great flood arrives. This too, because of its standing filling the sky and its being moistened only once or twice after the lapse of one or two years, [is called a "tree"].
And having descended into the Ganges... [as before] ...he does not find it.
Furthermore, another tree born on an island in the middle of the Ganges—with soft trunk and branches—lay with the current when the flood arrived;
when the water had subsided, it raised its head and stood as if dancing. For whose sake the ocean thus [treated] the Ganges... [as before].
She spoke as if she were angry, saying, "Lady Gaṅgā, you bring me various kinds of timber such as sandalwood, sara-wood, and laḷa-wood, yet you do not bring a block of wood!
She replied, "This is easily obtained, Your Majesty; I shall know on the next occasion.
On the next occasion, she came as if being embraced by water the color of copper. He likewise lay down with the current, and—
When the water has receded, he stands as if dancing with his head held high. Because of his own pliancy, he descends into the Ganges...
[and so on] ...but does not find it.
Another falls across the river Ganges and, covered by the sand, becomes like a bridge for many.
Once born there, bamboos, reeds, *karañja* trees, *kakudha* trees, and the like float toward both banks and become stuck right there.
Likewise, various kinds of shrubs being carried along, as well as the corpses of humans, pigs, dogs, elephants, horses, and so forth, also become stuck right there.
Even the Great Ganges, upon striking it, breaks apart and flows in two directions; even fish, turtles, crocodiles, *makara* monsters, and the like [are likewise affected].
They take up residence right there. But this [log], having fallen across [the river] and become a resource for the great multitude, descends into the Ganges;
though it sports in its bends, once it reaches the ocean, it cannot shine upon the surface of the waves, which have the color of jewels.
Thus, because he is free from these eight defects, the Blessed One [compares himself] to another log that has entered the stream.
In order to show the eight dangers that obstruct the attainment of the ocean, he said: "This great log was being carried away by the current of the river Ganges," and so forth.
In this context, "it will not run aground on the shore" means it will not come ashore.
"It will not be seized by men" means that those crossing in a raft, seeing it and thinking, "What a great log this is! [will not seize it].
Having gone there, humans will not take it for the sake of rafters and such;
nor will non-humans take it, thinking, "This is precious sandalwood essence; we shall place it at the door of our mansion.
In this way, the application of the simile should be understood together with the eight external defects.

One should understand that a person possessed of wrong view— such as the thought "there is no gift"— is like a log grown on a mountainside not far from the Ganges, which, being eaten away right there by termites and other insects, has reached a state of non-existence. For such a person,
having distanced themselves from the Dispensation, fails to descend upon the Noble Path and remains seated upon the raft of concentration.
He is unable to reach the ocean of Nibbāna.
Such a person—a monastic householder whose ties to the household life are unsevered—should be regarded as one who has grown up with roots outside and branches inside on the bank of the Ganges.
