For he thinks, "The mind is indeed unmoored; even while saying 'I am a monastic,' one remains a householder."
“Even while saying, ‘I am a householder,’ one becomes a recluse. Who knows what will happen?
Even one who goes forth in old age does not relinquish the bonds of a householder. For those who go forth in old age, there is no such thing as success.
If he obtains a robe, it is one with frayed edges or worn and discolored. As for his lodging—
At the edge of the monastery, he reached a leaf-hut or a pavilion.
Even while wandering for alms, he had to walk behind his grandchildren and children, and he had to sit on the outskirts.
Because of this, he became distressed and dejected, shedding tears as he thought, "I have wealth inherited from my family; would it be permissible to live by consuming that?"

Having reflected thus, he asked a certain Vinaya-master: "Venerable teacher, is it permissible to take what belongs to oneself and eat it, or is it not permissible? "There is no fault in this; it is permissible," he replied.
He then took several of his own disciples—monks who were difficult to speak with and of bad conduct—and at the time of evening, having gone into the village, [stood] in the middle of the village.
Standing there, he summoned the village folk and asked, "To whom shall you give the income arising from our enterprise? They replied, "Venerable sir, you have gone forth;
to whom shall we give it? He asked, "Is it not permissible for those who have gone forth to possess what belongs to themselves?
Then, taking spades and baskets, they performed various tasks such as binding the boundaries of fields and cultivating diverse kinds of grain and vegetables.
Having gathered various fruits during the winter, summer, and rainy seasons, he lives as a "monk-householder" (samaṇakuṭumbika), eating whatever he desires after having them cooked.
He has no wife other than a single female attendant who attends to his feet along with a young boy with five tufts of hair on his head.
Although this person touches water with the drooping branches [of his tree], [he does not actually bathe].
Like a tree with branches growing inward, it provides physical harmony for monks in the courtyard of the shrine, the courtyard of the Bodhi tree,

and other such places; however, because its roots are turned outward due to the unsevered bonds of household life, one cannot descend to the Noble Path and sit upon the raft of concentration to reach the ocean of Nibbāna.
One should see the person of broken livelihood as one who, though born in the midst of the Ganges, lives supported by the Saṅgha like a tree with crooked branches bound by external creepers.

A certain person, even when abandoning the bonds of a householder and going forth, does not obtain the going-forth in a suitable place; for this so-called "going-forth" is like the taking up of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). Just as people [seek a place] where—
They take rebirth and learn the very conduct of those families; likewise, monks who go forth in the presence of certain teachers adopt the conduct of those very teachers.

Therefore, some, having gone forth in an unsuitable place, become excluded from exhortation, instruction, recitation, interrogation, and so forth, and from early morning they take a water-pot and go to a watering-place [without attending] to their preceptors and teachers.
For the sake of food, he would carry his bowl on his shoulder and go to the dining hall;
he engaged in various games with the ill-behaved novices and lived in close association with the monastery boys.
During his time as a young bhikkhu, he shared the property of the Saṅgha with other young bhikkhus and monastery attendants who were suited to him.
Having gone there, [they said], "This property of the Saṅgha was received from King Asukaraṇa by those whose taints were exhausted;
you must not give this or that to the Saṅgha, for neither the king nor the royal ministers will be pleased upon hearing of your conduct.
Come now, take these spades and baskets and work on the lower embankments of the reservoir. Thus they had them take up their spades and baskets at the lower sluice-gates of the tank.

Having had the duties that ought to be performed carried out and having caused much food—both grain and cooked—to be brought into the monastery, he has the monastery attendants announce to the Saṅgha his own state of service.
The Saṅgha, thinking, "This youth has been very helpful;
give him a hundred or two hundred [pieces of cloth]," causes it to be given. Thus, increasing through the property of the Saṅgha from this side and that, he [grows] externally...
Bound by the twenty-one kinds of improper search, one who has descended onto the Noble Path and sits upon the raft of concentration is unable to reach the ocean of Nibbāna;
like a tree that has rotted away while being buried in sand at the very spot where it fell, such a person is overcome by indolence and gluttony.

It should be understood thus: with reference to such a person—one who has an eye for material gain, who is greedy for requisites, who has abandoned the duties toward teachers and preceptors, and who is devoid of recitation, interrogation, and wise attention—it is said in terms of meaning that there are five hindrances.
[They think: "O, to whom shall we go? Then, having arisen, sloth and torpor speak thus: "Do you not see?"
"This lazy person, residing in such-and-such a monastery, having gone to such-and-such a village and swallowed rice gruel at a gruel-stand,
cakes at a cake-stand, and alms-food at a meal-stand, returns to the monastery and, having cast aside all his observances and being devoid of recitation and other duties,
makes room for me as he approaches his bed."
Then the hindrance of sensual desire arose and said: "Sir, when you have made room for yourself, it is as if you have made room for me;
having just now fallen asleep and awakened still stained by defilements, you will now give rise to thoughts of sensual desire. Then the hindrance of ill will arose and said:
"When you have made room for yourselves, it is as if you have made room for me. Having just now fallen asleep and arisen..."

“Being told, ‘Perform your duties and services,’ he will wander about with his eyes popped out, uttering various kinds of harsh words such as, ‘Sir, these people are busy with our affairs instead of doing their own work! Then, the hindrance of restlessness arises, saying:
‘When you have made space for yourselves, it is as if you have made it for me; one who is called lazy is like a mass of fire fanned by the wind.’”
“...is as if agitated. Then the hindrance of restlessness and remorse arose and said: “When you have been given leave, it is as if I have been given leave;

one who is lazy is indeed characterized by restlessness and remorse, for he conceives the perception of what is allowable in what is unallowable, and the perception of what is unallowable in what is allowable.
Then the hindrance of doubt arose and said: “When you have been given leave...”
"Once it is done by me, it is as if it were already done. For such a person gives rise to great doubt regarding eight matters.
Thus, the five hindrances—characterized by laziness and greed—overwhelm and seize one, just as fierce dogs and other beasts of prey would seize an old bull with its horns cut off.
Having entered the stream of the Noble Path and sitting upon the raft of concentration, he [reaches] the ocean of Nibbāna.
He is unable to reach it.
A follower of wrong views (*diṭṭhigatika*) should be understood as one who stands having generated a view, like a tree whose roots are fixed between two rocks.
For he [holds that] "form exists in the formless realm, and consciousness functions in the non-percipient realm."
One who says, "The supramundane path consists of many moments of consciousness, while the underlying tendency (anusaya) is dissociated from consciousness;
yet it is these beings who run on and wander through saṃsāra," wanders about like Ariṭṭha and like the novice Kaṇṭaka.
Furthermore, he is one of malicious speech, wandering about dividing preceptors and others from their resident pupils and others. He too has descended into the stream of the Noble Path.
Sitting within the hollow of concentration, one cannot reach the ocean of Nibbāna.
Like a tree that has grown in the open air, filling the sky, and remains bound by creepers, which—after one or two years have passed—is drenched only once or twice when the great flood arrives;
so too is one who, having gone forth in old age, dwells in a border region.
One should understand that a person living [in such circumstances] has both a rare opportunity to see the Saṅgha and a rare opportunity to hear the Dhamma.
For instance, someone might go forth in old age, receive full ordination after a few days, become proficient in the Pātimokkha by the time he is five years [ordained],
and then, at the age of ten, while listening to a discourse on the Vinaya in the presence of an elder who is a master of the Vinaya, [be like] pepper...
Or, having placed a piece of *harītakī* in his mouth and covering it with his hand, he sits down as if sleeping;
thus becoming one who has performed the legal act (*vinaya*) by means of a mere pretense, he takes his bowl and robes and goes to a border region.
There, people honor him, and because the sight of a monk is rare, they build a monastery for him, saying, "Venerable sir, please dwell right here."
Having had [the site] cleared and having planted flowering and fruit-bearing trees, they dwelt there.
Then, learned bhikkhus who resembled those of the Mahāvihāra went there, thinking, "We shall go to the countryside to perform the dyeing of robes and other such tasks.
Seeing them, he was delighted and joyful; having performed his duties and services, on the following day, taking [them with him],...
Having entered the village for alms, he says, “Such-and-such an elder is a master of the Suttantas; such-and-such is a master of the Abhidhamma; such-and-such is a keeper of the Vinaya;
such-and-such is a master of the Three Piṭakas. When will you have the opportunity to see elders of this kind? You should arrange a hearing of the Dhamma.
The lay devotees, thinking, “We shall arrange a hearing of the Dhamma,” clear the path to the monastery and take along ghee, oil, and other provisions.

Having approached the Mahāthera and said, "Venerable sir, we shall cause a hearing of the Dhamma to be held; please select the preachers of the Dhamma," they returned on the following day and listened to the Dhamma.
Meanwhile, the resident elder, while putting away the bowls and robes of the visiting monks, spent the day right inside the inner chamber.
He passes the time. When the speaker of the day’s discourse rises—having delivered his recitation like one pouring water from a jar—he does not know that he has risen.
When the speaker of the night’s discourse rises—having spoken through the night as if agitating the ocean—he does not know that he has risen.
When the speaker of the dawn discourse rises after having spoken, he too does not know it.
He knew this. Rising early in the morning, having washed his face and offered alms-bowls and robes to the elders, as he was about to go on his alms-round, he said to the Great Elder:
"Venerable sir, what Jātaka did the reciter of the day recite?
What Sutta did the reciter of the morning recite? And what Dhamma discourse did the reciter of the night recite?"
"What Jātaka did the Paccūsakathika recite? How many aggregates (khandhā) are there? How many elements (dhātuyo)?

How many sense-bases (āyatanā) are there? Even though such a person might wait for one or two years to obtain the sight of a monk and the hearing of the Dhamma, he is like a tree that has been soaked once or twice by water when a flood arrives.

He is like this: having turned away from both seeing the Saṅgha and hearing the Dhamma, and dwelling at a distance, he is unable to descend into the Noble Path, sit upon the raft of concentration, and reach the ocean of Nibbāna.
He should be understood as a person with a sweet voice who is like a tender tree grown on an island in the middle of the Ganges.
For he, having mastered the well-known Jātakas such as those beginning with Vessantara, went to the border regions where it was difficult to encounter monks;

there, being attended by people whose hearts were gladdened by his Dhamma discourse, he dwelt in monasteries that were delightful like the Nandana Grove, filled with trees abundant in flowers and fruits, and built for his own sake. Then, for him—
When the monks Bhāra and Hāra heard this report, they said, "It is said that such-and-such a monk dwells with his mind attached to his attendants.
That monk is wise and capable of either learning the Buddha’s word or attending to his meditation subject.
Let us bring him here and learn the Dhamma together with him in the presence of the Elder So-and-so. [They went] into the presence of the Elder So-and-so.
They go there [thinking], "This is the meditation subject.

Having performed his duties for them, when they went out for an evening walk around the monastery and asked him, "Friend, this cetiya was built by you," he replied, "Yes, venerable sirs. "This is the Bodhi tree; this is the pavilion..."
“This is the Uposatha hall; this is the fire-hall; this is the walkway built by you.
Having had these trees planted, you have made this monastery as delightful as the Nandana Grove. “Yes, venerable sir,” he replies.
In the evening, he goes to attend upon the Elder, pays homage, and asks: “Why have you come, venerable sir?”

“Friends, we have come for this purpose: having gone there and learned the Dhamma from such-and-such an elder, and having received a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from such-and-such an elder, we shall practice the duties of a recluse together in harmony in a certain forest.
“It is well, venerable sirs; it is indeed good that you have come for my sake. As for me, because of my long residence here—”
“Venerable sir, I am weary here; I shall go and take my bowl and robes. “Friend, these young novices are exhausted from the journey.
Let us stay today and go after the meal tomorrow. “Very well, venerable sir,” he replied, and on the following day he entered the village for alms together with them.
The villagers thought, “Our noble master has arrived bringing many visiting monks with him.”
Having prepared seats, served the rice gruel, and listened to the discourse while they were comfortably seated, the villagers gave them a meal.
The elders said, “Friend, you go out after giving the blessing; we shall finish our meal in a place convenient for water,” and so they departed.
When the village dwellers heard the blessing, they asked, “Venerable sirs, from where have the elders come? [They replied,] “These are our...”
"Teachers, preceptors, those with the same preceptor, those seen in person, and those who have shared a meal. "Why have you come? "Because we wish to take you with us.
"And do you wish for me to go? "Yes, venerable sir. "What are you saying, bhante?
For whom was the Uposatha hall built by us? For whom was the dining hall, the fire-hall, and so forth built? In all our auspicious and inauspicious occasions..."
“Whom shall we go to? Thinking this, even the Great Laywoman sat right there and shed tears.
The young man thought, “While you are thus suffering, what would I achieve by going? I shall urge the Elders [to leave],” and he went to the monastery.
When the Elders had finished their meal duties and were sitting with their bowls and robes gathered, they saw him and asked, “Friend, why have you been so long?”
"It is daytime; let us go," they said. "Yes, venerable sirs, you are well.
At such-and-such a house, the foundation of bricks remains standing exactly as it was laid; at such-and-such other houses, there are the foundations for the mural paintings and so forth.
Even for one who has gone [there], there will be distraction of mind. You should go on ahead and perform the washing and dyeing of robes at such-and-such a monastery; as for me—"
"I shall reach that place. Knowing his desire to retreat, they departed, saying, "You may come later.
He followed them for a short distance and then turned back. Returning to the monastery itself, he looked about at the dining hall and other areas;
seeing the monastery’s delightful beauty, he thought: "It is well indeed that I did not go. Had I gone, O Lord, some preacher of the Dhamma..."
“Having arrived and divided the minds of all [the monks], he will make the monastery his own sect’s property;
then, having arrived later, I shall have to wander about eating the alms-food obtained from behind him.
At a later time, he hears: “It seems those monks, in the place where they went, [differ] by way of one sect or two sects, one Piṭaka or two Piṭakas, and so forth...”
“Having mastered the word of the Buddha, they became masters of the commentaries and masters of the Vinaya; they wander about with retinues of a hundred or even a thousand followers.

But those among them who went forth to practice the duty of a recluse, striving and exerting themselves, became stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arahants, and passed away into final Nibbāna with great honor. He then thought:
“If I too had gone there, this same prosperity would have been mine;
but being unable to leave this place, I have fallen away excessively. This person, because of his own dullness, does not leave that place;
having descended onto the Noble Path, he sits in the whirlpool of concentration and is unable to reach the ocean of Nibbāna.

One should understand the person of "contracted conduct" as one who, having fallen across the river Gaṅgā, stands like a bridge between the banks due to being covered by sand, and like a tree grown as a support for many;

such a person has mastered one of the various modes of practice—such as the similes of the chariot, the lineages of the noble ones, or the moon—and remains fixed therein. For he is dependent upon that very mode of practice.
Having mastered the Dhamma, he—whose natural voice was melodious—would go to a great place such as Cittala Mountain and perform the duties of the shrine courtyard and so forth.
Then, when he had reached the forefront of the Dhamma assembly, the visiting young monks would say to him, "Speak the Dhamma.
He would then speak, illuminating the practice of the Dhamma exactly as it had been correctly mastered. Then, for him...
All the monks— whether elders, novices, or those of middle standing, including those who wear rag-robes and subsist on alms-food— become delighted, thinking, "Oh, what a true person! He,
binding together young novices as if fastening them with an iron band by presenting to some merely the introductory words, to some half a verse, and to others a full verse,
would approach the great elders and say, "Venerable sirs, this..."
“There is an ancient monastery here; is there any income for it? he asked. The elders replied, “What are you saying, friend?
There is an income of twenty-four thousand *karīsa*. “Venerable sirs, you say such things, yet not even a fire burns in the hearth.
“Friend, what is received by those who dwell in the Great Monastery (*Mahāvihāra*) simply perishes in this very way; no one [takes care of it].”
"He settles it," [he said]. "Venerable sir, why do these people take away what was given by former kings and accepted by those whose taints were destroyed?
"Friend, it would be possible for such a person to obtain it if he were a preacher of the Dhamma. "Venerable sir, do not speak thus;
we are known as preachers of the Dhamma who illuminate the practice, while you are called 'the steward of the Saṅgha' and 'the protector of the monastery.'"
"Thinking, 'We wish to do it,' [they said]: 'Friend, is this indeed improper? But when you, such as yourselves, have spoken, it might arise for us.
[The other replied]: 'In that case, Venerable Sirs, when the monastery attendants arrive, place the burden on them;
we shall designate one as a proper gateway (kappiyadvāra).'"

Thus, having gone early in the morning and stood in the assembly hall, when the monastery attendants arrived, he would say things such as, "In such-and-such a field, where is the share? In such-and-such a field, where is the coin? and so forth;
having taken one person's field, he would give it to another. In this way, by successively refusing this and giving that, he acted accordingly.
Just as those with bowls of gruel, cakes, rice, or oil, honey, molasses, ghee,
and so forth in their hands came right up to him, the entire monastery became one great uproar, and the well-behaved bhikkhus grew weary and departed. He, for his part,
was ordaining many ill-behaved individuals who had been dismissed by their teachers and preceptors, thereby filling the monastery.

He fulfills [the requisites]. When visiting monks stand at the door of the monastery and ask, "Who lives in this monastery?", and upon hearing that "monks such as these live here," they depart by the very same outer gate.

This person, having become a support for the great multitude by lying across the path of the Teaching, has descended into the Noble Path and sits upon the raft of concentration, [heading toward] the ocean of Nibbāna.
He was unable to reach [the end].

He said this to the Blessed One: having understood that the teaching of the Dhamma had been concluded with the phrase "inclined toward Nibbāna," he spoke these words beginning with "But why, venerable sir?
because of his skill in discerning the sequence [of the discourse]. For the Tathāgata was also seated in this assembly.
Thinking, “There is a monk skilled in investigation who will ask me this question,” he brought the teaching to a conclusion at this point in order to provide him with the opportunity.
Now, regarding the internal sense bases and so forth mentioned by way of the method beginning with “the hither shore,” [there are] such things as approaching and not approaching.

These should be understood. Whether one relishes the eye on the basis of thinking, "My eye is clear; I am able to penetrate even a slight visual object," or whether one falls into dejection, thinking, "My eye is unpleasant;
I am not able to discern even a large visual object," because its clarity has been impaired by cataracts, wind-disorders, and so forth—[in both cases, it should be understood].
It is said that one "approaches" the eye-base. However, one who practices insight (vipassanā) by way of the three characteristics—impermanence, suffering, and non-self—does not approach it.
This same method applies to the ear-base and the others as well.
Regarding the mind-base, however: "My mind is indeed pleasing; having grasped nothing from the left, may everything [be seen] only from the right."

Whether one complies by saying, "I grasp it," or consoles oneself by thinking, "There is nothing that my mind has not obtained through its various thoughts," or whether one gives rise to dejection by thinking,
"My mind has taken a non-favorable turn toward what I have ill-considered"— in all such ways, one is said to approach the mind-base (*manāyatana*). Furthermore,
when giving rise to lust for a desirable form or aversion toward an undesirable one, one approaches the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*).
This is its name. The same method applies to the sense-base of sound and the others as well.

For this is a designation for delight-and-lust (*nandī-rāga*); just as a log that has sunk in the middle and reached dry land is covered over by fine and coarse sand so that it cannot raise its head again, even so [is one bound] by delight-and-lust.
A person bound [by this] falls into the four great states of misery and is overwhelmed by great suffering;
even for many thousands of years, they are unable to lift their head again. Therefore it is said: "This is a designation for delight-and-lust (*nandīrāga*).
"This is a designation for the conceit 'I am' (*asmimāna*)" means: just as a log of wood that has come ashore from the waters of the Ganges below...
Just as a stone, having been covered by dust and then by rain, gradually becomes overgrown with moss and comes to be called "a rock" or "a stump," even so,
a person who is puffed up with the conceit "I am" (asmimāna) becomes a refuse-rag wearer in the place of a refuse-rag wearer,
a Dhamma-preacher in the place of a Dhamma-preacher, a quarrelsome person in the place of a quarrelsome person, and a physician in the place of a physician.

The physician is malicious in the place of malice. Engaging in various kinds of improper search, he becomes entangled in this or that offense and thus comes to be subject to the question: "Is there any virtue within him, or is there none?
Therefore it is said: "This is a designation for the conceit 'I am'."
This is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure. For just as a log of wood fallen into a whirlpool is struck and battered by rocks and other obstacles within it,
and having broken apart, becomes a mere mass of powder and dust,

even so a person fallen into the whirlpool of the five strands of sensual pleasure is struck and battered for a long time by the sufferings of the four states of misery, such as torture, hunger, thirst, and the like.
It reaches a state of being crushed to powder. Therefore it is said: "This is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure.
"Immoral" means devoid of virtue. "Of evil nature" means of base character. "Impure" means not pure.
"Of suspect conduct" means one whose conduct must be remembered with suspicion by others, thinking, "I suppose he has done this; I suppose he has done that."
Or, he is one whose conduct is suspicious because he recalls the conduct of others; thus he is "one of suspicious conduct.

For when he sees two or three people talking, he suspects their conduct, thinking, "I suppose they are speaking of my fault," and so he recalls (or runs back to) their conduct; thus he is "one of suspicious conduct.

"One who claims to be an ascetic" means that when a count is begun by asking, "How many ascetics are in the monastery? during the distribution of voting tickets (*salāka*) and so forth, [he thinks], "I too..."
He gives his consent, saying, "I am an ascetic; I too am an ascetic," and he participates in the taking of voting tickets and other such acts.

One who consents to being a celibate practitioner (*brahmacāri*) is one who enters into those formal acts with the declaration, "I too am a celibate practitioner," during the observance days (*uposatha*), the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), and so forth.

"Rotten within" means that although the kidneys, heart, and other organs may not be putrid, they are considered rotten within due to the corruption of their qualities. "Lustful" means one who is soaked by passion.
“Become like rubbish” means to have become like refuse due to the defilements such as lust (*rāga*).

“He said this”: having turned the herd of cattle toward the bank of the Ganges and standing at the edge of the assembly, he heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma from beginning to end; [he understood it] by way of the Teacher not approaching the near shore and so forth.
He says, "It is possible to fulfill the practice. Thinking, "If it is indeed possible to fulfill it, I shall go forth and fulfill it," he spoke these words beginning with, "But I, venerable sir...
[The term] *vacchagiddhinīyo* means those who are affectionate toward their calves, with milk flowing from their udders due to their love for the calves.
“They will go by themselves. “Only when they have been driven out” means:
for if the cows have not been driven out, the owners of the cattle will come and, saying, “One cow is missing, one bull, and one calf is missing,” they will follow right behind you;
thus you will have no peace. And this going forth is not for one who is greedy.
He said this in order to show that the going-forth (pabbajjā) is blameless and has been praised by the Buddha and others. "Niyyātā" means "leading out.
In this sutta, the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) and its cessation (vivaṭṭa) are explained.
5. Commentary on the Second Simile of the Log (Dutiyadārukkhandhopamasuttavaṇṇanā)
242. In the fifth [case], it is in the city named Kimilā. "Defiled" (*saṃkiliṭṭha*) means that from the time it was concealed onward, there is no offense that can be called undefiled;

such is a defiled offense. "No purification is apparent" (*na vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati*) means that no purification is seen through the procedures of probation (*parivāsa*), penance (*mānatta*), and rehabilitation (*abbhāna*).
6. Commentary on the Avassutapariyāya Sutta 243.
Regarding the sixth sutta: "A new assembly hall" (*navaṃ santhāgāraṃ*) means an assembly hall recently built; the meaning is that it was a large hall (*mahāsālā*).
For on occasions such as when preparing for a military expedition, kings would stand there [and command], "Let so many go forward, let so many go back..."
They arrange it thus: "So many on both sides, so many elephants shall mount, so many horses, and so many shall stand in chariots";
they establish boundaries, and therefore that place is called a *santhāgāra*.
Furthermore, from the time they arrive at the departure site until they have the floors of their houses smeared with fresh cow dung and so forth, for that duration—two [periods].
It is called a *santhāgāra* because those kings used to occupy it there for three days; or it is called a *santhāgāra* because it was the house where those kings deliberated on affairs together.

For they were republican kings (*gaṇarājāno*); therefore, a matter that arose could not be settled by one alone, and the consent of all had to be obtained. Consequently, they would all assemble there and deliberate.
Therefore it was said: “A hall for deliberation (santhāgāra) is also called ‘a house together with instruction on affairs.
Furthermore, because they gather there and deliberate upon the duties of household life in such a manner as, “At this time it is proper to plow;
at this time it is proper to sow,” they therefore spread out their domestic life, in its entirety and in detail, within that place.
A meeting hall. "Not long built" means it has been recently completed, well-adorned like a celestial mansion through the work of bricklaying, plastering, painting, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "by a recluse," since deities take possession of their own dwelling place at the very moment the site of the house is acquired, the text says "by a recluse" rather than "by a deity. Or by a brahmin...
"or by anyone who has become human," it was said.

"They approached the Blessed One" means that having heard that the assembly hall (*santhāgāra*) was finished, they thought, "Let us go and see it," and having gone there, they surveyed everything starting from the gateway; [seeing that] "this assembly hall is exceedingly delightful..."
Thinking, "Who shall be the first to enjoy this exquisite [food], which will lead to our welfare and happiness for a long time?
he reflected: "Even if it were given first to our foremost kinsman, it would be more appropriate for the Teacher;
even if it were given according to the principle of those worthy of offerings, it would be more appropriate for the Teacher. Therefore, we shall have the Teacher enjoy it first."
"We shall cause the community of monks to come; when the community of monks has arrived, the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas will have arrived as well.
We shall cause the Teacher to deliver a discourse on the Dhamma to us throughout the three watches of the night.
Thus, we shall later enjoy that which was used by the Three Jewels; in this way, it will be for our welfare for a long time."
Having made the resolution, “It will lead to our happiness,” they approached.

As for the phrase “they approached where the new assembly hall was”: on that day, although the assembly hall had been well-adorned and well-maintained like a celestial mansion for the purpose of being seen by the royal families, it had nevertheless been prepared as a fit offering for a Buddha.
It had not yet been prescribed. For the Buddhas are indeed inclined toward the forest and delight in the forest; they may dwell within a village or they may not.
Therefore, thinking, "We shall prescribe this only after knowing the Blessed One's intention," they approached the Blessed One.
But now, having received his consent and wishing to prescribe it, they went to the assembly hall.
"Having spread the entire assembly hall" means having had it spread in such a way that the whole of it was covered.
First of all, thinking, "Cow dung is suitable for all auspicious occasions," he had even the floor already treated with plaster strewn with fresh cow dung;
then, knowing it had dried, [he arranged it] so that where one stepped, the footprint—
It appeared thus. Having had it smeared with four kinds of perfumes, they spread various colored rugs over it;

then, starting from a large leather bag on top of those, they had every available space covered with various colored rugs suitable for spreading, beginning with elephant-rugs, horse-rugs, lion-rugs, tiger-rugs, moon-rugs, sun-rugs, and variegated rugs. Therefore it was said:
“Having spread the entire assembly hall,” means:
having prepared the seats, first of all having prepared a magnificent Buddha-seat near the auspicious pillar in the center,
and having spread here and there whatever coverings were soft and beautiful.
Having prepared a beautiful red cushion on both sides, having fastened above it a canopy variegated with gold and silver stars,
having adorned it with garlands of perfumes, flowers, and leaves, having had a network of flowers made in an area twelve cubits all around,
and having had the space measuring thirty cubits enclosed by a curtain, [he reached] the western wall.
Having prepared long benches, stools, back-rests, and head-rests for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and having had them covered above with white spreads,
they arranged, against the eastern wall, their own large cushioned seats made of *kojava* cloth,
and placed beautiful pillows filled with swan’s down and other materials, thinking, "In this way, [the bhikkhus] will not be fatigued."
Thinking, "We shall listen to the Dhamma throughout the entire night," it was said, "having prepared seats.
"Having set out a water-jar" means having set out a large-mouthed water-vessel [thinking], "In this way,
the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus will wash their hands or feet, or rinse their mouths, as they please."

Having filled those various places with water the color of jewels, they placed various flowers and perfumed powders for the purpose of scenting it, covered them with plantain leaves, and set them out.
It is with reference to this that it is said, "having set out water-jars.
"Having lit oil-lamps" means [placing them] in lamp-stands made of silver, gold, and so forth, which had figures of Yonakas, Kirātas, and others.
The meaning is that they caused oil lamps to be lit in bowls made of gold, silver, and other materials placed in their hands.
Regarding the phrase "they approached the Blessed One," it should be understood that those Sakyan kings did not merely [clean] the assembly hall;
rather, throughout the entire city of Kapilavatthu, which was a league in extent, they had the streets swept, banners raised, and [lamps set] at the doors of the houses.
Having had full water-jars and plantain trees set out, and having made the entire city appear like a sky strewn with stars by means of garlands of lamps, he gave this command:
"Give milk to the children who drink milk; feed the young boys quickly and put them to sleep;
do not make a loud noise. Today, for one night, the Teacher will dwell within the village; Buddhas, indeed, desire little noise."
Having had the drum beaten, they themselves took up torches and approached the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed himself and taken his bowl and robe, approached the new assembly hall together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
When it was thus announced that it was the proper time, saying, "Venerable sir, let the Blessed One now do as he deems fit," [he entered].
The Blessed One, having donned a red double-layered upper robe with the color of a kovilāra flower dyed deep with lac juice—
arranging it so as to conceal the three circles like one trimming a lotus with a knife—

and having fastened a waistband resplendent as a flash of lightning as if encircling a cluster of lotuses with a golden sash, [he appeared] like an elephant’s frontal globe covered with a red woolen cloth.
It was as if enveloping [the Buddha]; like casting a net of coral over a golden pinnacle a hundred cubits high;
like donning a cloak of red woolen cloth upon a golden cetiya; like shrouding the full moon as it moves with a crimson-colored cloud;
or like pouring well-boiled lac juice over the summit of a mountain of gold.
As if encircling the summit of Mount Cittakūṭa with streaks of lightning, and having caused the great earth— including its world-systems, Sineru, and Yugandhara mountains— to tremble,

he donned a choice red rag-robe (paṃsukūla) the color of a banyan-tree sprout and emerged from the door of the Fragrant Chamber like a lion from a golden cave, or like the full moon from the peak of the Mountain of Sunrise.
And so it was. Having emerged, he stood at the entrance of the Perfumed Chamber.

Then, rays of light issued from his body like flashes of lightning from the mouths of clouds, making the trees of the grove appear as if their leaves, flowers, fruits, and branches were being drenched and turned golden-yellow by a stream of molten gold.
At that very moment, the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, each taking his own bowl and robe, [approached].
He surrounded the Blessed One. And those monks who stood surrounding him were such as these:

few in desire, contented, secluded, unattached, energetic, speakers, patient with speech, reprovers, censurers of evil, endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Surrounded by them...
The Blessed One shone like a mass of gold enveloped in red woolen cloth,
like a golden ship situated in the midst of a cluster of red lotuses, or like a golden palace surrounded by a coral railing.
The great elders, Sāriputta, Moggallāna, and others, having donned their cloud-colored rag-robes, surrounded him like great elephants clad in jeweled armor.
Free from passion, with defilements shattered, with their tangles disentangled and bonds severed, they are unattached to either family or group.

Thus the Blessed One—himself free from passion—is surrounded by those free from passion; himself free from hatred, by those free from hatred; himself free from delusion, by those free from delusion; himself without craving, by those without craving;
himself without defilement, by those without defilement; himself enlightened, surrounded by those enlightened through great learning.
Like a filament surrounded by petals, like a pericarp surrounded by filaments,
like the elephant king Chaddanta surrounded by eight thousand elephants, like the swan king Dhataraṭṭha surrounded by ninety thousand swans,
like a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) surrounded by the divisions of his army, like Sakka, the king of the gods, surrounded by hosts of Maruts, [he was] surrounded by a host of Brahmas.
Like the Great Brahmā Hārita, like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars,
he set out upon the road toward Kapilavatthu in the peerless garb of a Buddha and with immeasurable Buddha-majesty.
Then, a golden ray of light issued from his front body and reached a distance of eighty cubits.
From the back of his body, from his right hand, and from his left hand, golden-colored rays of light arose and reached a height of eighty cubits.
From the hairline at the top of his head, golden rays the color of a peacock’s neck arose through all the curls of his hair and reached a height of eighty cubits in the sky.
From the soles of his feet below, coral-colored rays of light arose...
He grasped a solid mass of earth extending eighty cubits. Thus, for a distance of eighty cubits all around, the six-colored rays of the Buddha shone and quivered;

issuing forth like golden-staffed torches, they spread out like a net leaping into the sky, or like flashes of lightning emerging from a great cloud covering the four continents. All the quarters of space were filled with golden campaka flowers.
They shone brilliantly, as if being scattered about, as if being sprinkled by streams of molten gold flowing from golden jars, as if draped with outstretched golden cloths,

and as if strewn with the pollen of *kiṃsuka* and *kaṇikāra* flowers stirred up by the *verambha* winds. And the Blessed One’s body, radiant with the eighty minor marks, the fathom-wide aura, and the thirty-two supreme characteristics, was like the sky when the stars have risen.
It shone as if it were the vault of heaven, like a forest of blooming lotuses, or like a *pāricchattaka* tree a hundred leagues in height in full bloom;
it gleamed as if overwhelming with its own splendor the majesty of thirty-two moons, thirty-two suns, thirty-two universal monarchs (*cakkavattī*),
thirty-two divine kings, and thirty-two great Brahmās, all arranged in successive order.
Just as it was adorned with the thirty perfections— namely, the ten perfections, the ten secondary perfections, and the ten ultimate perfections— all of which had been perfectly fulfilled; and how,
throughout four incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand aeons,
the merit of the gifts given, the virtue guarded, and the wholesome deeds performed, descended into a single existence to yield its fruit.
It was as if finding no place to stand, as if fallen into a narrow strait; it was like the time when the cargo of a thousand ships is loaded onto a single ship,
or when the goods of a thousand carts are loaded onto a single cart, or like the time when the floods of twenty-five Ganges rivers break through and become a single mass at their mouth.
And while the Blessed One was thus radiating with this splendor of a Buddha, they raised up many thousands of torches before him, as well as behind him, on his left side,
and on his right side. Furthermore, showers of rain— like clouds released from the four continents— fell consisting of flowers such as *jātisumana*,
campaka, jasmine, white lotus, red lotus, blue lotus, *bakula*, and *sinduvāra*, as well as fragrant aromatic powders of blue, yellow, and other colors.
They were scattered about like that. The sounds of the fivefold musical instruments and the cries of praise associated with the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha filled all directions.
The eyes of gods, humans, nāgas, supaṇṇas, gandhabbas, yakkhas, and others felt as if they had obtained the drink of the Deathless (amata).
Now, standing in this place, it is fitting to speak in praise of his journey by means of a thousand verses.
It is permissible. Herein, this is merely the beginning:
“Thus, endowed with all limbs, making the earth tremble, yet not harming living beings, the Guide of the World proceeds.”
“Lifting his right foot first, the Bull among Men,
moving with full majesty, shines as the supreme among bipeds.
As the Best of Buddhas walks, the soles of his feet are soft.”
It touches the earth evenly, yet is not defiled by dust.
As the Leader of the World walks, the low places rise up;
and the high places become level—even though the earth is insentient.
“Stones and pebbles, gravel, stumps, and thorns—
All these paths are cleared away as the Leader of the World proceeds.
He does not lift [the foot] too far, nor does he set it down too close.”
He goes forth without clattering, with both knees and ankles [kept close together].
The Sage, whose conduct is perfected, does not set out too quickly, nor does he walk too slowly; as he goes, he remains concentrated.
“Neither above, nor below, nor across, nor toward the cardinal or intermediate directions does he look as he walks;
for the Victor looks only the distance of a yoke’s length.
With the gait of a majestic elephant, the Conqueror is resplendent in his movement.”
The Chief of the World went gracefully, bringing joy to the world including the devas.
Shining like the king of stars and walking with the fourfold grace of a lion,
gladdening many beings, he approached the most excellent city.

This is indeed called "the time for praise. In such times, whether regarding the physical beauty of the Buddha’s body or the praise of his qualities, the measure is simply the strength of the preacher of the Dhamma.
Whether by means of prose verses or metrical composition, he should say as much as he is able; it should not be said that he has spoken poorly.
For the Buddhas are beyond measure; even the Buddhas themselves cannot fully describe their praises in their entirety.

They were unable even to speak, let alone any other people. Having entered the Sakyan royal palace, which was adorned and prepared with such splendor and luxury, the Blessed One—being honored by the people with hearts full of faith with perfumes, incense, scents, powders, and so forth—entered the assembly hall.
Thus it is said: "Then the Blessed One, having dressed himself and taken his bowl and robe, together with the community of bhikkhus..."
"He approached the new assembly hall.
"Placing the Blessed One at the head" means having placed the Blessed One in front.
There, the Blessed One sat in the midst of both the monks and the lay followers, and after bathing him with scented water and wiping away the moisture with a *dukūla* cloth cushion—
Having been polished with cinnabar and placed upon a seat draped with a crimson woolen cloth, he shone exceedingly like a solid image of red gold.
Now, this is the manner of the ancient eulogy:
"Having gone to the circular pavilion, he who moves with the gait of a majestic elephant..."
Illuminating the world, the Foremost One sat upon the excellent seat.
Seated there, the Charioteer of men to be tamed,
the God above gods, endowed with the marks of a hundred merits—
Seated in the center of the Buddha’s throne,
he shines like a golden necklace upon a pale woolen rug.
Like a necklace of Jāmbūnada gold placed upon a pale woolen rug, he radiates light.
He shines, free from stain, like a radiant gem.
Like a great sal tree in full bloom, like King Neru adorned,
he resembles a golden sacrificial pillar, like a red lotus.
“Like a blazing lamp-tree, like a fire on a mountain peak,
or like the Pāricchattaka tree of the devas in full bloom, he shines forth.

Regarding the phrase “for much of the night [the Blessed One] [spoke] a discourse on the Dhamma to the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu,” here a “discourse on the Dhamma” refers to one connected with the expression of appreciation for the assembly hall.
The miscellaneous discourse (pakiṇṇakakathā) is to be understood. For at that time, as if causing the celestial Ganges to descend, as if drawing up the essence of the earth,
as if taking a great rose-apple tree by its crown and shaking it, and as if pressing a jar of honey a league in size with a millstone and making the inhabitants drink the honey-drink,
the Blessed One delivered the miscellaneous discourse which brings welfare and happiness to the Sakyans dwelling in Kapilavatthu.
He spoke: “Great King, this gift of a dwelling is indeed great.
Your dwelling has been used by me, and it has been used by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
and when it has been used by both me and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, it is truly used by the Jewel of the Dhamma. For when a gift of a dwelling is given, all gifts [are fulfilled].”
It is indeed given. It is impossible to limit the benefits of a leaf-hut standing on the ground or even a bower of branches.
By the power of the gift of a dwelling, even when one is reborn in various existences, there is no confinement in the womb;
rather, the mother’s womb becomes as unconfined as a twelve-cubit chamber. Thus, [he spoke] in a manner variegated by various methods.
Having delivered an extensive discourse on the Dhamma,
he said: “It wards off cold and heat, as well as predatory beasts,
And snakes, mosquitoes, the chill, and even rains.”
“Then, when fierce wind and heat arise, one is shielded from them;
for the sake of shelter, for the sake of comfort, and in order to meditate and practice insight.
The gift of a monastery to the Saṅgha is praised as supreme by the Buddha.”
Therefore, a wise person, seeing their own true interest,
should have delightful monasteries built and cause those learned in the Dhamma to dwell therein;
and they should provide them with food, drink, clothing, and lodgings.
“One should give with a serene mind to those who have become upright;
they will teach him the Dhamma that removes all suffering,
by knowing which Dhamma here, he attains final Nibbāna, free from taints.”

Thus, thinking, "This too is a benefit of the monastery; this too is a benefit of the monastery," he spent much of the night—more than one and a half watches—discoursing on the benefits of the monastery.
Among these, only these verses were included in the collection (*saṅgaha*), whereas the miscellaneous teachings on the Dhamma were not included.
The phrases beginning with "having shown" (*sandassetvā*) have already had their meaning explained.
"Abhikkanta" means "passed beyond"; two watches of the night have gone by. "Yassa dāni kālaṃ maññathā" means:
for whatever journey you deem it to be time, the time for your departure has come; "go," is what is being said.
But why did the Blessed One dismiss them? Out of compassion. For they were delicate, having spent the three watches of the night sitting [in meditation].
"A physical ailment might arise; furthermore, the community of monks is large, and it is necessary to find space for them to stand and sit.
Out of compassion for both, he urged [the Buddha] on.
"Free from sloth and torpor": it is said that there, the monks remained unmoved even while standing or sitting for two watches of the night, until the final watch.
However, it is not the case that the bhikkhu-saṅgha became free from sloth and torpor simply because the food was digested;
for when one listens to the words of the Buddhas, physical and mental distress do not arise, and lightness of body and mind and so forth emerge.
Therefore, even while they remained standing or sitting for two watches of the night listening to the Dhamma, sloth and torpor did not affect them.
It had vanished; when the final watch arrived, it likewise became vanished. Therefore he said, "free from sloth and torpor.
As for the statement, "my back aches," why did it ache? For while the Blessed One was exerting himself in the Great Struggle for six years, there was great physical pain;
subsequently, in his later years, a wind arose in his back.
Or rather, this was not the reason. For the Blessed One was capable of suppressing arisen pain and remaining seated cross-legged for even one or two weeks;
however, he desired to use the Assembly Hall by means of all four postures.
He proceeded from the place for washing his feet as far as the Dhamma throne; it was over that distance that the act of walking was accomplished.
He stood for a short while on the Dhamma-seat and sat down; at that point, standing was accomplished.
He sat on the Dhamma-seat for two watches of the night; at that point, sitting was accomplished.
Now, thinking, "If I lie down for a short while on my right side, lying down will be accomplished," he thus desired to utilize all four postures.
It cannot be said that "the body, being subject to grasping, does not become weary";
therefore, he spoke thus by taking into account even a slight weariness produced by sitting for a long time.
"Having spread out the outer robe" means, it is said, that those kings had a curtain (paṭasāṇi) draped around one side of the assembly hall.

Having prepared a lawful couch, spread it with a lawful coverlet, and hung above it a canopy adorned with golden stars and garlands of perfumes and flowers, they set up a lamp fed with scented oil, thinking:
"Perhaps the Teacher, rising from his Dhamma-seat, might lie down here for a short while to rest; thus this assembly hall would be used by the Blessed One. For four...
“Used in the postures of daily life, it will lead to his welfare and happiness for a long time.
The Teacher, intending that very thing, spread out his outer robe there and lay down. “Having fixed his mind on the perception of rising” means:
having established the perception of rising in his mind, thinking, “I shall rise after this much time has passed,” and doing so while remaining awake.
While listening to the elder’s discourse on the Dhamma:
“The way of the lustful” means the manner of one who is lustful; the sense is the cause of lust.
“Becomes intent” means he becomes intent through the clinging of defilements; he becomes greedy. “Becomes corrupt” means his mind becomes putrid through the influence of ill will (*byāpāda*).
"By means of the eye" (cakkhutoti) means by way of the state of being the eye. "Māra" refers both to the Māra of defilements (kilesa-māra) and the Māra who is a son of a god (devaputta-māra).
"An opening" (otāraṃ) means a vulnerability. "An object" (ārammaṇaṃ) means a condition. For the sense bases accompanied by their respective objects are like a house of reeds or a house of grass;
the object capable of giving rise to defilement is like a grass torch; and the blazing of embers in whatever place a grass torch is set down is like [the arising of defilement].
When an object comes into the range of perception, there is the arising of defilements. Therefore it was said: "Māra would find an opportunity.
In the bright side of the simile, the sense bases devoid of bait are like a gabled house plastered with thick layers of clay; the aforementioned object is like a grass torch;
and the extinguishing of the fire in each place where the grass torch is set down is like the [extinguishing] of the sense bases devoid of bait.
When the objects of the sense bases come into range, there is no arising of the fever of the defilements. Therefore it was said: "Māra would find no opportunity. 7.
Commentary on the *Dukkhadhamma-sutta* (Sutta 244).
"Of things that are subject to suffering" (*dukkhadhammānaṃ*) means of things that have the nature of originating suffering. For when the five aggregates exist...

Suffering arises through various forms such as cutting, killing, binding, and so forth; therefore, because they possess the nature of giving rise to suffering, they are called "states of suffering" (*dukkhadhamma*).
"In that manner" (*tathā kho panassa*) means in that way for him.

"As he sees sensual pleasures" (*yathāssa kāme passato*) means by whatever mode he perceives those sensual pleasures. "As he moves about" (*yathā carantaṃ*) means following his conduct and his dwelling in whatever manner.
As he wanders about, sensual pleasures are seen as being like a pit of glowing embers.

This means they are seen as having a great feverish heat, like a pit of glowing embers, by way of the suffering rooted in seeking and the suffering rooted in rebirth. For those who seek sensual pleasures, there is [suffering] by way of plunging into the great ocean in a ship, entering a desert path, treading upon a path of stakes, charging into a battle arrayed on both sides, and so forth.
Furthermore, for those who indulge in sensual pleasures, there arises the suffering of great fever based on the volition of enjoying those pleasures—
which results in rebirth in the four states of misery (apāya) rooted in their search [for them]. Thus, by way of these two kinds of suffering,
they are seen to be like a pit of glowing embers, characterized by great fever.
He enters the forest. "A thorn in front" means a thorn standing right in the vicinity, as if wishing to pierce him from the front side.
The same method applies to "behind" and so forth. But "below" means near the place where he has stepped with his feet, not at the very spot where he has stepped.
In this way, he would be as if he had entered a thicket of thorns. "May no thorn [pierce] me."
"May a thorn not pierce me"—thus he guards against being pierced by a thorn.
"The arising of mindfulness is slow, monks": the arising of mindfulness itself is indeed slow;
yet, as soon as it has arisen, various defilements are restrained and are unable to persist. For when [defilements] such as lust arise at the eye-door...

When defilements have arisen, having recognized them with the second impulsion (javana) by thinking, "Defilements have arisen in me," one performs the restraint-impulsion itself during the third impulsion.
And this is not surprising—that a practitioner of insight (vipassaka) should suppress defilements during the third impulsion.

However, when a desirable object enters the range at the eye-door, after the life-continuum has turned toward it and after adverting and the other processes have occurred, immediately following the determining consciousness (voṭṭhabbana):
Having turned back the series of impulsions consisting of defilements that have arisen, one produces only the wholesome. For this is the benefit for those who have begun insight:
the state of being established in the reflective discernment of meditation.
"They should offer by bringing it forward" means, as in the case of the Elder Sudinna and the noble youth Raṭṭhapāla, [one offers] with the body.
Or they might offer the seven treasures, or invite [him] by saying with their words, "Take as much as you desire from our wealth.
"They burn" means that because they envelop the body, they produce a feverish heat and burn it;
or the meaning is that, clinging to the body when it has become moist with sweat, they ooze away. For that which, monks—
"Citta" (mind): This is because as long as the mind does not turn back, there is no such thing as a person turning back.
For it is such a mind that does not turn back; therefore, this was said. Thus, in this sutta, only the power of insight (*vipassanā*) is illustrated.
8. Commentary on the *Kiṃsukopama-sutta* (The Simile of the Flame Tree)
245. "Vision" (*dassana*) in the eighth [verse] is a designation for the first path.
For the first path, while accomplishing the task of abandoning the defilements (*kilesa*), sees Nibbāna for the first time; therefore, it is called "vision.

Although the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu-ñāṇa*) sees [Nibbāna] even earlier than the path, it does not perform the task of abandoning the defilements that must be accomplished after seeing.
“Because of non-existence, it is not called ‘seeing. Furthermore, all four paths are indeed seeing. Why?

Because for those monks who say, ‘At the moment of the stream-entry path, seeing is purified; at the moment of the fruit, it is purified. At the moments of the once-return, non-return, and arahant paths, it is purified;
at the moments of their fruits, it is purified,’ that monk, having heard them speak thus...”

Thinking, "I too, having purified my vision, will abide having realized Nibbāna—the purification of vision—after being established in the fruit of Arahantship," he approached that bhikkhu and asked him thus.

That bhikkhu, who practiced the meditation subject of the bases of contact, had attained Arahantship after discerning both material and immaterial phenomena by way of the six bases of contact. Herein—
For the former five bases are form (*rūpa*), while the mind-base (*manāyatana*) is formless (*arūpa*). Thus, he spoke only of the path he himself had realized.
He was "not satisfied" because he spoke while remaining within limited conditioned phenomena (*padesasaṅkhāra*); for it occurred to him:
"This one speaks while remaining within limited conditioned phenomena. Is it possible, while remaining within limited conditioned phenomena, [to attain] purification of vision?"

"to attain Nibbāna"? Then he asked him: "Friend, do you alone know this Nibbāna consisting in purification of vision, or are there others who also know it? "Friend, there is a certain elder named so-and-so in such-and-such a monastery.
He went to him and asked the same question. By this means, he went to yet another, and then to yet another.

And here, the second person, who was a practitioner of the meditation subject of the five aggregates, defined name-and-form by way of the aggregate of form as "form" and by way of the remaining aggregates as "name," and having done so, he gradually attained Arahantship. Therefore, he too spoke only of the path he himself had realized.
But this [third person] said: "These two do not agree with each other; for while the first remained within conditioned states that include a location..."
Having been told, "It has been explained by this [method] without omission," he remained unsatisfied; thus, having asked the same question again, he departed.
The third practitioner of the meditation subject on the great elements (mahābhūta-kammaṭṭhānika), having comprehended the four great elements both in brief and in detail, attained Arahatship;
therefore, he too spoke only of the path he himself had realized. But this one—of these...
“It does not agree with one another: the first was spoken standing on the side of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) that have a limited scope;
the second, those without limitation; and the third, those with excessive limitation. Being dissatisfied, he asked him the same question in that very manner and departed.

This was the fourth teacher, a practitioner of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) pertaining to the three planes (*tebhūmaka*). It is said that his elements were in perfect equilibrium and his body was healthy.
He is capable; indeed, all meditation subjects are suitable for him. Whether they concern past formations, or future, or present;
whether they belong to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere—all are indeed suitable. There is no meditation subject that is unsuitable for him.
Regarding times as well, whether it be before the meal, after the meal, or during the first watch of the night and so forth—[all are suitable].
Or rather, there is no such thing as an "inappropriate time. Just as a great elephant who has entered a foraging ground plucks with its trunk what is to be plucked with the trunk,
and tramples with its feet what is to be trampled with the feet before seizing it, even so,
by grasping all phenomena of the three planes as single groups and contemplating them, he attained Arahatship.
Therefore, he too spoke only of the path he himself had attained. However, being dissatisfied with the thought, "The statements of these [four] do not agree with one another;

by the first it was spoken while standing within limited conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), by the second without limitation, again by the third within limitation, and by the fourth only without limitation," he asked him: "What then..."
"Friends, is this Nibbāna, which consists in the purification of vision, known by you through your own natural capacity, or was it told to you by someone?
"Friends, what could we know? However, there is a Perfectly Enlightened One in the world with its devas;
it is by depending on him that this has been known by us. He thought: "These bhikkhus have grasped my underlying intention."
“They were unable to explain it; I shall ask the All-Knowing Buddha himself and become free from doubt.
Having said this, he approached the Blessed One.
Upon hearing his words, the Blessed One said, “Those who posed the questions to you were all four of them arahants whose taints were exhausted; they have explained it well.”
"You did not perceive that because of your own blindness and folly"—he did not cause such distress [with these words].

However, having understood his capacity as a recipient (*kārakabhāva*), [the Buddha thought], "This man seeks the true goal; I shall awaken him through the teaching of the Dharma alone," and thus he brought forward the simile of the *kiṃsuka* tree.
Therein, making it a factual account, the meaning should be explained as follows: In a certain great city...
A wise brahmin physician, who was the sole master of all medical treatises, lived there.
Then, a man afflicted with jaundice who lived in a village at the eastern gate of the city came into his presence, paid homage to him, and stood before him.
After the wise physician had exchanged greetings with him, he asked, "For what purpose have you come, good sir? [The man replied: "I am oppressed by a disease, noble sir."

"Tell me a medicine," he said. "In that case, sir, go, cut down a *kiṃsuka* tree, dry it, burn it, take its alkaline water, mix it with this and that medicine, prepare an elixir (*ariṭṭha*), and drink it;
by that you will become well. Having done so, he became free from disease, strong, and handsome.
Then another man, a resident of a village at the southern gate, who was afflicted by that same disease, heard it said:
"It is reported that such-and-such a person became healthy after preparing a medicine. Having approached him, he asked: "My friend, by what means did you become well?
"By the power of the *kiṃsuka* tree," he replied, "go and you too do the same. He also did so, but he became just like the other.
Then another man, a resident of the western gate village... [and so on] ...a man from the northern gate village, afflicted by that same disease, heard:
"It is said that such-and-such a person became healthy after preparing medicine. He approached him and asked: "My friend, by what means did you become well?
"By doing what is called 'kiṃsukāriṭṭha' (the act of making the *kiṃsuka* tree); go, you too do it. He also did it accordingly, and he became exactly like the other.
Then another man, a border-dweller who had never before seen a *kiṃsuka* tree, became afflicted by that very same disease.

After long applying various medicines without the disease being pacified, he heard it said: "A certain man living in a village at the eastern gate of the city has become healthy after preparing a medicine.
Upon hearing this, he thought: "Let us go; we too shall prepare the medicine made by him."
Taking his staff, he went gradually into that man's presence and asked, "Friend, how have you come to be at ease? "By doing what, friend?
"What kind of *kiṃsuka* tree is it? "It is like a pillar of burnt wood standing in a village that has been consumed by fire.
Thus, that man described the *kiṃsuka* tree exactly according to the form he had seen it in. Therefore, at the time of seeing it...
The *kiṃsuka* tree, having shed its leaves at the time it appears as a mere stump, remains just like that.
However, because that man was one for whom omens were auspicious, he was dissatisfied with the man’s explanation, thinking: "He says, 'This is like a burnt pillar in a burnt village';
this is inauspicious. For even if I take this medicine, my illness will not be cured."
He asked him: “Sir, do you alone know the *kiṃsuka* tree, or is there another who does too?

“There is, sir; in the village by the southern gate, there is one named so-and-so. He approached him and asked, and because he had seen it when it was in bloom, he replied in accordance with his own observation:
“The *kiṃsuka* is red. The other [said]: “This contradicts what the former said...”
He said, "The black one is very far indeed from the red one.
Unsatisfied with that answer as well, he asked, "But sir, is there anyone else who has seen a *kiṃsuka* tree, by whom a *kiṃsuka* has been seen before?

Having thus inquired, when it was told to him, "There is such a person named so-and-so in the village at the western gate," he approached that man and questioned him. Since he had seen it during its flowering time, [he described it] to himself...
In accordance with what he had seen, he said, "The *kiṃsuka* tree has recently come into flower, its buds having been taken up.
For at the time of flowering, the *kiṃsuka* tree appears as if wearing hanging rags, like a sword-sheath held with its opening downward, and like a *sirīsa* tree with its fruit hanging down.
[The king thought], "This man has spoken in contradiction to the previous ones; his word cannot be accepted," and thus, by way of refuting his explanation as well—
Not satisfied, he asked, "But sir, is there anyone else who has seen a *kiṃsuka* tree, by whom a *kiṃsuka* has been seen before?
Having asked this, when it was said, "There is one named so-and-so in the village at the northern gate," he approached him as well and questioned him.
Since that man had seen it when its leaves were fully covered, he described it according to his own vision as "having thick foliage and spreading branches, with dense shade."
He said: "Sandacchāyo means a shadow that remains when [the objects] have come together.
Thinking, "This man also has spoken in contradiction to those before; it is not possible to accept his word," and being dissatisfied with his explanation as well, he said to him:
"How is it, sir, do you know the *kiṃsuka* tree by your own nature?"
“Or was it told to you by someone? “What could we know, sir?
However, in the middle of that great city there is our teacher, a wise physician; it is from him that we have learned.
“In that case, I too shall approach my own teacher and become free from doubt. Having approached his presence, he paid homage to him and stood there.
The physician, having exchanged greetings with him, asked, "For what purpose have you come, good sir?
"I am afflicted by a disease, noble sir; tell me a remedy," he replied.
"In that case, my friend, go, cut down a *kiṃsuka* tree, dry it, burn it, take its alkaline water, and mix it with this and that medicine."
“Make it into an *ariṭṭha* (antidote) and drink it; by this you will become comfortable. Having done so, he became free from disease, strong, and handsome.
In this context, the city of Nibbāna should be seen as like a great city, and the Perfectly Enlightened One as like a skilled physician.
For it has been said: “‘Physician, surgeon’—this, Sunakkhatta, is a designation for the Tathāgata.”
“The Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Thus, like four medical students in the four neighboring villages, there are four *khīṇāsavas* who have attained purification of vision.
The first man living in the borderland is like the monk who asks the question.
When that borderland dweller, dissatisfied with the discourse of the four medical students, approaches the teacher himself—

The time for questioning is like this monk’s time for approaching the Teacher and questioning him, being dissatisfied with the discourse on the four who have attained purity of vision and whose taints are exhausted.
"In whatever way they were intent" means in whichever manner they were inclined. "Vision well-purified" refers to the vision of Nibbāna.
"Completely purified. "In whatever way those true persons have declared it"—in that very manner it was spoken to you by those true persons.

For just as one saying "the *kiṃsuka* tree is black" does not speak of anything else, but speaks of the *kiṃsuka* itself according to the method he has seen, even so, one who has attained purity of vision through the six bases of contact and whose taints are destroyed [speaks] in the same way.
While speaking on this question, he did not speak of anything else; he spoke only of Nibbāna, the purification of vision, by means of the path he himself had realized.
And just as when one says, "The *kiṃsuka* tree, red, with fresh shoots, thick leaves and foliage," one does not speak of anything else, [so too did he speak].
Just as he spoke only of the *kiṃsuka* tree according to the method he himself had seen, so too,

when one who has attained purity of vision and whose taints are destroyed explains this question by way of the five aggregates of clinging, the four great elements, or the phenomena of the three planes,
he does not speak of anything else; he speaks only of Nibbāna, which is the purity of vision, by means of the path he himself has realized.
In this regard, just as when it is dark, even one who sees a *kiṃsuka* tree has a vision that is real and true,

and by that vision nothing else is seen— only the *kiṃsuka* tree is seen— in the same way, for the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) who has attained purity of vision through the six bases of contact,
his vision is real and true; he says nothing other than what he himself has realized through the path he has attained.

Only Nibbāna itself is described as the purification of vision. And just as when a *kiṃsuka* tree is seen at the time it is red, at the time its buds appear, or at the time its leaves and foliage are thick,
that vision is real and true— even though nothing other than that is seen,
for only the *kiṃsuka* tree is seen— in the very same way, by way of the five aggregates of clinging, by way of the four great elements, and by way of the phenomena of the three planes...
Even for one whose taints are destroyed who has attained purification of view, that vision is real and true;
nothing else was spoken by him, but rather, by means of the path he himself had realized, only Nibbāna—the goal of purification of view—was spoken of.
Why was this begun with the words, "Bhikkhu, it is as if there were a king’s frontier city"? If by that bhikkhu...
If it was already understood, then this [discourse] was undertaken for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to him.
If it was not understood, then this city simile was undertaken for the purpose of illustrating and clarifying that very same meaning.
In that regard, as for the middle part of the city, whether the walls and so forth are firm or weak, in every respect—
Or let them not exist; there is no fear of thieves. Therefore, without including that [city], he said, "a border city.
"Strongly fortified" means having firm walls. "With strong walls and gateways" means both firm walls and firm gateways.
For gateways (toraṇa) are made to the height of a man for the purpose of decorating the city, and also for the purpose of warding off thieves.
They indeed exist. Alternatively, *toraṇa* is a name for a wooden framework (*piṭṭhasaṅghāṭa*);
the meaning is also "a firm wooden framework. Regarding "six gates": a city gate may be one, two, a hundred, or even a thousand;
however, here the Teacher spoke thus while pointing out a city with six gates. "Wise" means endowed with wisdom. "Skilled" means...
"Endowed with proficiency" means possessed of clear knowledge. "Wise" means endowed with *medhā*, which is defined as the wisdom that arises on the spot (*ṭhānuppattika-paññā*).
Regarding the phrase "in the eastern direction," and so forth, the meaning should be understood by taking it as a factual account:
it is said that in the prosperous great city of Samiddha, a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) endowed with the seven treasures was ruling; this [place] was his frontier city.
The city was devoid of an official (*āyuttaka*). Then, men came and said, "Sire, there is no official in our city; grant us some official.
The king gave one of his sons and said, "Go, take him there, have him consecrated, and dwell there establishing the courts of justice and other such matters.
They did accordingly. Through association with evil friends, the prince—

After only a few days, having become a drunkard, he stripped away all his judicial and administrative duties and spent his time in the center of the city, surrounded by profligates, drinking liquor and indulging in the pleasures of dancing, singing, and the like. Then they came and reported this to the king.
The king commanded a wise minister: "Go, admonish the prince and [restore] his judicial and administrative duties."
"Having had him brought back and performed the consecration once more, come! [The king said. "It is not possible, Your Majesty, to advise the prince;
the prince is fierce and might even kill you. Then he commanded a warrior endowed with great strength:
"Go with him, and if he does not abide by the advice, cut off his head. Thus, that minister and the warrior—this was swift.
The two messengers went there and asked the gatekeeper, "Sir, where is the prince, the lord of the city?
[He replied,] "He is sitting here in the center of the crossroads, drinking liquor, surrounded by rogues, and enjoying the pleasures of song and so forth.
Then that pair of messengers went and said to the minister, "Master, it is said that after having the judicial seats and other such places established..."
“Rule the kingdom well,” he said. The prince sat there as if he had not heard him.
Then the soldier, seizing him by the head, drew his sword, saying, “If you will carry out the king’s command, do so; if not, I shall strike off your head right here.
The attendants and ruffians immediately fled in all directions. Terrified, the prince accepted the message.
Then, having performed his consecration right there and raised the white parasol,
they delivered to him the king’s words of truth, saying, “Rule the kingdom rightly,” and then returned by the very same path by which they had come.
Revealing this matter, the Blessed One said, “From the eastern direction.”
Herein, this is the correlation of the similes: the city of Nibbāna should be seen as like a great, prosperous city;
the Dhamma-king, the Fully Enlightened One, endowed with the seven jewels of the factors of enlightenment, is like a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) endowed with the seven treasures;
the city of personal existence (sakkāya) is like a frontier town; and in that town, the son of a counterfeit king—
The fraudulent thought-arising of this bhikkhu is like that of the fraudulent prince;

his time of being possessed by the five hindrances is like the time when the fraudulent prince was surrounded by rogues; the two swift messengers are like the meditation subject of serenity and the meditation subject of insight;
and his state with the first-jhāna concentration arisen is like the time when the great warrior was seized by the head.
The time when the mind has been made immovable and grasped is like the moment a warrior seizes [his enemy] by the head, while the rogues flee in all directions and move far away;
the distancing of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) as soon as the first absorption (*paṭhamajjhāna*) has arisen is like that.

The time of emerging from absorption is like the moment [the warrior] is released as soon as he has accepted the king’s command, thinking, “I shall carry out the king’s instruction,” by the minister for the king.

The time when the mind has been made pliable through concentration and the meditation subject for insight (vipassanā) has been developed should be understood as being like the time of announcing the royal decree;

and the raising of the white parasol of liberation for one who has attained Arahatship by relying on the meditation subjects of serenity (samatha) and insight should be understood as being like the raising of the white parasol for him after he had been consecrated by those two messengers right there.

In such passages as, "Monk, 'city' is a designation for this body composed of the four great elements," the meaning of the phrases beginning with "composed of the four great elements" has already been explained in detail above. However,
because it is the dwelling place of the prince of consciousness, the body is here called a "city," and because they serve as its gates, the six sense bases [are called the city-gates].
Regarding the phrase "the gates": because mindfulness is always well-established at those gates, it is called the "gatekeeper.
