Because they were sent by the Dhamma-King who proclaims the meditation subject, serenity and insight are called the "swift pair of messengers.
Here, serenity should be understood as like a great warrior, and insight as like a wise minister.
“In the middle of the crossroads” means at the crossroads in the center of the city.

“Of the great elements” refers to the great elements that serve as the support for the heart-basis (*hadayavatthu*). Indeed, this mention of the four great elements is made specifically for the purpose of showing the condition for the materiality of the basis.
However, like that prince in the center of the city, he sits in the crossroads of the heart-materiality in the middle of the body, [conveyed] by the messengers of serenity and insight.
The son of the king, who is the consciousness of insight (vipassanā-viññāṇa), should be consecrated with the consecration of Arahatship;
however, because Nibbāna is the unshakable true nature of things and the ultimate goal, it is called "the statement of things as they really are" (yathābhūta-vacana).
As for the Noble Path, just as the preliminary path of insight was, this one is exactly the same, owing to its possession of the eight factors.
Having done so, it is said: "by the path as it came. This, first of all, is the correlation of the simile brought forward here for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.
However, for the purpose of making that same meaning clear, the correlation regarding the side of the simile brought forward is as follows:

here, the simile of the six doors is brought forward by way of the six bases of contact (*phassāyatana*) to show the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) who has attained purity of vision; the simile of the master of the city... [is brought forward].
By way of the five aggregates, the simile of the crossroads is presented; by way of the four great elements, the simile of the city is presented;

and by way of the phenomena of the three planes, it is brought forth to show the one whose taints are destroyed who has attained purification of vision. In brief, however, only the Four Noble Truths are taught in this sutta.
For by means of the entire collection of city-components, only the Truth of Suffering is taught through the expression "as it really is."
The truth of cessation, the truth of the path by means of the way it has been traversed, and the craving that brings about suffering are the truth of origination.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the monk who had asked the question was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
9. Commentary on the Lute Simile Sutta.

246. "Bhikkhus, for any bhikkhu or bhikkhunī whatsoever"—this was said by the Teacher as if a great householder, having performed extensive agricultural work and harvested the crop, were to erect a pavilion at his house door and distribute alms to both Saṅghas.
Although he had established alms-giving for both Saṅghas, [the Teacher spoke thus].
When two assemblies have been satisfied, he surely satisfies the remaining people as well; in the same way, the Blessed One,
having fulfilled the perfections for more than four incalculable eons, having attained omniscient knowledge at the seat of enlightenment, and having set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma,
sat in the great monastery of Jetavana and performed a great sacrifice of Dhamma for both the assembly of monks and the assembly of nuns.
While sacrificing, they began the Vīṇopama Sutta. Although this was undertaken with reference to two assemblies, it is not restricted to those four assemblies.
Therefore, it should be heard and believed by everyone; and having thoroughly investigated it, the flavor of its meaning should be experienced.
In this context, regarding "desire" (*chanda*) and the others: "desire" (*chanda*) refers to weak craving that arises first; it is not capable of causing passion (*rañjeti*).
However, the strong craving that arises repeatedly is called "passion" (*rāga*); that is capable of causing passion.

"Hatred" (*dosa*) refers to weak anger that arises first and is incapable of performing acts such as taking up a staff; whereas that which arises repeatedly and is capable of performing those acts is [called "hatred"].
Strong anger is called *paṭigha*. Delusion (*moha*), however, is ignorance that has arisen by way of deluding and thoroughly bewildering.
Thus, in this context, all three unwholesome roots are included by these five terms. When these are taken, all defilements rooted in them are necessarily included as well.
Furthermore, by the two terms "desire" (*chanda*) and "lust" (*rāga*), the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed are included; "hatred" (*dosa*)...
By the two terms “paṭigha,” the two types of consciousness-arising accompanied by displeasure (*domanassa*) are included;

by the term “moha,” the two types of consciousness-arising accompanied by restlessness and doubt, which are devoid of greed and hatred, are included. Thus, all twelve types of consciousness-arising are indeed shown.

It is “with fear” (*sabhaya*) because it is a dwelling place for the thieves that are the defilements (*kilesa*). It is “with peril” (*sappaṭibhaya*) because of [the presence of] execution, imprisonment, and so forth.

It is "frightening" because it is a cause of fear. It is "thorny" because it is thorny with the thorns of lust (*rāga*) and so forth. It is "overgrown" because it is overgrown with the thickets of lust and so forth.
It is a "wrong path" because it is not the way for one going to the world of the gods, the world of humans, or *nibbāna*.
It is a "by-path" because, like a narrow footpath leading to a place that is base and loathsome, it leads to the states of deprivation (*apāya*).
"A bad road. Regarding "duhitika": here, *ihiti* means "wandering" (*iriyanā*). It is called *duhitika* because wandering there is painful (*dukkhā ihiti ettha*).
For on a path where there is no edible food such as roots and fruits, or food to be chewed and swallowed, wandering is painful;
one cannot reach the desired destination by following it. Likewise, having set out upon the path of the defilements (*kilesa-magga*), one cannot [reach the goal].
The path of defilements is called "a drought" because it leads to a state of existence characterized by misfortune. There is also a reading *dvīhitiko*, which has the same meaning.
"Frequented by bad people" means frequented by bad people such as Kokālika and others.
"Restrain the mind from that" means restrain the mind—which is proceeding toward those forms cognizable by the eye—by way of desire and so forth.

One should restrain [the mind] by means of methods such as the contemplation of foulness (*asubha*). For when lust arises toward a desirable object at the eye-door, the mind turns back for one who contemplates it as foul;
when hatred arises toward an undesirable object, the mind turns back for one who contemplates it with loving-kindness (*mettā*);
and when delusion arises toward a neutral object, the mind turns back for one who contemplates the recitation, the inquiry, and the dwelling under a teacher.
The mind turns back. However, for one who is unable to do so, the greatness of the Teacher, the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma, and the good practice of the Saṅgha should be brought to mind.

For the mind turns back even in one who reflects upon the greatness of the Teacher, and also in one who reflects upon the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma and the good practice of the Saṅgha. Therefore it was said: "By means of the contemplation of the foul, etc."
“...one should ward them off by means of skillful methods.
“Grain” (*kiṭṭha*) refers to the crop produced in a place where grain grows. “Ripe” (*sampanna*) means fully developed and well-formed. “A grain-eater” (*kiṭṭhāda*) is one who eats the crop.
“In the same way,” in this context, the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*) are to be regarded as being like the ripe grain.

The deceptive mind is like the ox that eats the grain; the time when the guard of the grain is negligent is like the time when a bhikkhu wanders about having abandoned mindfulness at the six sense-doors.

Just as the owner of the crop fails to obtain the fruit of the harvest because the ox eats the grain from its interior due to the negligence of the grain-guard, so it is through the departure of the mindfulness that guards the six doors.

It should be understood that for a bhikkhu whose mind relishes the five strands of sensual pleasure, there is an absence of attainment of the fruits of recluseship because he has abandoned the side of the wholesome.

"Above the yoke" means between the two horns. "He should restrain it well restrained" means that once the nose-rope is fixed in the yoke, he should restrain it by holding it very firmly. "With a stick" means with a thick stick resembling a club.
"In this way, monks, that ox— having been brought to a state of docility through being restrained, beaten,
and released whenever he desired to descend upon the grain at whatever moment he wished to do so due to his negligence regarding the protection of the grain—
became an ox devoid of unruly behavior."
"Even so," it is said; here too, the five strands of sensual pleasure are to be seen as like the grain, the deceitful mind as like the grain-eater,
the non-release of mindfulness at the six sense-doors by this bhikkhu as like the vigilance of the grain-guard,
and the Sutta as like the staff— the striking of the ox with the staff when it is heading toward the grain being like the striking of the mind externally.

At a time when the mind is directed toward various objects, one should bring to mind the relevant Sutta— such as those on the "No-End-of-Time" (Anamatagga), the "Divine Messengers" (Devadūta), the "Burning Snake" (Āditta-āsīvisa), or the "Fears of the Future" (Anāgata-bhaya)— and, having turned the arising of consciousness away from those various objects,
one should understand how to introduce it back into the primary meditation subject (mūlakammaṭṭhāna). Thus said the ancients:
“Having heard well-spoken words, the mind becomes serene;
it tames itself and finds joy and happiness.
Thus, the mind remains fixed upon that object.”
"Like an ox eating chaff, driven by the whip.
*Udujita* means "driven. *Sudujita* means "well-driven," though it also has the meaning of "well-subdued. *Udu* and *sudū* are merely particles.
*Ajjhatta* refers to the internal range of the sense-spheres (*gocarajjhatta*). In the phrases beginning with "he settles," [the explanation] is according to the first jhāna.
It remains steady; it settles down by way of the second jhāna; it becomes unified by way of the third jhāna;
it becomes concentrated by way of the fourth jhāna. Or rather, all of this should be understood by way of the first jhāna.
To this extent, what is called the virtue of restraint of the faculties through the preservation of serenity has been explained by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"Of a king" means of any bordering king whatsoever. "Hear the sound" means that having woken up at the time of dawn, one hears the sweet sound of a lute being played by a skilled lute-player.
Regarding the terms "alluring" (*rajanīya*) and so forth: it is "alluring" because it delights the mind;
it is "desirable" (*kamanīya*) because it is fit to be desired; it is "intoxicating" (*madanīya*) because it intoxicates the mind; [and] it is as if the mind were swooning...
It is called *mucchanīya* because one becomes intoxicated (*mucchiyati*) by playing it. It is called *bandhanīya* because it binds (*bandhati*) by grasping as if with a tether.
"Enough for me, sir," he said thus, unwilling [to accept] upon seeing the shape of the lute. *Upadhāraṇa* refers to the pegs.
*Koṇa* refers to the square sounding-board staff.
Thus, regarding that lute: the king, thinking, "Bring that lute; I shall see its sound," took the lute.
In the phrases beginning with "cut it into ten pieces," first he would cut it into ten pieces;
then, not seeing its sound, he would cut it into a hundred pieces; even then, not seeing it, he would reduce it to small fragments; even then, not seeing it—
“‘The fragments will burn away, but the sound will escape and flee; then I shall see it,’ he might thus scorch it with fire. Still not seeing it, [he thinks:
‘The fine powder of lac will be scattered by the wind, but the sound will fall at my feet like solid grain; then I shall see it,’ and so he might expose it to a great wind.”

Nevertheless, not seeing [him], he might think: "The powdered lac will go with the water, but the sound will emerge like a man crossing to the other shore and will cross over; then I shall see him," and he would cast it into the swift current of a river.

"He would speak thus" means that, failing to see him by all these means, he would speak to those people in this way. "Asatī kirāyaṃ" means "this lute is indeed asatī"; the meaning is "it is wretched. *Asatī* is a synonym for something wretched, as it has been said:
“Worldly women are indeed unreliable; no fixed limit exists for them.
They are lustful and shameless, like a fire that consumes everything.
Just as this is so, it is not only the lute (*vīṇā*) that is base; rather, even this very lute is [unreliable] in the same way.
The meaning is that whatever else is bound by strings is likewise merely inferior. "In the same way" (evameva kho):
here, the five aggregates are to be regarded as the lute, and the practitioner of yoga (*yogāvacara*) as the king.
Just as that king, having analyzed that lute starting from its tenfold dissection and finding no sound, becomes indifferent to the lute;
In this way, the practitioner of yoga, while comprehending the five aggregates, sees nothing that can be grasped as "I" or "mine," and thus becomes indifferent to the aggregates.
Therefore, demonstrating that comprehension of the aggregates to him, [the Buddha] said: "He investigates form to the extent that is the range of form," and so forth.
In this context, "he seeks" means he searches for. "To the extent that is the range of form" means as far as the range of form extends. Therein, "range" (*gati*) is fivefold:

the range of destination (*gatigati*), the range of birth (*sañjātigati*), the range of specific characteristic (*salakkhaṇagati*), the range of dissolution (*vibhavagati*), and the range of disintegration (*bhedagati*).
Among these, what is called "this form" extends downward to the limit of the Avīci hell and upward to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma-world.
Having made these its limits, it transmigrates and revolves within this interval; this is what is called its "going and coming.
Furthermore, this body is not born within the calyx of a lotus, nor among white, blue, or other varieties of water-lilies;
rather, it is born in a place between the stomach and the intestines, a region of dense darkness, pervaded by foul-smelling winds, utterly loathsome, like that of putrid fish and the like.
That which arises like this is called the "mode of arising" (*sañjātigati*) of matter.

Furthermore, the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) of matter is twofold: the individual characteristic (*paccattalakkhaṇa*), known as "being afflicted" (*ruppana*), as stated in the passage, "Bhikkhus, it is called 'matter' because it is afflicted";
and the universal characteristic (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*), which consists of the divisions such as impermanence and so forth. This is its [characteristic].
This is called the movement of specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇagati*):
“The forest is the movement of deer, the sky is the movement of birds;
non-existence is the movement of phenomena, and Nibbāna is the movement of the Arahant.”
When it is stated thus, the non-existence of form is called its "state of dissolution" (*vibhavagati*). Its disintegration, however, is called its "state of breaking up" (*bhedagati*).

This same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates as well. However, here, from the top down to the peak of existence (*bhavagga*), their "state of birth" (*sañjātigati*) and their "state of individual characteristics" (*salakkhaṇagati*) should be understood according to their respective specific characteristics by way of feeling, perceiving, volitional formation, and cognizing.

"Even that does not exist for him": this refers to the triad of grasping at views, craving, and conceit—which is designated as "I," "mine," or "I am" with respect to form and so forth—and even that does not exist for that one whose taints are destroyed;
thus it is found in the Sutta according to its own sequence. Therefore, it is said in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*:
“Virtue is taught at the beginning, the cultivation of concentration in the middle, and Nibbāna at the end—this is the discourse on the simile of the lute. 10.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Simile of the Six Animals.

247. "One with a wound" (*arugatta*) means one whose body is ulcerated. Because those very wounds have become suppurating, he is "one with suppurating limbs" (*pakkagatta*). "A thicket of reeds" (*saravana*) means a thicket of *kaṇḍa* reeds.
"In the same way" refers to how a person of immoral character is to be understood like a man with a wound:
when his limbs are pierced by blades of *kusa* grass and scratched by arrow-points resembling the edge of a sword, his suffering and mental distress increase all the more.
The suffering that arises for one who is pointed out here and there by fellow celibates (sabrahmacārīs) as "this is the doer of such-and-such deeds" should be understood.
"He receives a rebuker" means he receives one who reproaches him. "One who acts thus" refers to those who perform such acts as medical treatments, serving as a messenger, and so forth.
The doer. "One of such conduct" means one whose range of activity (gocara) is of this kind by way of frequenting widows and so forth.
"A village-thorn that is impure" means it is impure in the sense of being unclean; it is a "village-thorn" in the sense of piercing those who dwell in the village.

"Pakkhin" refers to the bird with an elephant's trunk. "Should let go" means should release. "Should pull toward" means should draw near. "I shall enter" means I will go inside. "I shall fly into the sky" means I will leap up into the air.
Among these, the snake desires to enter the anthill, thinking, "I will coil my coils into a circle and sleep.
The crocodile desires to enter the water, thinking, "I will enter a distant hole and lie down.
The bird desires to fly into the sky, thinking, "I will move freely in the cloudless atmosphere. The dog [desires to enter] the hearth, having piled up ashes...
The dog, thinking, "I shall lie down taking hold of a pillow," desired to enter the village.
The jackal, thinking, "Having eaten human flesh, I shall stretch out my back and sleep," desired to enter the raw charnel ground.
The monkey, thinking, "Having climbed a high tree, I shall leap in every direction," desired to enter the forest.
"Anuvidhāyeyyuṃ" means they would follow; "anuvidhiyeyyuṃ" is also a reading, meaning they would conform to.
The sense is: "wherever it goes, there they too would go.
"Even so"—here, the six sense-bases (āyatana) are to be seen as like the six creatures, craving (taṇhā) as like the strong rope, and ignorance (avijjā) as like the knot in the middle. In which...
Whichever door the object is strong at, that respective sense base draws [the mind] toward that respective object.
Now, the Blessed One might bring forward this simile either by way of analogy or by way of showing the diversity of the sense bases (*āyatana*).
Regarding these, first, there is no separate function of absorption (*appanā*) by way of analogy; it is already included within the text itself. As for the sense bases...
Furthermore, this absorption is characterized by the perception of diversity: this snake does not delight in a place that is sprinkled and well-swept outside;
rather, it enters only into rubbish heaps, thickets of grass and leaves, or ant-hills, and when lying there, it finds delight and attains one-pointedness.
In the same way, the eye has an uneven inclination; it does not delight in smooth surfaces such as gold walls and the like.
He finds no delight and does not even wish to look; rather, he delights only in the various forms of mind, flowers, fruits, creepers, and so forth.
For in such places, even when his eyes cannot reach them, he wishes to look by opening his mouth wide.
Even a crocodile that has gone out does not see what should be seized; it wanders about with its eyes closed. But when—
When one has plunged into water a hundred fathoms deep and, having entered a cave, lies down, then his mind becomes one-pointed and he sleeps happily.
In the same way, this hearing (sota) is inclined toward a cave and dependent upon space;
it makes its abode only in the hollow of the ear-cavity, and the space within that ear-cavity alone is the condition for its perception of sound. Unobstructed space as well...
It is indeed permissible. For when recitation is being performed inside a cave, the sound does not go out by breaking through the roof of the cave;

rather, it goes out through the openings of the doors and windows, comes along striking the succession of the elements, and strikes the sense-faculty of hearing. At that time, those sitting on the surface of the cave know, "So-and-so is reciting."
This being so, there is the state of having a present object as its domain. But what is this "having a present object as its domain"? Yes, it is having a present object as its domain.
If that were so, then when drums and such are being struck at a distance, the cognition "the sound is far away" would not occur.
It is not the case that it does not occur. For when the sensitive matter of the ear is struck, [one knows] "the sound is far," "the sound is near," or "it is on the further bank or the near bank."
In whatever way one knows, that is the mode of its appearance; such is the nature of things (*dhammatā*). What is the significance of this nature of things?
Just as there is hearing from whichever opening there is, and the seeing of the moon, sun, and so forth, so too this [mind] does not reach its proper range.
Even a bird finds no pleasure in a tree or on the ground; but when it has passed beyond one or two throws of a clod, [it settles].
Just as one who leaps into the cloudless sky attains one-pointedness of mind, so too the nose has space as its inclination, wind as its support, and odors as its domain.

For instance, when it has rained newly, cows sniff the ground again and again and, facing toward the sky, draw in the wind. This is also the case when one takes a mass of fragrance between the fingers and smells it.
Not drawing in the wind, it does not perceive its scent at all.
Even when wandering outside, the cockerel does not see a safe place and is harassed by clods, sticks, and the like;
yet, having entered the village and lain down upon ashes piled up at the hearth, he finds comfort. In the same way...

The tongue also has its inclination toward the village, with taste as its object, supported by water. For even after performing the duties of a recluse throughout the three watches of the night, one must still enter the village at dawn, taking bowl and robes.
Furthermore, it is impossible to know the flavor of dry solid food unless it is moistened by saliva.
Even a jackal wandering abroad finds no rest; it is only when it has eaten human flesh in a charnel ground and lies down that it finds comfort.
In the same way, the body also has a craving for what is clung-to (*upādiṇṇaka*) and takes as its object tactile sensations dependent upon earth.
For this reason, beings who do not obtain another [body] to cling to lie down with their own heads placed upon the palm of their own hands.
Both internal and external earth serve as conditions for the apprehension of its object.
For even in the case of a well-spread bed, it would be impossible for one who is neither sitting nor pressing down to know the hardness or softness of the wooden planks situated beneath;
thus, both internal and external earth serve as the condition for his knowledge of the tangible.

Even a monkey, while wandering upon the ground, finds no pleasure; however, having climbed a tree a hundred cubits high and sitting upon the branch, it becomes comfortable as it gazes toward the cardinal and intermediate directions.
In the same way, the mind has various underlying tendencies (*adhiṣṭhāna*) that serve as conditions for the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*);
even regarding things previously seen, it forms an underlying tendency toward various objects, while its fundamental life-continuum remains.
"Is a condition": this is the summary here. In detail, however, the diversity of the sense bases (*āyatana*) has already been explained in the *Visuddhimagga* in the "Description of the Sense Bases.

"He does not incite the eye" means that he does not drag it along because it has become devoid of activity, having been bound to the pillar of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) by the leeches of the sense bases which are the cords of craving (*taṇhārajjuka*). In this sutta, only preliminary insight (*pubbabhāgavipassanā*) is discussed.
11. Commentary on the Yavakalāpi Sutta (248).
In the eleventh [verse], *yavakalāpī* means a heap of barley that has been harvested and set aside. *Byābhaṅgihatthā* means having clubs in their hands.
*Chahi byābhaṅgīhi haneyyuṃ* means they would strike them with six broad club-staffs. *Sattamo* refers to the seventh among those.
When six men had pounded the barley, filled their bags, and departed, a seventh man might arrive.
Thinking, "Let them be better off," he would strike even more thoroughly for the sake of seizing whatever remained there, even if it were merely a bit of chaff and husk.
"In the same way" means that here the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) are to be seen as like the crossroads, and the bundle of barley placed at the crossroads...
The being is like the man; the eighteen objects—classified as desirable, undesirable, and neutral—are like the six types of hammers;
and the defilements consisting of the craving for existence are like the seventh hammer.
Just as a sheaf of barley placed at a crossroads is struck by the six hammers, so too are these beings struck in the six sense bases by the eighteen rods of objects.

They are being slain. Just as [the oxen] become more exhausted by the seventh [lap], so too beings, while experiencing the suffering rooted in existence, become more exhausted by the defilements that long for existence.
Now, in order to show those defilements that long for existence, he said, "Once upon a time, monks," and so forth. Therein—
“Sudhammāyaṃ” means on the ground of Sudhammā; the meaning is “at the door of the divine assembly hall (devasabhā) called Sudhammā.
“Dhammikā kho devā” means these gods are indeed righteous (dhammika), referring to those who, having seized a lord of the asuras such as myself, did not even inflict a wound upon me.
“Adhammikā devā” means these gods are indeed unrighteous (adhammika), referring to those who [seized] a lord of the asuras such as myself.
They bind him with five bonds, including the neck-bond, like a young pig in excrement and force him to sit down. "Thus, monks, the bond of Vepacitti is subtle," they say;
for it is said that it is as fine as a lotus-stalk fiber or a spider's web, and it cannot be cut either by an axe or by a hatchet. However, because it can be severed by the mind alone—
One is bound by it and liberated by the mind; therefore, it is called the "fickle-minded bond" (*vepacittibandhana*).
Even subtler than that is the bond of Māra, namely the bond of the defilements (*kilesabandhana*), which is even more subtle than that;
it does not come within the range of the eye, nor does it obstruct one's postures (*iriyāpatha*). Bound by this, sentient beings [remain] even upon the surface of the earth.
They go and come even through space for a hundred leagues or a thousand leagues.
Furthermore, this bond is severed by knowledge alone and not by anything else; thus it is called "the bond that has knowledge as its release.
"One who conceives" means one who conceives of the aggregates by way of craving, views, and pride. "Bound by Māra" means bound by the fetters of Māra.
"Baddho" (bound): this is a genitive case used in the sense of the instrument;

the meaning is "bound by the Māra of the defilements. "Mutto pāpimatā" (freed from the Evil One): freed from the bondage of Māra. Or, this genitive case is used in the sense of the instrument itself; the meaning is "freed from the bondage of the defilements by the Evil One.
By the word "asmi" (I am), the conceit of craving is expressed. "Ayamahamasmi" (this I am) is the conceit of views. "Bhavissam" (I shall be) is by way of eternalism.

It is precisely conceiving through views (*diṭṭhimaññitam*). They will not exist by way of annihilation (*uccheda*). "Possessing form" (*rūpī*) and so forth are merely indicators of the various divisions of eternalism (*sassata*).
Therefore—because conceiving is an affliction (*ābādha*), a disease, a tumor, and a dart, by way of cutting off internal faults—therefore.
"Quivering" (*iñjita*) and so forth: because by these defilements beings quiver, tremble, and are obsessed (*papañcita*).
And because they have reached a state of negligence, these [states] are mentioned for the purpose of showing their specific modes.

In the section on "the course of conceit" (*mānagata*), however, the meaning is: the course of conceit is *mānagata*, which is to say, the occurrence of conceit. Conceit itself is *mānagata*, just as excrement is *gūthagata* or urine is *muttagata*.
Therein, the phrase "I am" (*asmīti*) is stated by way of the conceit associated with craving (*taṇhā*).
[It is] by way of the view: "This I am. But is it not the case that there is no conceit associated with views? Yes, there is none;
however, because conceit has not been abandoned, what is called "view" arises. This was said with reference to a view rooted in conceit.
The rest is clear in all respects.
The Chapter on the Venomous Snake.
The Fourth Fifty.
The Commentary on the Connected Discourses on the Six Sense Bases is finished.
2. Saṃyutta Nikāya: Connected Discourses on Feeling 1.
Sagāthāvagga: Chapter with Verses 1.
Samādhisutta: The Discourse on Concentration—Exegesis
249. In the first chapter of the Sagāthāvagga in the *Vedanāsaṃyutta*, "one who is concentrated" (*samāhita*) means one who is concentrated either by access (*upacāra*) or by absorption (*appanā*).

"And he understands feeling" (*vedanā ca pajānāti*) means he understands feeling by way of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*). "And the origin of feelings" (*vedanānañca sambhavaṃ*) means he understands their origin—that is, their arising—by way of the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*).
"And where these [feelings] cease" (*yattha cetā*): this refers to where these feelings cease.

One understands that Nibbāna by way of the truth of cessation. One understands the path leading to their destruction—that is, the path leading to the destruction of those very same feelings—by way of the truth of the path.
"Free from hunger, completely extinguished" means that, having become free from craving, one is completely extinguished through the extinction of the defilements (*kilesa-parinibbāna*).

Thus, in this sutta, the feeling pertaining to the range of comprehension (*sammasanacāra-vedanā*) is explained. In the verses, serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) are expressed by two phrases.

[The first] has been explained; by the remaining [terms], the Four Truths have been explained. Thus, herein, the comprehensive classification of phenomena belonging to the four planes has been stated.
2. Commentary on the *Sukhasutta* 250.

In the second [verse], "together with the neither-painful-nor-pleasant" (*adukkhamasukhaṃ saha*) means together with the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling and with pleasure and pain. And internally...

"And externally" means both one's own and another's. "Subject to decease" (*mosadhamma*) means having the nature of perishing. "Dissolving" (*palokina*) means that which dissolves, having the nature of breaking up.
"Seeing its fall as they repeatedly touch it" means seeing its fall by touching it again and again with wisdom.

"Thus one becomes dispassionate toward it" means one becomes dispassionate toward those feelings. Here too, in this sutta, it refers to the feelings in the course of comprehension (*sammasanacāra-vedanā*).
Thus it was said; in the verses, this refers to the touching of knowledge.
3. Commentary on the *Pahāna-sutta* (251).
In the third verse, "he cut off craving" means he severed and completely eradicated all craving. "He shook off the fetters."
He overturned even the tenfold fetter and rendered it rootless. "Sammā" means by way of cause or reason.
"Mānābhisamayā" refers to the realization through vision of conceit and the realization through its abandonment. For the path of arahantship, by way of its function, perceives conceit;
this is its realization through vision. Once it has been seen by that [path], it is abandoned at that very moment, just as one is by the poison of a [poisonous] sight.
It is like the life of beings who have been seen. This is his "clear realization through abandoning.

Regarding the phrase "he has made an end of suffering": because he has thus seen and abandoned conceit by means of the path of Arahantship, there is also the "final limit" (antima-ariyadanta) spoken of as:
"The end of the body’s binding wears away, like the tip of a green reed."
There are four "extremes" (*anta*): the "low extreme" spoken of as, "Bhikkhus, this is one extreme of livelihood"; the "partial extreme" spoken of as, "Personal existence (*sakkāya*) is one extreme";
the "limiting extreme" spoken of as, "This alone is the end of suffering, the destruction of all conditions" (*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 2.51;
2.4.71; *Udāna* 71); and [the fourth]. Among these, regarding the entirety of the suffering of saṃsāra...
"He made an end of that which is reckoned as the fourth limit" means he made a boundary, a demarcation;
it is said that he left nothing remaining but the final mass of suffering.

"He does not neglect clear comprehension" means he does not abandon clear comprehension. "He does not come to be counted [as one who is]" means [he is not counted] as one who is lustful, hateful, or deluded.
It does not conform to such a designation; having abandoned that designation, one is called "one whose taints are destroyed"—this is the meaning.
In this sutta, the underlying tendency toward the object (*ārammaṇānusaya*) is discussed. 4. Commentary on the Pātāla Sutta.
252. Regarding "the fourth, *pātāla*": it is called *pātāla* because it is sufficient (*alaṃ*) for falling (*pāta*), meaning there is no footing (*patiṭṭhā*) here.

"Non-existent" (*asantaṃ*) means not having come into being (*asambhūtattaṃ*) and not being perceived (*apaññāyamānattaṃ*). "He speaks such words" refers to the speech: "There is a *pātāla* in the great ocean.
For he [speaks thus] regarding that mouth of the whirlpool (*balavāmukhaṃ*) into which the water of the great ocean plunges with great force.
Having risen as far as one, two, or ten *yojanas*—even up to the edge of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) or Mount Sineru—it falls back again into the great ocean;
at the place where it falls, it is like a precipice into the great hell. This is what is called in the world "the mouth of the powerful" (*balavāmukha*).
It is with reference to this that he speaks thus.
However, because it serves as a resting place for such fish, turtles, devas, and dānavas, and is also a pleasant dwelling,
one speaks of that [place] as being present and existing, even though it is non-existent and not actually found there. Furthermore,
because all ordinary worldlings (puthujjana) are unable to endure physical painful sensations, therefore— [the word "āyu"] has this very meaning in the sense of "it is enough for the morning."
Showing what "the underworld" (pātāla) is, he said, "Monks, this refers to the bodily [remains]," and so forth.
"He did not stand firm in the underworld" means he did not find a footing within the underworld. "They find a foothold" (gādhanti) means they find a support.
"He cries out" means he wails, uttering unbridled and confused lamentations. "Weak" means having weak knowledge. "Lacking strength" means lacking the strength of knowledge.
"By way of limitedness, one who has a limited measure. In this sutta, "noble disciple" refers to a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*). For here, the stream-enterer is the primary subject;

however, it is also appropriate for a practitioner (*yogāvacara*) who possesses powerful insight (*vipassanā*), even if his intelligence is not sharp, provided he is capable of establishing himself without following after arisen feelings.
5. Commentary on the Daṭṭhabba Sutta 253.
In the fifth [sutta], "to be seen as suffering" means they are to be seen as suffering by way of their subjecting one to change (*vipariṇāma*).

"As a dart" means they are to be seen as a dart in the sense of piercing and causing pain. "As impermanent" means that, having been neither-painful-nor-pleasant, they exist in the mode of non-existence.
They are to be seen as impermanent. *Addā* means he saw. *Santam* means having the nature of peace.
6. Commentary on the Salla Sutta. 254.
In the sixth [verse], *tatra* refers to those two persons. *Anuvedham vijjheyya* means he would pierce right through that very opening of the wound.
Or, in a location adjacent by a finger’s breadth or two finger’s breadths, there is a piercing that follows through.
For one who has been pierced in this way, that subsequent piercing sensation is stronger than the initial sensation;
likewise, the painful feeling arising later is even stronger than the preceding feeling. "The escape from painful feeling" refers to [the escape] from painful feeling.
For concentration, the path, and the fruits are the escape; he does not know that, but knows only sensual pleasure as the escape.
"Of those feelings" means of those pleasant and painful feelings. "Being fettered, he feels it" means that being associated with defilements, he feels that feeling, not dissociated from them.
"Fettered in suffering": here the ablative case (*nissakka*) is used in the sense of the instrumental (*karaṇatthe*).
The meaning is: "associated with suffering. "Of one who has reckoned the Dhamma" means of one who has understood the Dhamma, who has weighed the Dhamma.
"Of one who is well-versed" means of one who is well-versed in the scriptures (*pariyatti*) and well-versed in realization (*paṭivedha*).
"He understands rightly, having gone to the further shore of existence": he has gone to Nibbāna, the further shore of existence; he understands that very Nibbāna rightly. In this [verse] as well...

In this sutta, only the underlying tendency toward the object (*ārammaṇānusaya*) is mentioned. Among the noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*), it is said that one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is the primary subject here, though they also say that a non-returner (*anāgāmī*) is likewise included.
7. Commentary on the First Gilāna Sutta (Sutta 255).
"Where the sick ward was, he approached": even the Tathāgata, the supreme person in the world with its gods...

He approached [the sick monk], thinking: "They will go to attend to the sick; they will believe and be convinced that 'the sick are indeed those who ought to be attended to,' and thus they will consider the sick as worthy of attendance.
And he thought: "I shall teach the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) to those for whom it is suitable there.
Regarding the passage beginning with "contemplating the body in the body," that which is to be said has been stated.
We shall explain this further below. "Contemplating impermanence" means contemplating impermanence (*aniccatā*). "Contemplating vanishing" means contemplating vanishing (*vaya*).

"Contemplating dispassion" means contemplating dispassion (*virāga*). "Contemplating cessation" means contemplating cessation (*nirodha*). "Contemplating relinquishment" means contemplating relinquishment (*paṭinissagga*).
What is shown by this much? It is the path of practice leading to the arrival of this bhikkhu.

For the foundations of mindfulness are indeed preliminary; and as for clear comprehension, these three contemplations—contemplation of impermanence, contemplation of vanishing, and contemplation of dispassion—are also preliminary.
Furthermore, these two—contemplation of cessation and contemplation of relinquishment—are also [preliminary].
[The section on] "mixed" [factors]. Up to this point, the time for the development of this bhikkhu has been shown;
the remainder is exactly as previously stated. 8–9. Commentary on the Second *Gelañña-sutta* and others (Suttas 256–257).

In the eighth sutta, the phrase "dependent on this very contact" is stated according to the inclination of those who would understand it thus; however, in terms of meaning, there is no difference between this and the previous. For here, the body itself is called "contact. The ninth sutta is self-evident.
10. Commentary on the Discourse Rooted in Contact (Phassamūlakasutta) 258.

In the tenth [discourse], "to be experienced as pleasant" (*sukhavedaniya*) means that which serves as a condition for pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*). The same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. Furthermore, the word-by-word commentary (*anupada-vaṇṇanā*) here has already been explained in detail below. In these two discourses, the feeling pertaining to the range of comprehension (*sammasanacāravedanā*) is discussed.
The first chapter, the Chapter with Verses (*Sagāthāvagga*), is concluded.
2. The Chapter on Being Gone into Solitude (Rahogatavagga) 1.

Commentary on the Discourse on Being Gone into Solitude (Rahogatasuttavaṇṇanā) 259. In the first discourse of the Chapter on Being Gone into Solitude, regarding the statement "whatever is felt, that is suffering": whatever is felt...

The meaning is that all of that is suffering. In such passages as "the impermanence of formations alone," etc., he points out that it was with reference to this very impermanence of formations—their nature of exhaustion, their nature of vanishing, and their nature of change—that I said, "Whatever is felt, that is suffering.
For whatever is the impermanence of formations, that is also [the impermanence] of feelings.
It is simply impermanence. And this impermanence is death; with the intention that there is no suffering greater than death, it is said that "all feelings are suffering.
Furthermore, the phrase "I, monks" is used to show that it is not only the cessation of feelings that I proclaim, but I also proclaim the cessation of these other phenomena as well.
It has been undertaken. The "subsiding" (*vūpasama*) and the "tranquillities" (*passaddhiyo*) are spoken of here according to the inclination of those who would awaken through such a teaching.
Furthermore, it should be understood that by the mention of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññā-vedayita-nirodha*), the four formless attainments (*āruppa*) are already included.
2–3. Commentary on the First Discourse on Space, etc. (*Paṭhama-ākāsasutta-vaṇṇanā*)

260–261. In the second [verse], “many winds blow” (*puthū vāyanti mālutā*) means many winds blow. The rest is self-evident. This third [section] was spoken with the intention of helping those who understand without [further] verses.
4. Commentary on the *Agārasutta* (The Discourse on the Householder) 262.
In the fourth [verse], “eastern” (*puratthimā*) means from the east. The same applies everywhere. Regarding the phrases “even worldly pleasant feelings,” and so forth:

"Sensual pleasure" (sāmisā sukhā) refers to feeling associated with the bait of sense-desires (kāmāmisapaṭisaṃyuttā vedanā). "Spiritual pleasure" (nirāmisā sukhā) refers to feeling arisen by way of the first jhāna and so forth, and by way of insight (vipassanā) and recollection (anussati).
"Sensual pain" (sāmisā dukkhā) refers to feeling that is sensual precisely because of the bait of sense-desires.
"Spiritual pain" (nirāmisā dukkhā) refers to [the pain] arising from the condition of longing for one who establishes a longing for the unsurpassed liberations (anuttare vimokkhe).

The arisen feeling of mental distress (*domanassa*). The "unworldly" (*sāmiṣā*) neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is a feeling that is unworldly precisely because of the bait of sensual desire (*kāma*).
The "unworldly" (*nirāmiṣā*) neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that arises by way of the fourth jhāna.
5–8. Commentary on the First *Ānanda-sutta* and others.

263–266. The four beginning with the fifth are exactly as explained above. However, of these, the first two possess complete tranquility (*passaddhi*), while the latter two possess only partial tranquility. They were spoken according to the inclinations of those who would attain awakening through the teaching.
9–10. Commentary on the *Pañcaṅga-sutta* and others:

267–268. In the ninth [sutta], "the householder Pañcaṅga": *Pañcaṅga* is his name; it refers to him by means of the five items consisting of an axe, a hatchet, a chisel, a staff, a mallet, and a black cord.
Or, because he was endowed with five factors, he was known as Pañcakaṅga. *Thapati* means a chief carpenter.
*Udāyī* refers to the wise Elder Udāyī. *Pariyāya* means a reason. "Both Ānandas" means both, Ānanda, by way of a *pariyāya*, that is, by way of a reason.
And here, they should be understood as two in terms of body and mind; or as three in terms of pleasure and so forth; or in terms of the faculties.
There are five beginning with the faculty of pleasure; six beginning with eye-contact-born [feeling], according to the doors;
eighteen beginning with "having seen a form with the eye, one investigates a form that is a basis for joy," according to the modes of investigation;
six joys based on the household life, six based on renunciation; six sorrows based on the household life, and six based on renunciation.
There are six kinds of equanimity based on the household life and six based on renunciation; thus there are thirty-six.
These are thirty-six in the past, thirty-six in the future, and thirty-six in the present; thus one hundred and eight types of feeling are to be understood.
"Ānanda, these five cords of sensual pleasure"—this is a separate connection. For it is not only beginning with two that feelings [are to be understood].
The Blessed One has taught that, by way of exposition, even a single feeling has been spoken of;
demonstrating this, he began this teaching in order to support the argument of the householder Pañcakaṅga. "More excellent" means more beautiful. "More sublime" means more tranquil.
And here, starting from the fourth jhāna, there is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; that too, in the sense of being peaceful...
And it is called "pleasure" in the sense of being sublime. Cessation (nirodha) is termed "pleasure" by way of the pleasure of non-experience.

For that which arises by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure and by way of the eight meditative attainments is called "pleasure of experience," whereas cessation is called "pleasure of non-experience.
Thus, whether it be the pleasure of experience or the pleasure of non-experience, it is [termed] "pleasure" in the sense of the state of being free from suffering.
It has arisen as exclusively pleasant.
"In whatever place" means in whichever location. "Pleasure is found" means that either felt pleasure or un-felt pleasure is found.
The Tathāgata designates all of that as pleasure; all of that the Tathāgata [designates].

"He describes the state of being without suffering as being in happiness itself. Here, the Blessed One, taking the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) as the heading, concluded the teaching by means of the pinnacle of Arahantship, according to the person who is to be guided (*neyya-puggala*). The tenth [sutta] is thus of plain meaning.
This is the second chapter, the Chapter on Seclusion.
3. The Chapter on the Mode of Exposition of One Hundred and Eight:
1. Commentary on the Sīvaka Sutta 269.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the third chapter, "Moliyasīvaka": *Sīvaka* is his name; however, he also has a crest (*cūḷā*).
Therefore he is called Moḷiyasīvaka. "Wanderer" refers to the wanderer Channa. "Arising from bile" means having bile as their condition.
"Feelings" refers to sensations (*vedanā*). In that regard, three kinds of feelings arise conditioned by bile. How so?
For someone might give a gift or observe virtue [thinking], "My bile is disturbed, and my life is indeed difficult to maintain."
One undertakes the precepts and performs the Uposatha ceremony; thus, wholesome feeling arises for him.
Another person, thinking, "I will prepare a bile-medicine," kills a living being, takes what is not given, speaks falsehood, and commits the ten unwholesome actions;
thus, unwholesome feeling arises for him. Another person [thinks], "Even by preparing this much medicine, my bile..."
"It subsides; let it be as it must be. Thus, remaining equanimous and enduring bodily feeling, he lies down;
in this way, indeterminate feeling arises for him.
"This is to be known by oneself" means that upon seeing each of those various bile disorders, this should be understood by oneself. "Agreed upon as truth" means...
"Agreed upon by the world": for even the world, seeing a disorder of bile such as discoloration and so forth in the body, knows, "His bile is deranged.
Therefore: because they overstep what is known by oneself and agreed upon as true by the world, therefore [it is said].
This same method applies to those arising from phlegm (*semha*) and so forth. Here, however, "arising from a combination" (*sannipātika*) refers to all three—bile and the others.
"Arising from cold" means those produced by an unsuitable temperature (*visabhāga-utu*).
For instance, an unsuitable temperature arises for those living in a dry region who dwell in a non-desert area, and likewise for those living in a non-desert area who dwell in a dry region;

in this way, an unsuitability of temperature certainly arises even by way of places such as the Malaya mountains or the shores of the ocean. "Produced from that" means they are called "arising from the transformation of temperature."

"Born from the avoidance of uneven ground" means those born from avoiding uneven terrain such as carrying heavy loads, pounding lime, or walking at improper times, or from pitfalls containing snakes or thorns.

"Caused by external means" means those arisen by making the condition of being beaten with shanks, iron bars, mallets, and so forth, after having been seized on the grounds that "this person is a thief" or "this person is an adulterer. This is the external [classification].
Having encountered an external effort, one person performs a wholesome deed, another an unwholesome one, and another lies down enduring it—just according to the method already described.
"Born solely from the ripening of kamma" means they have arisen purely from the maturation of kamma.

For when even these [kamma-born states] arise, one person performs a wholesome deed, another an unwholesome one, and another lies down enduring it, just according to the method already described. Thus it is in all instances.
There are three kinds of feelings.
Among them, bodily feelings arising from the first seven causes can be warded off;

however, for those born as the ripening of kamma (*kammavipākaja*), even all medicines and all protective charms (*paritta*) are not capable of providing a defense. In this sutta, what is called "worldly convention" (*lokavohāra*) is being discussed.
2–10. Commentary on the Eight Hundred Suttas, etc. (270–278).
Regarding the second [sutta], "the method of eight hundred" means that which serves as the cause for the eight hundred. "The method of the Dhamma" means the cause of the Dhamma.
In the phrase "both bodily and mental," here "bodily" is found only in the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), while "mental" [is found in the fine-material and immaterial spheres].
They also belong to four planes. Regarding "pleasant" and so forth: pleasant feeling does not exist in the formless realm (*arūpāvacara*), but is found in the remaining three planes;
painful feeling belongs only to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*); the others belong to all four planes.

In the pentad, the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, and the faculty of mental grief belong only to the sense-sphere; the faculty of mental joy belongs to the [first] three planes; the faculty of equanimity belongs to all four planes. In the hexad...
In the five doors, feeling belongs only to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*); in the mind-door, it belongs to all four planes.

In the eighteenfold set, they are called "investigations accompanied by joy" (*somanassūpavicāra*) because they proceed with joy in relation to the six desirable objects. The same method applies to the other two [types of investigation].
Thus, while this teaching is presented by way of the investigation (*vicāra*), here the eighteen feelings should be understood by way of the joy and so forth associated with them.

Regarding the passage beginning with "six kinds of joy based on the household," it is said: "Joy arises when one regards the acquisition of forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, charming, and connected with worldly gain;
or when one recollects what was previously acquired, which has passed away, ceased, and changed."

“Whatever kind of mental joy (*somanassa*) of this nature there is, this is called ‘joy based on the household life. Thus, the joys based on the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) mentioned in relation to the six sense-doors are called the six types of joy based on the household life.
“But having understood the impermanence of forms, their change, fading away, and cessation: ‘Formerly, indeed, as well as now, forms...’”
And when one sees with right wisdom, as it truly is, that ‘all these forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change,’ joy arises.
That kind of joy is called ‘joy based on renunciation.
Thus, when a desirable object enters the range of the six sense doors, one practices insight by way of impermanence and so forth.
For one who is able to arouse and intensify [insight] after having established it, the joy that arises with the thought,
"My insight has been intensified," consists of six types of joy based on renunciation (*nekkhammasita*).
These are the joys associated with worldly material things (*lokāmisa*) regarding forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, and pleasing.

“Or, when one regards what is not obtained as not obtained, or when one recollects what was previously obtained but is now past, ceased, and changed, sorrow arises. Such sorrow as this is called ‘sorrow based on the household life.
Thus, regarding the six sense doors, [the thought occurs]: “I shall not experience a desirable object,” or “I am not experiencing [one].”
The sorrows arising from one who reflects, which are based on the strands of sensual pleasure,
are called the six household sorrows. "Having understood the impermanence of forms, their change, fading away, and cessation— both formerly and now,
all those forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change"— thus one understands this as it really is with right wisdom.
Having seen this, he conceives a longing for the unsurpassed liberations, thinking:
"When indeed shall I enter upon and abide in that sphere which the noble ones now enter upon and abide in?
Thus, for one who conceives a longing for the unsurpassed liberations, sorrow arises conditioned by that longing. Such sorrow as this—this is [the sorrow].
This is called "dejection based on renunciation. Thus, when a desirable object has entered the range of perception at any of the six doors,

if one fails to arouse longing for the noble fruit-dhammas known as the supreme liberation, and fails to exert oneself by establishing insight through the contemplation of impermanence and so forth in order to attain them—
thinking, "Having exerted myself in insight for this fortnight, this month, or even this year..."

The states of dejection that arise in one who grieves, thinking, "I was unable to reach the plane of the noble ones," are called the six types of dejection based on renunciation (*nekkhammasita-domanassa*).

"Having seen a form with the eye, equanimity arises in the fool, the deluded worldling—unconqueror, unconqueror of karmic ripening, not seeing the danger, the uninstructed worldling. Such equanimity regarding form..."
It does not transcend them; therefore, that equanimity is called "based on the household life.

Thus, when a desirable object enters the range of the six sense doors, the equanimity that arises dependent on the strands of sensual pleasure—remaining stuck and clinging right there without transcending the forms and so forth, like flies clinging to a ball of sugar—is what is known as the sixfold equanimity based on the household life.

“Having understood the impermanence of forms, their change, fading away, and cessation—both past forms and those of the present—one who sees this as it really is with right wisdom, thinking, ‘All those forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change,’ gives rise to equanimity.
Such equanimity as this transcends form; therefore, it is called equanimity.”

"...is called 'based on renunciation' (nekkhammasita). Thus, when desirable and other objects have entered the range of the six sense doors, the equanimity that arises—being without lust for the desirable, without hatred for the undesirable, without looking on with indifference, and without delusion—is the equanimity associated with insight-knowledge (vipassanāñāṇa) known as "equanimity based on renunciation.
In this discourse, the section defining the phenomena of the four planes is all-inclusive.
It has been explained. The third and subsequent sections have their meanings already clarified.
11. Commentary on the Nirāmisasutta (The Discourse on the Non-Material):

In the eleventh [sutta], "with material" (*sāmisā*) means with the material of the defilements (*kilesāmisena*). "More non-material" (*nirāmisatarā*) refers even to the rapture of meditative absorption (*jhānapīti*), which is itself non-material.

It is more spiritual (nirāmisatarā). But surely, in two of the jhānas, joy (pīti) is both sublime (mahaggatā) and supramundane (lokuttarā), while the joy of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇapīti) is purely mundane (lokiyā);
why then is that [reviewing joy] said to be more spiritual? Because it arises through the reviewing of peaceful and sublime states (dhamma).
For just as a king’s favorite minor attendant, entering the royal palace at will and without obstruction, [is considered more distinguished than others].
The treasurer, the general, and the others do not count even when struck with a foot. Why? Because they are the king’s immediate attendants.

Thus, he is superior to them; in the same way, it should be understood that this [joy] is also superior even to supramundane joy because it arises through the reviewing of peaceful and sublime states. This same method applies to the remaining sections as well.

In the section on the liberations (*vimokkha*), however, a liberation associated with form is called "with the bait of form" (*sāmisa*) precisely because it has form as its object; one associated with the formless is called "without the bait of form" (*nirāmisa*) due to the absence of the bait of form.
The commentary on the Connected Discourses on Feeling is finished.
3. The Connected Discourses on Women (*Mātugāmasaṃyutta*).
1. The First Section on the Series of Repetitions (Paṭhamapeyyālavagga) 1–2. Commentary on the Discourses on Women (Mātugāmasuttādivaṇṇanā) 280–281.

In the first discourse of the Saṃyutta on Women (Mātugāmasaṃyutta), "by means of factors" (aṅgēhi) refers to unwholesome factors. "Not possessed of beauty" (na ca rūpavā) means not endowed with physical beauty.
He is ugly and unsightly. He is not wealthy, meaning he is not possessed of riches but is destitute. He is not virtuous, meaning he is not endowed with moral conduct but is immoral.
And he is lazy; he is unable to perform tasks such as tilling and cooking.

Being indolent and slothful, he merely sleeps while sitting in his sitting place, or while standing in his standing place. Furthermore, he does not obtain offspring—meaning for this man—there are no children.

One who does not obtain a son to establish the family lineage is called a barren woman (*vañjhitthī*). The "white side" (*sukkapakkha*) should be understood by reversing what was stated [for the dark side].
The second [section] should be transposed according to the same method as stated for the first.
3. Commentary on the Discourse on Exclusive Suffering (*Āveṇikadukkhasutta-vaṇṇanā*)
282. Regarding the third [section], "exclusive" (*āveṇika*) means individual, not shared with men. "Service" (*pāricariya*) refers to the state of being an attendant.
4. Commentary on the Sutta beginning with "By three qualities," etc. (283–303).

In the fourth [sutta], regarding the phrase "overwhelmed by the stain of stinginess": for at the time of the morning meal, women [are occupied] with the preservation of milk and curd, cooking, boiling, and so forth.
He began to give, yet even when entreated by his own children, he did not wish to give anything. Therefore it was said:
"In the morning, with a mind overwhelmed by the stain of stinginess. But at midday, women are as if overcome by anger;
finding no quarrel within their own home, they go even to the house of a neighbor to engage in a dispute, [and so too] the husband’s...
And he wandered about, looking at the places where [people] stood or sat. Therefore it was said: “At the time of midday, with a mind obsessed by envy.
But in the evening, her mind inclines toward the practice of unrighteousness. Therefore it was said:
“In the evening, with a mind obsessed by sensual lust. The fifth and subsequent [sections] have their meaning already explained.
3. The Chapter on Strength (Balavagga) 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Confidence (Visāradasuttavaṇṇanā) 304.

Regarding the tenth [discourse], in the phrases "the strength of form" and so forth: the excellence of physical form is the strength of form; the excellence of wealth is the strength of wealth; the excellence of kinsmen...
The strength of kinsmen; the strength of children, which is the excellence of having children; and the strength of virtue, which is the excellence of moral conduct.
For one who guards the five precepts and the ten precepts by keeping them unbroken, it is precisely this excellence of virtue that is called the "strength of virtue.
"These, monks, are the five strengths"—these five are called strengths in the sense that they provide support.
2–10. Commentary on the *Pasayha-sutta*, etc., §§305–313.
*Pasayha* means having overcome. *Abhibhuyya vattati* means he overcomes; he overwhelms.
*Neva rūpabalaṃ tāyati* means he is not able to protect or preserve the power of form. He simply destroys it.

“They do not let her live in the family” means that they seize her by the neck and expel her, saying, “She is immoral, her conduct is corrupt, and she has transgressed the bounds of propriety,” and thus they do not let her live in that family.
“They let her live in the family and do not expel her” means that having recognized, “What does it matter whether she is beautiful or possesses wealth and so forth?
She is pure in virtue and perfected in conduct,” the relatives let her live in that very family and do not expel her.
The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the Mātugāma-saṃyutta is finished.
4. Jambukhādaka-saṃyutta.
1. Commentary on the Nibbānapañhā Sutta 314.
In the Jambukhādaka Saṃyutta, "Jambukhādaka the wanderer" refers to the wanderer Channa, who was the nephew of the Elder.
Regarding the statement, "Friend, as for the destruction of lust": it is by coming to nibbāna that lust is destroyed; therefore...
Nirvana is called the destruction of lust; the same method applies to the destruction of hatred and delusion as well.
However, one who would claim on the basis of this very sutta that nirvana is merely the destruction of defilements should be asked:
"Whose defilements are destroyed? Are they one's own, or those of others? Certainly, he will say, "One's own. Thereupon, he should be questioned:
“What is the object of the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhuñāṇa)? Knowing [the answer], one would say, “Nibbāna.

But at the moment of the knowledge of change-of-lineage, have the defilements already been destroyed, are they being destroyed, or will they be destroyed? They cannot be said to have “been destroyed” or to be “being destroyed,” but it can be said that they “will be destroyed.
However, while those defilements are still undestroyed, does the knowledge of change-of-lineage [bring about] the destruction of defilements?
"Does it take an object? Certainly, when this is said, he will be left without an answer.

This should also be applied to path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*). For even at the moment of the path, the defilements cannot be said to be "extinguished" or "will be extinguished," but they can be said to be "being extinguished. And there is no extinction of defilements while the defilements themselves have not yet been extinguished.
It becomes an object; therefore, this must be accepted. That which, by depending upon it, lust and the other defilements are exhausted is Nibbāna.

Furthermore, because it is included among the "formless phenomena" (arūpino dhammā) in the pairs such as "form-possessing phenomena and formless phenomena," it is not merely the exhaustion of defilements.
2. Commentary on the Arahattapañhāsutta 315.

In the explanation of the Arahattapañha, because arahantship arises at the end of the exhaustion of lust, hatred, and delusion, it is therefore stated: "the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion.
3–15. Commentary on the Dhammavādīpañhāsutta and others.
316–328. They are called "Sugatas" (Well-Gone) in the world because, having abandoned passion and the other defilements, they have gone well; thus they are Sugatas.

"For the full understanding of suffering, friend," means for the sake of thoroughly knowing the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*). "The nature of suffering" (*dukkhatā*) is the essential quality of suffering. Regarding "the suffering of suffering" (*dukkhadukkhatā*) and so forth:
the essential quality of suffering that is designated as "suffering" is the "suffering of suffering. The same principle applies to the remaining two terms as well.
16. Commentary on the *Dukkarapañhā-sutta* 329.
*Abhirati*: This means being without weariness regarding the life of renunciation (*pabbajjā*). “Not long, friend”:

Friend, a bhikkhu who practices in accordance with the Dhamma thinks, “One instructed in the morning will attain distinction by evening; one instructed in the evening will attain distinction by morning.”
By stating this, it is shown that one who exerts effort and strives will, before long, easily become an Arahant and become established in Arahantship.
The rest is entirely clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the Jambukhādaka Saṃyutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Sāmaṇḍaka Saṃyutta 330–331.
In the Sāmaṇḍaka Saṃyutta as well, the meaning should be understood by this same method.
The commentary on the Sāmaṇḍaka Saṃyutta is finished.
6. Moggallāna Saṃyutta, 1–8.
Explanations of the First Jhāna Question Sutta and others, 332–339.
In the Moggallāna Saṃyutta, the phrase "accompanied by sensual desire" means accompanied by the five hindrances. For when he has emerged from the first jhāna...
The five hindrances appeared to him continuously. Consequently, that first jhāna of his became known as "partaking of decline.
Knowing of that negligence, the Teacher gave him the exhortation: "Do not be negligent!

The meaning should be understood in this same manner regarding the second jhāna and the others as well. For here, it is that which is accompanied by the object of meditation itself that is called "accompanied" (sahagata).
9. Commentary on the Animittapañhā Sutta (340).
"Signless concentration of mind": this was said with reference specifically to the concentration of insight (*vipassanā-samādhi*) that occurs after abandoning the signs of permanence and so forth.
"Consciousness follows after a sign": thus, by means of this dwelling in the concentration of insight...
While he was dwelling with insight-knowledge sharp, bold, and flowing— just as when a man cutting a tree with a sharp axe thinks,
"My axe is indeed working well," and because he looks at the edge of the axe at every moment,
the task of felling it is not accomplished; even so for the Elder, [while thinking] "My knowledge is indeed bold..."
“...flows along,” attachment arises with reference to insight.
Then, being unable to accomplish the task of insight, it is said with reference to that: “consciousness follows after signs.
By not attending to any signs, one enters and dwells in the signless concentration of mind; this is by way of not attending to all signs of permanence, pleasure, and self.
I entered and dwelt in the signless concentration of mind associated with insight leading to emergence, having Nibbāna as its object, which is the concentration of the higher paths and fruits.
10–11. Commentary on the Sakkasutta and others.

341–342. *Aveccappasādena* means with unshakable confidence (*acalappasādena*). *Dasahi ṭhānehi* means by way of ten reasons. *Adhigaṇhanti* means they overcome; they stand having transcended [them]. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the Moggallāna Saṃyutta is finished. 7. The Cittasaṃyutta.
1. Commentary on the Saṃyojana Sutta. 343.

Regarding the first sutta of the *Cittasaṃyutta*, "In Macchikāsaṇḍa"—that is, in a forest grove of that name—the phrase "this conversation arose" refers to the ancient elders (*porāṇakattherā*), who were not prone to frivolous talk; for wherever they sat, they would give rise to a question.
Not knowing, they asked; knowing, they answered. Thus this discussion arose among them.
"Migapathaka" was the name of his own village of property. It is said that it was situated on the back side of the Ambāṭakārāma.
He approached [the elders] thinking, "Having answered the question of the elders and having ensured their comfortable stay, I shall give [it to them]. In the deep...
"In the Buddha’s word" means in the Buddha’s word which is profound in meaning and profound in the Dhamma.
"The eye of wisdom traverses it" means that the eye of knowledge carries across and proceeds through it.
2. Commentary on the First Isidatta Sutta.
344. Regarding the second [question], "the venerable elder" refers to the eldest among those elders, the Great Elder (Mahāthera).

"He remained silent" means that although he knew [the answer], he did not say anything because of his lack of confidence. "I shall explain it, venerable sir," [he thought]: "This elder neither explains it himself nor requests others;
furthermore, this lay follower is harassing the Saṅgha of monks. I shall explain this for him..."
Thinking, "I will give [him] a comfortable dwelling," he rose from his seat, went to the Elder, and thus requested permission.
Having been granted permission, he sat down on his own seat and gave the explanation. *Sahatthā* means with one's own hand.
*Santappesi* means he thoroughly satisfied him by giving as much as he desired. *Sampavāresi* means...
“Enough! Enough! he made him desist by both a gesture of the hand and by speech. “With bowl removed from his hand” means that the bowl had been taken away from his hand;
the sense is that, having washed it and placed it in a bag, he had hung the bowl over his shoulder.
3. Commentary on the Second Isidatta Sutta.

345. Regarding the third [question], "In Avanti": this refers to the kingdom of Avanti in the southern region (Dakkhiṇāpatha). "'A blessing is spoken' means: 'We shall attend to you with the four requisites'—this statement is said to be faultless and blameless"; he says this with the underlying intention, "O lay follower.
4. Commentary on the Mahākapphiṇa-pāṭihāriya Sutta: 346. Regarding "Dispose of the remainder":
it is said that he had already wiped the bronze bowl together with the Elders.
Having increased the quantity of milk-rice (*pāyāsa*), they gave it to him. Having eaten the milk-rice, he thought, wishing to go together with the elders alone:
"In the house, the female lay devotee (*upāsikā*) will distribute the leftovers;

but here, these slaves and laborers will not distribute them unless told by me, and thus this excellent milk-rice will be lost. Granting them permission, he spoke as follows: "Kuthitaṃ" means "boiled" (*kudhitaṃ*).
The meaning is that it was becoming extremely hot due to the sand heated from below and the sun’s heat from above.
Furthermore, this is a phrase not found elsewhere in the Buddha’s word consisting of the Three Baskets (*Tepiṭaka*). Regarding the word *paveliyamānena*: it means being urged on;
he spoke thus, saying “It would indeed be well, venerable sir,” having thought, “I shall provide them with a comfortable dwelling.”
“He performed a feat of supernormal power by means of volitional formation” means he exercised the supernormal power of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāniddhi*).
In this context, there is both a variety of preliminary preparations—such as, “Let a very gentle, cool breeze blow;

let the rain fall, forming a canopy of clouds, and touch [the area] one by one”—and a single resolution, such as, “Let the rain fall with wind. Thus, “let the rain fall with wind” is an example of a single preliminary preparation.
"Let a very gentle, cool breeze blow; let the rain fall drop by drop, forming a pavilion of clouds"—such is the variety of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
In the manner already described, there is both a variety of preliminary work (*parikamma*) and a variety of resolutions;

likewise, there is also the case where the preliminary work is performed in one way and the resolution is made in another. However, for one who acts in whatever way [is appropriate], having emerged from the foundational jhāna—
For one who has performed the preliminary work (*parikamma*), that [attainment] succeeds by means of the mind fixed upon the sublime (*mahaggata*) immediately after the preliminary work.
"He cleared away" means he scattered it. 5.
Commentary on the First Kāmabhū Sutta 347. In the fifth [verse], *nelaṅgo* means faultless. *Setapacchādo* means having a white covering. *Anīghaṃ* means free from suffering.

“Having been silent for a moment” means: having remained silent for a moment in order to examine the meaning—investigating by turning the three Piṭakas over in his mind like earrings, thinking, “This is the meaning of this; this is the meaning of that. “By way of liberation” means:
by way of the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship. Furthermore, while speaking this question, the lay follower performed a difficult task.
The Fully Enlightened One spoke according to what he had actually seen, saying: "Behold, monks, this monk coming toward us—white-skinned, thin, and with a prominent nose.
But this [author], by grasping the underlying principle, said: "This is a designation for an arahant."
6. Commentary on the Second Kāmabhū Sutta (348).
Regarding the sixth [sutta], the question, "Venerable sir, how many kinds of volitional formations are there?"—it is said that this householder was practicing toward cessation (*nirodha*);
therefore, thinking, "I shall ask about the volitional formations that have cessation as their basis," he spoke thus. The Elder [Mahākaccāna] understood his intention.

Having understood that although many formations such as the formative volitions of merit exist, he spoke the passage beginning with "There are, householder, three... while specifically pointing out the bodily formation and so forth.
Therein, it is called a "bodily formation" (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) because it is bound to the body and is formed—that is, produced—by means of the body.
It is called a "verbal formation" (*vacīsaṅkhāra*) because it forms or produces by means of speech. Because it is bound to the mind, [it is produced] by means of the mind...
It is called "mental formation" (*cittasaṅkhāra*) because it is formed and produced by the mind.
But what is being asked here by the question, "But which, venerable sir"? [The answer is: "These formations are mixed together, intermingled, indistinct, and difficult to illustrate.
For instance, at the door of the body, there arise eight wholesome sense-sphere volitions (*kāmāvacara-kusala-cetanā*) following upon taking up, grasping, releasing, and moving."
The twelve unwholesome volitions—thus, these twenty wholesome and unwholesome volitions, as well as inhalation and exhalation, are called simply the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*).

At the door of speech, the twenty volitions of the aforementioned type that arise after reaching vocal articulation by means of the movement of the jaws, as well as applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), are called simply the verbal formation (*vacīsaṅkhāra*). [This occurs] without reaching movement at the doors of body or speech.

“Even the twenty-nine wholesome and unwholesome volitions that arise when one is sitting in private and reflecting, as well as these two factors—perception and feeling—are called mental formations (*cittasaṅkhāra*).
Thus, these formations are mixed together, agitated, indistinct, and difficult to illustrate;
I shall explain them by making them clear and manifest,” he asked.
"But why, venerable sir?"—here he asks for the word-meaning of "bodily formations" (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) and so forth. In the reply to that:
"bound up with the body" means dependent on the body; they exist when the body exists and do not exist when it does not. "Bound up with the mind" means dependent on the mind;
they exist when the mind exists and do not exist when it does not.
Now, asking in order to know whether "does this person enter the cessation of perception and feeling (saññā-vedayita-nirodha), or does he not? Is he one who has mastered it there, or is he not?
he said: "But, venerable sir, how does the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling come about?
In the reply to that, by the two phrases "they will attain" or "I shall attain," the time of attaining the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) is indicated.

It has been explained. By the word "attained" (*samāpanno*), internal cessation is indicated. Likewise, by the first two words, the period with consciousness is indicated, and by the last, the period without consciousness.
"Previously the mind was developed in such a way" means at the very time of delimiting the duration prior to the attainment of cessation.
The mind has been developed with a determination for a specific duration, thinking, “I shall remain without consciousness for this long.
As for the phrase “it leads to suchness,” that mind which has been developed in this way leads the person toward suchness—that is, toward the state of being without consciousness.
Regarding the statement “the verbal formation ceases first,” it means that among the remaining formations, it ceases first even in the second jhāna itself.
