It ceases. "Then the bodily formation" means that thereafter, in the fourth jhāna, the bodily formation ceases.
"Then the mental formation" means that thereafter, at internal cessation, the mental formation ceases. "Life-span" refers to the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*).
"Dissolved" means impaired and destroyed.
In this regard, some say: "Because of the statement that 'for one who has attained the attainment of cessation, the mental formation has ceased,' the mind is not ceased;
therefore, this attainment is also accompanied by mind. They should be told:
"Since there is the statement that 'his verbal formation also has ceased,' speech would likewise be unceased; therefore, one who has attained cessation could even speak Dhamma."

One may even have to sit while reciting the scriptures. Furthermore, since it is stated that for one who has died and passed away, "the mental formation (cittasaṅkhāra) has ceased," it would follow that the mind has not ceased [in the case of the other person].

Consequently, one who burns his deceased parents or Arahants would be committing an act of immediate retribution (ānantariyakamma). Thus, without adhering to the literal expression, [one must rely on] the teachers...
One should examine the meaning by standing upon the method; for the meaning is the refuge, not the letter.

Regarding the phrase "the faculties are serene": when the process consisting of kamma-formations is occurring and the sensory sensitivities (pasāda) are being struck by external objects, the faculties become fatigued and as if impaired or defiled by dust raised by the winds and other elements.

It is like a mirror placed at a crossroads. However, just as a mirror placed inside a casket or a chest after being put into a bag shines even more brilliantly within, so too do the five translucent organs (pasāda) shine exceedingly within the cessation of one who has attained the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpanna).
Therefore it is said: "The faculties are serene."

By the two phrases "they will emerge" (*vuṭṭhahissanti*) or "I am emerging" (*vuṭṭhahāmi*), the time of internal cessation is described; by the phrase "emerged" (*vuṭṭhito*), the time of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) is described.
Likewise, by the first two phrases the period of mindlessness is described, and by the last one, the period of possession of mind.
"Previously the mind was developed in such a way" refers to the very time of delimiting the duration prior to the attainment of cessation.
“Having remained without consciousness for this long, thereafter I shall become possessed of consciousness”—thus the mind is cultivated with a delimited duration.
That which "leads to suchness" means that the mind thus cultivated leads the person to suchness, that is, to the state of being possessed of consciousness.
Thus, below [this] is the time of entering the attainment of cessation.
It has been grasped; here, it is the time for emerging from cessation.
Now, as it is the time to discuss the discourse on cessation, the discourse on cessation should be explained. Furthermore, this [discourse] proceeds by way of:
"Because of being endowed with two powers, because of the subsiding of three formations, and by means of sixteen modes of knowledge and nine..."

Having established the heading: "The knowledge of the attainment of cessation is the wisdom consisting in mastery through the practices of concentration," this has been explained in every detail in the *Visuddhimagga*;
therefore, it should be understood according to the method explained therein. But what is this so-called "cessation"?
It is the non-occurrence of the four aggregates following their analytical reflection. Now, for what purpose do they enter into this attainment?
"Being weary of the occurrence of formations, we shall dwell happily for seven days remaining without consciousness;
this is indeed Nibbāna in the present life, namely cessation"—it is for this purpose that they attain [the attainment of cessation].
As for the statement "the mental formation arises first": for one emerging from cessation, the fruit-attainment consciousness (phalasamāpatti-citta) [arises first].
It arises first. Referring to the perception and feeling associated with it, he said, "The mental formation arises first.
Then, as for "the bodily formation": after that, at the moment of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the bodily formation arises.
But does the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) not arouse inhalation and exhalation? It does arouse them. However, of this...
The attainment of fruition belonging to the fourth jhāna does not arouse [the breath]. But what is the point of this?

Whether the attainment of fruition belongs to the first jhāna, or to the second, third, or fourth jhāna, for a bhikkhu who has emerged from a peaceful attainment, inhalation and exhalation are beyond reckoning;
their state of being beyond reckoning is illustrated by the case of the Elder Sañjīva.

This should be understood. For when the Elder Sañjīva emerged from attainment and walked while treading upon glowing embers resembling *kiṃsuka* flowers, not even a thread of his robe was burned, nor was there even the slightest appearance of heat. They say, "Such is the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-bala*).
In the very same way, for a bhikkhu who has emerged from the attainment of fruition (*phala-samāpatti*), the inhalations and exhalations [do not occur].
"It is called 'utterance' (abhohārika)" should be understood as being said with reference to the moment of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
"Then there is verbal formation" means that thereafter, at the time of the manifestation of the functional process consisting of action, verbal formation arises.

Does the life-continuum not arouse applied thought and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra)? It does arouse them. However, the applied thought and sustained thought that arise from it [are those produced by the functional process].
The statement "they are unable to formulate speech" refers specifically to the moment of cognizing [an object] during the occurrence of a process consisting of activity.
"Contact through emptiness" (*suññato phasso*) and so forth should be explained both in terms of their qualities and their objects. First, regarding the qualities:

"emptiness" (*suññatā*) is the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*); referring to the contact co-arising with that, it is called "contact through emptiness. This also applies to the signless (*animitta*) and the desireless (*appaṇihita*).
The same method applies here. However, as for the object: Nibbāna is called "emptiness" (suññatā) because it is empty of lust and the other defilements;
it is "signless" (animitta) because of the absence of the signs of lust and so forth; and it is "desireless" (appaṇihita) because of the absence of longing for lust, hatred, and delusion.
The contact of the attainment of fruition that arises having made emptiness-Nibbāna its object is called "empty. The same method applies to the signless and the desireless as well.
There is another discourse called "The Discourse on What is to be Realized. For insight is also called emptiness (*suññatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and desirelessness (*appaṇihita*).

In this context, when a bhikkhu, having discerned formations as impermanent and having seen them as impermanent, emerges [from concentration] by way of impermanence, his insight leading to emergence is called "signless" (*animittā*). When one, having discerned them as suffering and having seen them as suffering...

Having perceived [the aggregates] as suffering, one emerges from them; for such a person, this is called the signless (appanihita). Having comprehended them as non-self and having perceived them as non-self, one emerges from them as non-self;
for such a person, this is called emptiness (suññatā). In that context, the path associated with signless insight is called the signless path;
the fruit of the signless path is called the signless fruit; and the contact co-arising with the attainment of the signless fruit is likewise so named.
When touching, it is said that "signless contact touches. The same method applies to wishless and empty contact as well.
However, if it were spoken of by way of what is to be arrived at, one would fall into the alternative view that "contact is either empty, or signless, or wishless";
therefore, it must be spoken of by way of both its quality and its object. For in this way, it is consistent that "three types of contact touch."

In such passages as "inclined toward seclusion" (*vivekaninna*), Nibbāna is called "seclusion. That which is inclined toward, or bent down toward, that seclusion is "inclined toward seclusion" (*vivekaninna*).
That which, without going elsewhere, stands as if curved toward seclusion is "sloping toward seclusion" (*vivekapoṇa*).
That which stands as if falling toward seclusion is "leaning toward seclusion" (*vivekapabbhāra*).
7. Commentary on the Godatta Sutta 349.

Regarding the seventh [sutta], "both different in meaning and different in phrasing": for these [teachings], there is difference both in the phrasing (*byañjana*) and in the meaning (*attha*). Among these, the difference in phrasing is evident.
As for the meaning, however, the measureless liberation of mind (*appamāṇā cetovimutti*) is sublime (*mahaggatā*) because it belongs to a different plane of existence.

The "signless" (animitta) is, in terms of plane, belonging to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara); in terms of object, it has the seven designations as its object. The "nothingness" (ākiñcañña) is, in terms of plane, sublime (mahaggata) and belongs to the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara);
in terms of object, its object is not to be specified. The "emptiness" (suññatā) is, in terms of plane, belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara);
in terms of object, it has formations (saṅkhāra) as its object—for here, "emptiness" is intended in the sense of insight (vipassanā). The "signless" is, in terms of plane, supramundane (lokuttara).
In terms of its object, it has Nibbāna as its object.
In such passages as, "Lust, venerable sir, is a maker of measure," and so forth— just as there is water at the foot of a mountain consisting of decaying leaves and moss which is black in color,
and which appears to those looking down as if it were a hundred fathoms deep, even though [there is no depth]— whether it be a staff or a rope...

Just as there is not even enough space on the back of one's foot to cover it for someone measuring with a scale, even so, as long as lust and the other defilements have not arisen, it is impossible to perceive the individual;
he appears like a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner.
But when lust and the others arise in him, then he is known as "lustful," "hateful," or "deluded."
Thus, because they arise merely to show the measure of a person by saying, "This one is this much," they are called "measure-makers.
As for the statement, "Venerable sir, as to how immeasurable are the deliverances of mind": however many deliverances of mind there are that are immeasurable.
But how many are they? They are twelve: the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra), the four paths, and the four fruits. Among these, the divine abodes...

They are immeasurable because of their boundless nature; and Nibbāna is also immeasurable because it is devoid of those defilements that create limits, yet it is not "liberation of mind" (cetovimutti), and therefore it was not included here. "Unshakable" refers to the liberation of mind that is the fruit of Arahantship.
For that is the most senior of them all, and therefore it is said to be "declared the foremost. "Lust, venerable sir, is indeed a possession."
Lust, having arisen, afflicts, crushes, and binds a person; therefore it is called "affliction" (*kiñcana*).
It is said that when people have oxen trample a threshing floor, they say, "Trample it, Kapila! Trample it, Kāḷaka! Thus, the sense of crushing should be understood as the sense of affliction.
The same method applies to hatred and delusion as well.
The so-called "liberations of mind through nothingness" (*ākiñcaññā cetovimuttiyo*) consist of nine things: the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*), the paths, and the fruits.
In this context, the base of nothingness is called "nothingness" (*ākiñcañña*) because it has no "anything" (*kiñcana*)—that is, no object—remaining.

The paths and fruits are "nothingnesses" (*ākiñcaññāni*) because of the absence of "anythings," namely the defilements that crush and fetter; Nibbāna is also "nothingness," as is the liberation of mind.
However, it does not exist [in that way], and therefore it was not included.
In passages such as "Lust, venerable sir, is the making of signs," it is as if there were two calves similar to one another from two different families.
As long as their distinguishing marks have not been made, one cannot say, "This is the calf of such-and-such a family; this is..."

It is not possible to know [the person] by thinking, "He belongs to such-and-such a family. However, when one of their identifying marks, such as a trident, has been made, then it is possible to know.

In the same way, as long as lust has not arisen in a person, it is not possible to know whether they are "an Ariya" or "a worldling. But when lust arises in them, [they are known as] "one possessed of lust."
It arises as if making a sign for recognition, thinking, "This is such-and-such a person"; therefore, it is called "making a sign.
The same method applies to hatred and delusion as well.
The so-called "signless liberations of mind" consist of thirteen factors: the three types of insight, the four formless attainments, and the four paths.
There are four fruits. In that context, insight is called "signless" because it dispels the sign of permanence, the sign of pleasure, and the sign of self.
The four formless attainments are called "signless" due to the absence of the sign of form. The paths and fruits are signless by virtue of the absence of the defilements that produce signs;
Nibbāna likewise is signless, yet it is not the liberation of mind (cetovimutti).

Therefore, it was not included. Now, why was the emptiness liberation of mind (*suññatā cetovimutti*) not included? Because, according to such statements as "empty of lust," it is already fully incorporated in all [the other liberations];
therefore, it was not mentioned separately.
They have the same meaning means they have the same meaning by way of their object; for all these—“the immeasurable,” “nothingness,” “emptiness,” and “the signless”—[share this commonality].
These are indeed names for Nibbāna itself. Thus, by this method, they have the same meaning.

However, in another context it is "the immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*), in another "nothingness" (*ākiñcañña*), in another "emptiness" (*suññatā*), and in another "signlessness" (*animitta*); by this method, they have different verbal expressions.
8. Commentary on the Discourse to Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.

350. Regarding the eighth [sutta], "he approached him": being himself one who has arrived at the goal, one who has understood the teaching, and an Ariyan disciple who is a non-returner (*anāgāmī*), why did he approach the Nigaṇṭha, who was naked, devoid of dignity, and stripped of his robes?
It was for the purpose of clearing away slander and for the purpose of establishing a formal debate.
For it was said that the Nigaṇṭhas claimed, "The disciples of the ascetic Gotama are like stiff khadira-wood posts; they do not engage with anyone..."

“They do not even offer a hospitable welcome,” they say, censuring him. It was for the sake of being released from that censure, and thinking, “I shall bring a charge against him,” that he approached.

“Venerable sir, it is not out of faith in the Blessed One that I go to him regarding this”—this refers to one who has not yet realized it through direct knowledge. Such a person might go on the basis of another’s faith, thinking, “It is indeed so”; but by me, however—
He spoke thus, demonstrating: "This has been realized by me through direct knowledge; therefore, I do not proceed here on the basis of faith in the Blessed One.
"Looking up" means: having raised the body, drawn out the belly, and extended the neck, looking about in all directions.
"One might think it should be obstructed" means: it should be warded off in such a way that it does not emerge after having pierced through.
"One might think it should be bound. "In accordance with the Dhamma" means having a valid reason. "Then you should respond to me together with the assembly of Nigaṇṭhas":
once the meaning of these [terms] is understood, then you should approach me together with the assembly of Nigaṇṭhas;
the meaning is that, having come to me for the purpose of responding, you should make known the fact of your own arrival. "A single question" means...
"One question-path" means one way of seeking a question. "One summary" (uddesa): what is called "one"?
This is the one summary. "One exposition" (veyyākaraṇa): "All beings subsist by nutriment"—this is the one exposition.
In this manner, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.
9. Commentary on the Acelakassapa Sutta 351. Regarding the phrase "How long has it been since he went forth?":
the meaning is, "What length of time has elapsed since he went forth? "Superhuman states" (*uttari manussadhammā*):

"human states" (*manussadhamma*) refers to the ten courses of wholesome action; [the phrase means] beyond those human states. "A distinction of noble knowledge and vision" (*alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso*): [this refers to the attainment of the fruits of the path].
The distinction of knowledge and vision termed "adept" (*alam-ariya*) is so called because of its capacity to achieve the state of a noble one (*ariya-bhāva*).
"Nakedness" (*naggeyya*) is due to the state of being naked. "Shaven-headedness" (*muṇḍeyya*) is due to the state of being shaven.

"For the purpose of brushing away gravel" (*pavāḷanipphoṭanāya*) means for the sake of brushing away the dust, dirt, and sand that stick to the seat when one is sitting on the ground; it refers merely to a peacock-feather whisk held for that purpose.
10. Commentary on the Discourse on Visiting the Sick (Gilānadassanasutta) 352.
In the tenth [discourse], "garden deity" (*ārāmadevatā*) refers to a deity dwelling in flower gardens or fruit gardens. "Forest deity" (*vanadevatā*) refers to a deity dwelling in forest thickets.
"Tree deity" (*rukkhadevatā*) refers to Vessavaṇa during the time of King Mātta, and so forth; thus, in those various [contexts]...

"Deities dwelling in trees": deities dwelling in medicinal herbs, grasses, and forest giants—such as the *harītakī* and *āmalakī* trees, the *muñja* and *pabbaja* reeds, and the preeminent trees of the forest. "Having gathered together" means having assembled.
"Having come together from here and there. "Make a resolve" means establish it by way of aspiration. "The mental resolve of the virtuous person will succeed."
The heart’s aspiration of one possessed of virtue will succeed. "Righteous" (*dhammika*) means endowed with the ten wholesome qualities and free from going upon wrong paths.
"King of Dhamma" (*dhammarāja*) is a synonym for that very same person; or, he is a King of Dhamma because his sovereignty was obtained through the Dhamma.
Therefore, when you say, "In that case, noble son, please instruct us as well," it is because of this. "Undivided" (*appaṭivibhatta*)...
Thinking, "We will give this to the monks, and we ourselves will eat this," it remains undivided and shall indeed be shared in common with the monks.
The commentary on the *Cittasaṃyutta* is finished.
8. Gāmaṇisaṃyutta 1.
Commentary on the Caṇḍasutta 353.
In the first discourse of the Gāmaṇisaṃyutta, "Caṇḍo gāmaṇī" (The Fierce Headman) is the name adopted by the elders who compiled the Dhamma.
"O village headman, one person. "He makes himself manifest" means he shows himself by quarreling with one who quarrels, reviling one who reviles, and striking back at one who strikes.
"He does not make himself manifest" means he shows that even when reviled or struck, he does nothing in opposition.
2. Commentary on the Tālapuṭa Sutta 354.
In the second [sutta], "Tālapuṭa" is one who has such a name. It is said that the color of his face was as clear as the color of a palm fruit released from its stalk;
therefore, they gave him the name Tālapuṭa. He was one who had perfected his resolution (*abhinīhāra*).
He was a person destined for his final existence. Since rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) is indeed indeterminate, like a stick thrown into the air, he was consequently born into a family of actors.
Having reached maturity, he became the preeminent master of the art of acting and became famous throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.
His retinue consisted of five hundred carts and five hundred women; even his wife—
Whenever he entered a city or a town accompanied by those many thousands of women and a thousand carts,
they would give him a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] even before his arrival. Furthermore, when he assumed the dress of a festival-goer and sported with the thousand women,
whatever collection of ornaments there was— such as those for the hands and feet— [he received].

They hurl [insults] at him, yet there is no end to it. On that day, having sported in Rājagaha surrounded by a thousand women, he—because his knowledge had reached full maturity—approached the Blessed One together with his retinue.
"By truth and falsehood" means by both truth and untruth. "Let this be" means let this remain. "Lust-inducing" means as a condition for lust.

There are dramatic gestures (*abhinaya*) such as the display of drawing five-colored threads from the mouth, or the appearance of wind and rain, and other such modes associated with the gratification of sensual desire (*kāmasāda*).
"To a greater degree" means by way of their excessive magnitude. "Provocative of hatred" refers to modes of display such as the cutting off of hands and feet caused by hatred.
"Provocative of delusion" refers to acts such as taking water and making it into oil, or taking oil and making it into water, which are caused by delusion.
These and others are the various divisions of Māyā.
Regarding what is called the "Pahāsa" hell: there is no separate hell specifically named Pahāsa;

rather, it refers to a certain section of the Avīci hell itself where beings are tormented while dancing and singing as if they had assumed the guise of actors. It is with reference to this that [the term is used].

It is said: "Venerable sir, I do not weep for this. Here, the meaning should be understood in the sense of having an object (*sakammaka*), namely, "I do not weep for this answer of the Blessed One," and not merely as the shedding of tears.
Furthermore, other conventional expressions such as "weeping for the dead" (*matam amma rodantī*) should also be understood in this context.
3–5. Commentary on the *Yodhājīva-sutta* and others (355–357).
In the third [sutta], a *yodhājīva* is one who makes his living by means of warfare; this is the name adopted by the Theras who compiled the Dhamma.
"Exerts" (*ussahati*) or "strives" (*vāyamatī*) means he exerts effort or makes an endeavor. "They cause to perish" (*pariyāpādentī*) means they cause him to undergo death.
*Dukkaṭa* means badly done; *duppaṇihita* means badly placed. "The defeated hell" is not a separate hell in itself;

rather, it refers to a certain section of the Avīci hell where beings are roasted like those clad in fivefold armor and carrying shields, mounted on elephants, horses, and chariots, as if engaged in battle. It is with reference to this that it was said. The same method applies to the fourth and fifth [sections] as well.
6. Commentary on the Asibandhakaputtasutta 358.

In the sixth [verse], "those from the western lands" (*pacchābhūmakā*) means those who dwell in the western regions. "Carrying water-pots" (*kāmaṇḍalukā*) means those who possess their own water-pots (*kamaṇḍalu*).

"Wearing garlands of water-moss" (*sevālamālikā*) means that early in the morning they take water-moss as well as blue lotuses and other flowers from the water, and wear them as a garland for the purpose of knowing whether they have been purified by the water.
"Adorned with ornaments. "Those who descend into the water" means those who descend into the water morning and evening. "They urge them on" means they cause them to go upward.
"They instruct them" means they cause them to know correctly. "They lead them to heaven" means standing around [the dying person], saying, "Go, sir, to the Brahma-world!
Go, sir, to the Brahma-world! they cause them to enter heaven. "They should walk around" means...
One should go around following it. "Ummujjā" means emerge; rise up. "Thalamuplavā" means ascend to dry land.
"Tatra yāssā" means whatever might be there. "Sakkharā vā kaṭhalā vā" means gravel and pebbles.
"Sā adhogāmī assā" means that would go downwards; it would be something going to the bottom. "Adhogacchā" means go downwards.
7. Commentary on the Khettūpama Sutta (The Simile of the Field) 359.
In the seventh [verse], *jaṅgala* means hard, not soft. *Ūsara* means saline soil where salt has formed. *Pāpabhūmi* means a portion of land that is inferior. Regarding *maṃdīpā* and so forth:
those for whom I am the island (*dīpa*) and the support (*patiṭṭhā*) are *maṃdīpā*. Those for whom I am the shelter (*leṇa*) and the place of refuge (*allīyanaṭṭhāna*) are [likewise so called].
"Maṃleṇā": they have me as their refuge and protection; thus they are "maṃtāṇā. "Maṃsaraṇā": they have me as their resort for the destruction of fear; thus they are "maṃsaraṇā. "Viharanti":
they dwell having made me [their refuge] in this way. "Gobhattanapi":
in the summer season, when there is a lack of grain and fruit, [the fodder] is gathered, tied into bundles, and set aside.
The meaning is: "There will even be the eating of meat. *Udakamaṇiko* is a specific type of vessel so named because of a girdle of jars (*maṇika*) around its belly.
*Ahārī aparihārī* means it does not bring water nor carry it about; the meaning is that it does not contain [the water].
Thus, in this sutta, only careful preaching of the Dhamma is discussed. For careless preaching of the Dhamma by the Buddhas—
There is no such thing. For Buddhas are of a nature equal to a lion;

just as a lion exerts the same identical speed whether for the sake of seizing a mighty rutting elephant or even a hare or a wildcat, so too do the Buddhas teach with equal care whether teaching one person, two, many, or an assembly of monks, an assembly of nuns, laymen, laywomen, or even followers of other sects.
They listen having first placed their faith and having gained conviction. Thus, the teaching given to them is called "careful teaching.
8. Commentary on the *Saṅkhadhamasutta* (The Conch-Blower Sutta) In the eighth [sutta], by the phrase "whatever is much, whatever is much," the Nigaṇṭha himself contradicts his own doctrine.

Therefore, since this is so, the Blessed One said: "In that case, no one at all is destined for the states of deprivation," and so forth. However, the first four phrases are conditions for [wrong] view.
Therefore, showing the danger even in those, he said: "Here, headman, a certain teacher holds such a doctrine," and so forth.
In that context, *ahampamhi* means "I also am."

Regarding "accompanied by loving-kindness" (*mettāsahagatena*) and so forth, everything that needs to be said—including the method of meditation (*bhāvanānaya*)—has already been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.
However, the passage beginning with "Just as if, headman, a powerful conch-blower... is new here.

In that context, "powerful" (*balavā*) means endowed with strength; "conch-blower" (*saṅkhadhamo*) means one who blows a conch shell; and "without difficulty" (*appakasirena*) means without hardship or suffering.
For a weak conch-blower, even while blowing the conch, is unable to make himself known by his sound in the four directions;
his conch-sound does not pervade everywhere. But for one who is strong, it is far-reaching. Therefore, he said, "strong.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the liberation of mind through loving-kindness" (*mettāya cetovimuttiyā*): here, when "loving-kindness" (*mettā*) is mentioned, both access concentration (*upacāra*) and absorption (*appanā*) are acceptable; however, regarding "liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*), [only absorption is intended].

But when it has been stated, absorption itself is required. Regarding "action performed with a limited measure": action performed with a limited measure is said to be that of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), while action performed without a limited measure is that of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).

For the latter is called "performed without a limited measure" because it is performed by extending it beyond limits through the methods of directional pervasion—whether specifically directed or not specifically directed.

"It does not remain there, it does not persist there" means that this sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) kamma neither lags behind nor stands still within that fine-material or immaterial-sphere (*rūpārūpāvacara*) kamma.
What is meant? That sense-sphere kamma cannot cling to or stand between that fine-material or immaterial-sphere kamma;
rather, having been overwhelmed and exhausted by the fine-material or immaterial-sphere kamma, it makes no room for itself.

Having taken hold [of it], one is unable to remain established. Rather, it is only the karma of the fine-material and immaterial spheres that, like a great flood, pervades and exhausts the limited water of the sense-sphere, making way for itself and remaining there;
having warded off its own result, it leads one by itself to companionship with the Brahmās. Thus, this sutta begins with the defilements (kilesa).
Having emerged at the conclusion [of the discourse], because it was taken up by way of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra), it proceeded according to the natural sequence.
9. Commentary on the Kula Sutta (Discourse on Families) 361.
In the ninth [sutta]: "Famine" means that alms-food is difficult to obtain. "Drought" means [a state where one thinks] "Shall we live, or shall we not?"

Thus it proceeds as "pavattaīhitikā. There is also a reading, "duhitikā," which has the same meaning. It is called *duhitikā* because here one cannot perform any activity with ease; suffering (*dukkha*) is the striving (*īhiti*) here.
It is called *setaṭṭhikā* because there are white bones (*seta-aṭṭhikāni*) scattered here and there of people who have died.
It is called *salākāvuttā* because it subsists on mere sticks (*salāka-matta-vuttā*); whatever is placed or sown there [is merely a stick].
It was merely like a tally-stick; the meaning is that it did not produce fruit.

"He could not spit it out" means that, being unable to speak after releasing the two ends, he was unable to spit it out—that is, to bring it outside. "He could not swallow it down" means that, seeing the fault in his answer, being unable to withdraw it, he was unable to swallow it down—that is, to make it enter within.
"O village headman, from ninety-one aeons ago," while the Blessed One was thus speaking, [the time passed] until the breath exhaled through the nose had ceased.
He entered again, and in that same amount of time he recollected ninety-one eons for the purpose of full understanding:

"Has there ever been anything in this family that was spoiled by the giving of cooked alms-food to a bhikkhu? Then, seeing not even a single instance, he said, "From here on, village headman," and so forth.
Now, while speaking of the benefits of giving and so on, he said: "Then those families which are wealthy..."
He began the teaching on the Dhamma. In this context, "born of giving" means produced or brought forth by giving.
The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. Here, "truth" refers to truthfulness; "recluseship" refers to the remaining virtues.
"Scatters" means that one disperses them by employing them improperly. "Blows away" means he destroys them as if blowing upon them. "Shatters" means he destroys them.
“Impermanence” means non-existence after having existed; it is the vanishing in a mere moment of those who have been joined together, even over a long period of time.
362. Commentary on the Maṇicūḷaka Sutta:
Regarding the tenth [sutta], “He said this to that assembly,” it is said that he thought thus: “When sons of noble family go forth, they leave behind their wives and children...”
"Having abandoned gold and silver, they go forth into homelessness; and it is not possible for those who have gone forth to take back what they have abandoned.

Standing on this principle, he spoke the words beginning with "Do not, noble sir. "One should hold this to be absolute" means that one should maintain with certainty that the practice of the five strands of sensual pleasure is contrary to the dhamma of a recluse and contrary to the dhamma of a follower of the Sakyan son.
"Grass" refers to the grass used for covering a lodging.
"Should be sought" means that when a house—whether covered with grass or covered with bricks—is falling into ruin, one should go to those by whom it was built and inform them:
"The lodging built by you is leaking; it is not possible to live there. If people are able, they will repair it.
If they are unable [to do it themselves], they will say, "You yourselves take a carpenter and have it built; we shall persuade him.
When this has been said, having had it built, it should be pointed out to them. People will give what is to be given to the carpenters.

If there are no owners of the dwelling, it is permissible to have it built after announcing it to others as well by means of the conduct for alms-round (*bhikkhācāra-vatta*). It is with reference to this that [it was said].
"It should be sought after" is what was stated.
"Wood" refers to timber for the purpose of repairing a dwelling when rafters and other parts are decaying. "A cart" refers to a temporary cart made by modifying a household vehicle.
And it is not only a cart; other implements such as axes, adzes, and spades may also be included.
It is proper to seek [a donor] in this way. Regarding "a man": a man should be sought by means of manual labor (*hatthakamma*).

For if one says to any man whatsoever, "Friend, you will give after performing manual labor," and he replies, "I will, venerable sir," it is proper to have him do whatever one desires, saying, "Do this and that. But, Gāmaṇi, I would not [allow it] by anyone...
"By way of a method" means: I do not say that gold and silver should be sought for any reason whatsoever.
**Commentary on the Bhadraka Sutta, Chapter 11** 363.
"In the Mallas": in the country of that name. "By execution" means by killing. "By loss" means by the loss of wealth.
"By one who has attained it without delay" means not by one who has attained it after an interval of time; the meaning is: by one who has attained it without exceeding the [proper] time.
"The youth named Ciravāsi" refers to his son, who bore that name. "He dwells in an outer residence" means he lives outside the city, learning some craft or other.
In this sutta, the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) is described.
12. Commentary on the Rāsiya Sutta 364.
Regarding the twelfth [sutta], it is called "Rāsiya" because the question was asked by grouping [the topics] together; thus it received this name from the Elders of the Dhamma-saṅgaha.
"Tapassin" means one who relies on austerity. "Lūkhajīvin" means one who lives a harsh life. "Antā" means sections or divisions.
"Village" means a village. There is also a reading "gammā," which means the practice (dhamma) of those living in a village.
"Devotion to self-mortification" means devotion to one's own mortification; the meaning is the infliction of physical suffering upon oneself.
But why is devotion to sensual pleasure mentioned here? Why is devotion to self-mortification mentioned? And why is the Middle Way mentioned?
What is the practice? First, devotion to the pleasure of sense-desires is mentioned for the purpose of showing those who enjoy sensual pleasures;

devotion to self-mortification is mentioned for the sake of those who rely on austerity; and the middle way is mentioned for the purpose of showing the three bases for the wearing away [of defilements].
What is the purpose of showing these? It is so that the Tathāgata, having abandoned these two extremes, might proceed by the middle way.
Having attained perfect enlightenment, he neither censures nor praises all those who enjoy sensual pleasures, nor does he censure or praise all those who rely on self-mortification;
rather, he censures only those who deserve censure and praises only those who deserve praise.
It should be understood that the purpose of showing these [examples] is to illustrate this meaning.
Now, in order to clarify that meaning, he said: "There are three types of sensual enjoyers, village headman," and so forth. Therein, "by violence" means by a violent act.
"Does not share" means he does not make a distribution among friends, companions, those seen together, and those with whom he is associated.
"Does not perform meritorious deeds" means he does not perform meritorious deeds that serve as conditions for future existence. "By what is righteous and unrighteous" means...
"Both by means of the Dhamma and by means of non-Dhamma. "By means of grounds" means by means of causes. How does he realize [the goal] by exerting and tormenting himself?
By way of the fourfold energy and by way of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga). Regarding the phrase "three kinds of visible weariness":
here, even though there is only one path, it is called "three kinds of weariness" because of its wearing away of the three defilements.
13. Commentary on the Pāṭaliya Sutta 365.
Regarding the thirteenth [verse], "messages" (*dūteyyāni*) refers to the duties of a messenger, namely both written communications and oral instructions.

Why was the phrase "I know [the taking of] life" (*pāṇātipātañca āhaṃ*) introduced? It is for the purpose of demonstrating his omniscience, showing that "not only do I know *māyā*, but I also know this and that other thing."
"It has been undertaken. For, headman, the statement "There are certain recluses and brahmins...
was undertaken to show the views of other recluses and brahmins and to cause their abandonment of them.

"Adorned with garlands and earrings" means: he is adorned with a garland (*mālī*) by means of a garland, and he is adorned with earrings (*kuṇḍalī*) by means of earrings. "With desires for women" means: desires together with women.

"Women's desires" means those women who are objects of desire. "A dwelling house" (*āvasathāgāra*) refers to a residence built in a particular spot within a family home for the comfortable living of each individual.
"Therefore, I share [it] according to my ability and according to my strength" means that I make a distribution to her in accordance with my own capacity and in accordance with my power.
"It is enough" (*alam*) means it is appropriate. In a matter that is doubtful...
"Place" (*ṭhāne*) means in a cause that should be doubted. "Concentration of mind" (*cittasamādhi*):
this shows that if you, established in that concentration of the Dhamma, should attain the concentration of mind by way of the four paths together with insight.
"By my infallibility" (*apaṇṇakatāya mayhaṃ*): this practice leads to my own infallibility, that is, to being without fault.
Meaning: "A lucky throw" means a winning throw.

"This, headman, is concentration on the Dhamma; if you were to obtain concentration of mind therein"—here, "concentration on the Dhamma" refers to the phenomena of the ten courses of wholesome action, and "concentration of mind" refers to the four [foundations of mindfulness] together with insight.

The paths. Alternatively, the five factors consisting of gladness, rapture, tranquility, happiness, and concentration—as spoken of in the passage, "Gladness arises; for one who is glad, rapture arises"—are called concentration of states (*dhammasamādhi*).
Concentration of mind (*cittasamādhi*), however, consists only of the four paths together with insight.
Alternatively, the ten courses of wholesome action and the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) are called concentration of states; that—
The one-pointedness of mind that arises in one fulfilling concentration on the Dhamma is called "concentration of mind.

Thus, "you should abandon this state of doubt" means: if you, established in this aforementioned concentration on the Dhamma, should likewise obtain concentration of mind, you would certainly abandon this doubt.
The remainder is exactly as explained everywhere else.
The commentary on the Gāmaṇisaṃyutta is finished. 9.
The Asaṅkhata-saṃyutta (Connected Discourses on the Unconditioned).
1. First Chapter 1–11.
Commentary on the Discourses on Mindfulness Directed Toward the Body, etc., 366–376.
In the *Asaṅkhata-saṃyutta*, "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*) means unmade (*akata*). "Seeking welfare" (*hitesinā*) means by one seeking what is beneficial (*hita*). "Compassionate" (*anukampakena*)...
"Out of compassion. "Taking compassion as the basis" means having embraced compassion with one's mind; it is also said to mean "depending upon" it. "That has been done for you by me":
that has been done for you by me while teaching this unconditioned state and the path to the unconditioned.
For this alone is the duty of a compassionate Teacher: namely, the teaching of the Dhamma without error.
From this point on, however, what is called "practice" is the duty of the disciples. Therefore, by saying, "These, monks, are the roots of trees... [etc]...
this is our instruction," he indicates the lodging at the root of a tree. By saying "empty huts," he indicates a place secluded from people.
By both of these, he describes a lodging suitable for yoga and hands over his inheritance.

"Meditate" means: meditate upon the thirty-eight objects by way of object-contemplation (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*), and meditate upon the aggregates, bases, and so forth as impermanent and so on by way of characteristic-contemplation (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*);
what is meant is that you should increase both serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). "Do not be negligent" means:
do not be heedless. "Lest you be remorseful later" refers to those who, in former times during their youth...
At a time when they are free from illness, when the seven requisites are available,
and while the Teacher is present in person, those who lack wise attention pass their days and nights as gluttons, experiencing the pleasure of sleep and the pleasure of sloth,

and thus they are heedless. Later, at the time of old age, the time of illness, the time of death, the time of misfortune, and when the Teacher has passed away into Parinibbāna, they [realize] that former...
Recalling their own dwelling in negligence and perceiving the gravity of dying with a rebirth-linking consciousness still remaining, they become full of remorse.
Showing that you should not be like them, he said, "Do not be remorseful later.
"This is our instruction for you" means: this is our instruction and exhortation to you from us, saying, "Meditate; do not dwell in negligence. This is what is meant.
2. The Second Chapter:
1–33. Commentary on the Discourses on the Unconditioned, etc., §§377–409.
Regarding the passage beginning with “contemplating the body in the body,” that which is to be said will be explained further below.

In the passage beginning with "anataṃ," it is *anata* (unbending) because of the absence of the bending of craving (*taṇhānati*). It is *anāsava* (taintless) because of the absence of the four taints (*āsava*). It is *saccaṃ* (truth) because of its ultimate reality.

It is *pāraṃ* (the further shore) in the sense of being the opposite side of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). It is *nipuṇaṃ* (subtle) in the sense of being refined. It is *sududdasaṃ* (very difficult to see) because of its extreme difficulty to perceive.

It is *ajajjaraṃ* (undecaying) because it is not subject to aging. It is *dhuvam* (stable) in the sense of being firm. It is *apalokitaṃ* (illuminated) because of its non-perishing nature. [It is seen] by eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*).
It is "non-manifest" (anidassana) because it cannot be seen. It is "without proliferation" (nippapañca) due to the absence of the proliferations of craving, conceit, and views.

It is "peaceful" (santa) in the sense of being a state of peace. It is "deathless" (amata) because there is no death. It is "sublime" (paṇīta) in the sense of being supreme. It is "auspicious" (siva) in the sense of being glorious. It is "secure" (khema) because it is free from danger. It is "the destruction of craving" (taṇhakkhaya) because it is the condition for the destruction of craving.
It is "wonderful" (acchariya) in the sense of being astonishing—that is, worthy of being struck with wonder. It is "unborn" (ajāta), having never come to be.

It is "wonderful" (*abbhuta*) because it has been offered up as "it exists. It is "free from calamity" (*anītika*) because it is devoid of suffering. It is "a state free from calamity" (*anītikadhamma*) because its intrinsic nature is devoid of suffering.

It is "nibbāna" due to the absence of craving (*vāna*). It is "harmless" (*abyābajjha*) precisely due to the absence of malice (*byābajjha*). It is "dispassion" (*virāga*) because it is the condition for the attainment of dispassion.

It is "purity" (*suddhi*) because of its ultimate purity. It is "liberation" (*mutti*) because of its release from the three realms of existence. It is [so called] due to the absence of attachment to sensual pleasures (*kāmālaya*).

It is without a home (*anālaya*). It is an island (*dīpa*) in the sense of being a firm foundation. It is a cave (*leṇa*) in the sense of being fit for clinging to. It is a refuge (*tāṇa*) in the sense of protecting.

It is a shelter (*saraṇa*) in the sense of being a place of safety from fear; the meaning is that it is the destruction of fear. It is the supreme resort, goal, and foundation, thus it is the "supreme resort" (*parāyaṇa*).
The rest here is exactly according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the *Asaṅkhata-saṃyutta* is finished.
10. The *Abyākata-saṃyutta*. 1.
The commentary on the *Khemā-sutta*.
410. Regarding the first sutta of the *Abyākata-saṃyutta*: Khemā was a female lay follower of Bimbisāra who went forth out of faith during her time as a householder.

She was a great elder (mahātherī) whom the Blessed One placed at the head of the list for great wisdom, saying: “Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my female disciples, the bhikkhunīs, in great wisdom; that is, Khemā. She is called “wise” because she is endowed with wisdom.
"Viyatta" means endowed with proficiency (*veyyattiya*). "Medhāvinī" means endowed with intelligence (*medhā*) and wisdom (*paññā*).
"Bahussutā" means endowed with both the abundance of learning through study (*pariyatti-bāhusacca*) and the abundance of realization through penetration (*paṭivedha-bāhusacca*).

"Gaṇaka" means skilled in calculation by counting without omission (*acchiddaka-gaṇanā*). "Muddika" means skilled in calculation by finger-mudrā (*aṅgulimuddā*). "Saṅkhāyaka" means... [skilled in calculation by counting].
"Skilled in counting by handfuls": it is deep, being eighty-four thousand *yojanas* deep;
it is immeasurable, being immeasurable by the measure of an *āḷhaka*; it is difficult to fathom, being hard to grasp for the purpose of determining its measure by the count of *āḷhakas*.
"By which form the Tathāgata [is defined]": by which form one might designate the Tathāgata—who is reckoned as a 'being'—as long, short, dark, or fair.
"That form has been abandoned by the Tathāgata" means that such form as described above has been abandoned by the All-Knowing Tathāgata through the abandonment of its origination.

"Released from reckoning of form" means that because there is no further arising of form in the future, and because even the conventional designation "one will become such-and-such a person" in terms of the categories of form and non-form has subsided, he is released even from the conceptualization of form. "Profound" means...
It is profound because of the profundity of its underlying intention and the profundity of its qualities.

Regarding that Tathāgata, who is thus profound in his qualities, for one who perceives the non-existence of that designation—seeing that the designation "Tathāgata" as a "sentient being" occurs only in dependence on [certain conditions] and would not exist in the absence of those conditions—the thought arises:
"This Tathāgata, who was reckoned as a sentient being, exists after death."
The meaning is that this statement is neither applicable nor logical; even the statement beginning with "the Tathāgata does not exist after death" is neither applicable nor logical.
"It will coincide" means it will become one. "It will merge" means it will become continuous. "It will not contradict" means...
There will be no contradictory term. Regarding the phrase "in the supreme term" (*aggapadasmiṃ*): here, it is the teaching (*desanā*) that is intended by the term "supreme term.
2. Commentary on the Anurādha Sutta: 411.
The second [sutta] has already been explained in detail in the Khandhika-vagga; however, it is mentioned here because it pertains to the section on the undeclared (*abyākata*).
3–8. Commentary on the First Sāriputta-Koṭṭhika Sutta, etc., §§412–417.
In the third [sutta], “Whatever has come to be form” (*rūpagatam etam*) means this is merely form. It shows that herein no being whatsoever other than form is found;
rather, it is only when form exists that there is this mere name. This is also the case in the passages beginning with “Whatever has come to be feeling” (*vedanāgatam etam*), and so forth.

The same method applies here. "This, friends, is the cause" means that this—the ungraspable nature [of the Tathāgata] apart from form and the other aggregates—is the cause by which this was left undeclared by the Blessed One.
The fourth and subsequent points have their meanings already explained.
9. Commentary on the Kutūhalasālā Sutta (The Hall of Inquiry)
418. Regarding the ninth [simile], the "Hall of Curiosities": there is no such thing as a private hall called a "Hall of Curiosities.

Rather, it is that place where various recluses and brahmins of different sects engage in all kinds of discourse. Because it is a place where curiosity arises among many people, who wonder, "What does this one say?
What does that one say?", it is called the "Hall of Curiosities. It goes even far away means...
He goes to the Ābhassara Brahma-world. "And he lays down this body" means he lays it down by means of the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*).
"He is not reborn" means that at the very moment of death, because the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*) has not yet arisen, he is not reborn.
10. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta.
419. "Would this have been in conformity with their view": according to their tenet, "this would have been in conformity.

"Would it be in conformity for the arising of knowledge that all phenomena are non-self?"—the meaning is: regarding this insight-knowledge that arises as "all phenomena are non-self," would it have been in conformity for me?
Would it have led to the arising [of higher knowledge]? Such is the sense.
11. Commentary on the Sabhiya-Kaccāna Sutta 420. Regarding the eleventh [verse]:

"Friend, by this much alone"—that is to say, for one who might give an answer such as, "By this much time alone, when a cause exists, there is the designation 'possessing form' and so forth; when it does not exist, there is none," for him there is only this much.

"Much more so," he said. "As for 'how much more so' regarding that which has transcended"—that is to say, when the manner of teaching the Dhamma has transcended [the ordinary] and is exceedingly agreeable, what further talk can there be?
There is no more talk; the discussion is ended.
The commentary on the *Abyākata-saṃyutta* is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the Saḷāyatanavagga of the Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathā, the Sāratthappakāsinī.
